title: Collective Superconducting-Qubit Interfaces For Microwave-to-Optical Quantum Transduction
authors: Nicolas Dirnegger, Matthew Guibord, William Munizzi, Chee Wei Wong, Prineha Narang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23383v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Microwave-to-optical quantum transduction is essential for connecting superconducting quantum processors through optical networks. Mechanically mediated transducers, however, remain limited by weak electromechanical coupling, dissipation, and added noise. In this work, we study a transducer in which an ensemble of superconducting qubits couples collectively to a shared optomechanical resonator. For weak signals, we show that ensemble size and optical pump strength together set the conversion efficiency, added noise, and bandwidth, with pump heating limiting efficiency to a finite optimal pump strength. Near half excitation, the collective coupling grows nearly linearly with ensemble size, accelerating transfer of an excitation into the mechanics. We show that this speedup is offset by relaxation of the additional excited qubits, so the single-qubit coupling and lifetime still set the coherence requirement. Transferring exactly one excitation also requires an anharmonic mechanical mode, which an auxiliary qubit coupled to the mechanics can provide. In a lossless prescribed-Kerr benchmark with four qubits and [MATH], a mechanical anharmonicity of [MATH] raises the final joint single-photon intracavity target probability from [MATH] to [MATH]. Finally, we quantify the effects of decoherence, disorder, residual qubit--qubit interactions, and pump-induced qubit noise, finding that pair-dependent interactions reduce the optical retrieval efficiency from 58\% to 35\%. These results establish the coherence and selectivity requirements for collective quantum transduction.
tldr: A theoretical study of a microwave-to-optical quantum transducer in which an ensemble of superconducting qubits couples collectively to a shared optomechanical resonator, quantifying how ensemble size, pump strength, anharmonicity and decoherence set efficiency, noise and bandwidth.
motivation: Microwave-to-optical transduction is needed to link superconducting quantum processors over optical networks, but mechanically mediated transducers suffer from weak electromechanical coupling, dissipation and added noise; collective enhancement via qubit ensembles is a promising route to overcome these limits.
method: The authors model an ensemble of superconducting qubits collectively coupled to one optomechanical resonator, analyzing the weak-signal conversion efficiency, added noise and bandwidth as functions of ensemble size and optical pump strength, benchmarking single-excitation transfer with a prescribed-Kerr anharmonic mechanical mode supplied by an auxiliary qubit, and simulating decoherence, disorder, residual qubit-qubit interactions and pump-induced noise.
result: Pump heating limits efficiency to a finite optimal pump strength; near half excitation the collective coupling grows nearly linearly with ensemble size but the speedup is offset by relaxation of extra excited qubits, leaving single-qubit coupling and lifetime as the coherence requirement; mechanical anharmonicity substantially raises the final single-photon intracavity probability, while pair-dependent interactions reduce optical retrieval efficiency from 58% to 35%.
conclusion: The work establishes the coherence and mode-selectivity requirements for collective superconducting-qubit transduction and shows that while ensemble scaling aids speed, anharmonic mode engineering and disorder control are decisive for high-fidelity microwave-to-optical conversion.

title: Quantum Resources And The Onset Of The Quantum Monte Carlo Sign Problem
authors: Naga Dileep Varikuti, Leela Ganesh Chandra Lakkaraju, Philipp Hauke
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23514v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Monte Carlo sign problem poses a fundamental obstacle to classical simulation of quantum many-body systems, yet its connection to quantum resources remains poorly understood. We probe this connection by systematically tuning the degree of nonstoquasticity in random k-local Hamiltonians. In numerical tensor-network studies, we find the sign complexity and the quantum resources of entanglement and nonstabilizerness of the ground state to be strongly suppressed in a broad regime up to substantial nonstoquasticity. As nonstoquasticity is further increased, the considered quantum resources experience sharp crossovers into a regime where they are strongly enhanced. Surprisingly, numerical quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations drastically deteriorate in the same region, even though the Hamiltonian is already considerably nonstoquastic well before it, indicating that the failure of ground-state QMC is correlated more with the resource content of the state than the sign structure of the Hamiltonian. We corroborate these findings analytically by constructing an approximate ground state of k-local Hamiltonians in the stoquastic limit. Moreover, we identify a distinct behaviour in graph states. Their nonstabilizerness always vanishes, but, as we demonstrate analytically, on bipartite graphs the sign can be easily cured while in multipartite graph states it cannot. Our results thus shed light on the highly subtle interplay between quantum resources and the computational difficulty encountered by QMC methods.
tldr: The paper links the quantum Monte Carlo sign problem to ground-state quantum resources, showing that entanglement and nonstabilizerness crossovers correlate more strongly with QMC failure than Hamiltonian nonstoquasticity alone.
motivation: The sign problem is a fundamental obstacle to classical simulation of quantum many-body systems, but its relationship to quantum resources such as entanglement and magic remains poorly understood.
method: The authors tune nonstoquasticity in random k-local Hamiltonians and use numerical tensor-network studies to compute ground-state entanglement and nonstabilizerness, comparing these with QMC performance and analytic constructions in the stoquastic limit and graph states.
result: They find a broad regime where sign complexity and quantum resources are suppressed up to substantial nonstoquasticity, followed by sharp crossovers where resources are enhanced and QMC deteriorates; graph states show that nonstabilizerness can vanish while sign-curability depends on bipartiteness.
conclusion: The failure of ground-state QMC is correlated more with the resource content of the state than with the sign structure of the Hamiltonian, clarifying the subtle interplay between quantum resources and computational difficulty.

title: Experimental Constraints On Gauge Hidden-variable Models In Bell Tests
authors: Li-Yu Shen, Lukas Scarfe, Carrie Rodriguez, Alessio D'errico, Andrea Aiello, Ebrahim Karimi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23418v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum mechanics assigns identical statistics to measurement procedures that realize the same final effect, irrespective of the transformations used to reach it. We test this operational equivalence with polarization-entangled photons by implementing one of Bob's analyzer settings either directly or through closed wave-plate trajectories [MATH] calibrated to produce the same measurement operator. Motivated by ontological descriptions in which a hidden frame is transported between contexts, we formulate a local path-memory model and derive the mixed-context bound [MATH]. The quantity [MATH] is a coupling-dependent counterfactual mismatch probability: it bounds a contextual Bell expression, but neither generates nor predicts the quantum Bell correlation. We therefore test path memory through the observable difference between direct and looped implementations, using a no-signaling phenomenological response in which a hidden holonomy [MATH] modifies one correlation term in [MATH]. The direct reference violates the Bell inequality, while the looped mixed-context curves remain indistinguishable from it within the experimental precision. Our results support the quantum equivalence of calibrated measurement implementations and constrain path-sensitive hidden-variable extensions that predict an observable memory of the optical history.
tldr: An experimental Bell test with polarization-entangled photons constrains path-sensitive hidden-variable extensions by comparing direct and looped implementations of the same measurement operator.
motivation: Quantum mechanics predicts that measurement procedures realizing the same final effect have identical statistics, but hidden-variable models with path memory could in principle produce observable context-dependent deviations.
method: The authors implement one of Bob's analyzer settings either directly or through closed wave-plate trajectories calibrated to yield the same measurement operator, formulate a local path-memory model, and test a no-signaling phenomenological response with a hidden holonomy modifying one Bell correlation term.
result: The direct reference violates the Bell inequality, while the looped mixed-context curves remain indistinguishable from it within experimental precision.
conclusion: The results support the quantum equivalence of calibrated measurement implementations and constrain hidden-variable extensions that predict observable memory of the optical history in Bell tests.

title: Spectral Engineering Of Charge Localization And Work Reliability In Collective Quantum Batteries
authors: G. D. de Moraes Neto He-Guang Xu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23789v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The performance of a quantum battery depends not only on how much energy it stores, but also on how rapidly useful charge can be restored after work extraction. We show how engineering the reservoir spectrum connects these properties in an interacting collective-spin battery. Interactions separate the Dicke transition frequencies, allowing frequency-selective pumping and loss to control where excitation accumulates and how populations move along the ladder. Analytical results relate the pump-to-loss ratio to charge localization, fluctuations, and extractable work. Two reservoirs producing the same mean charge can nevertheless exhibit markedly different localization and charging times. Under repeated extraction, finite-time recharging also generates correlations between successive work outputs. At matched mean work, these correlations can reverse the ordering of single-cycle and long-time fluctuations: a protocol with larger fluctuations in individual strokes can deliver more reliable accumulated work. An exact counting relation connects these statistics to net charging-energy transfer, while relaxation modes distinguish recovery of the stationary state from recovery of useful work. Finally, local dephasing redistributes population among collective-spin sectors, leading to an exact stationary symmetry-dilution law and a finite operating window for work extraction under a collective transverse controller.
tldr: The paper shows how reservoir spectral engineering controls charge localization, charging time, and work-output reliability in an interacting collective-spin quantum battery.
motivation: Quantum battery performance depends not only on stored energy but also on how quickly useful charge can be restored and how reliably work can be extracted under repeated operation.
method: The authors analyze an interacting collective-spin battery coupled to engineered reservoirs, deriving analytical relations between pump-to-loss ratio, charge localization, fluctuations, and extractable work, and using an exact counting relation for work statistics.
result: Reservoirs with the same mean charge can produce different localization and charging times; finite-time recharging generates correlations between successive work outputs that can reverse the ordering of single-cycle versus long-time fluctuations, and local dephasing yields a symmetry-dilution law and a finite work-extraction window.
conclusion: Spectral engineering provides a route to control charge localization and work reliability in collective quantum batteries, with implications for designing more reliable repeated-operation protocols.

title: Scrambling Leads To Entanglement Cost In Nlqc
authors: Alex May Atsuya Hasegawa
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23378v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In a non-local quantum computation (NLQC), shared entanglement along with a single simultaneous round of quantum communication is used to implement a joint channel. NLQC has many applications, most of which benefit from an understanding of lower bounds on the entanglement needed to implement a given channel as an NLQC. However, the properties of a channel that lead to it having an entanglement cost in NLQC have remained unclear, with most lower bounds only applying to specially constructed examples. Here, we give a new lower bound technique for unitaries based on scrambling: we find that a unitary has zero entanglement cost if and only if it does not scramble. Further, we find that the tripartite mutual information, an entropic object that quantifies the degree of scrambling, provides a quantitative lower bound on entanglement cost in NLQC. This is the first known lower bound on entanglement cost for unitaries in NLQC which is faithful. Our results also relate scrambling and NLQC for the first time. Leveraging the faithful scrambling based bound, we then show that the controllable correlation, an earlier studied quantity, is also a faithful lower bound, resolving an earlier conjecture of Cleve and May.
tldr: The paper establishes a faithful, scrambling-based lower bound on the entanglement cost of implementing unitaries in non-local quantum computation (NLQC), showing zero entanglement cost if and only if the unitary does not scramble.
motivation: Most known lower bounds on the entanglement required for NLQC applied only to specially constructed channels, leaving unclear which channel properties actually force a nonzero entanglement cost.
method: The authors derive a new lower-bound technique for unitaries based on the degree of scrambling, quantified by the tripartite mutual information, and use it to also prove faithfulness of the controllable correlation.
result: A unitary has zero NLQC entanglement cost exactly when it does not scramble, and the tripartite mutual information yields the first faithful quantitative lower bound on entanglement cost for unitaries; the controllable correlation is also shown to be a faithful bound, resolving a conjecture of Cleve and May.
conclusion: Scrambling is identified as the operative channel property driving entanglement cost in NLQC, connecting scrambling theory with NLQC and providing generally applicable, faithful lower bounds.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the entanglement cost of implementing unitaries in non-local quantum computation (NLQC), a model where shared entanglement and a single round of simultaneous quantum communication simulate a joint channel. The authors establish a fundamental connection between the entanglement cost and the scrambling properties of the unitary. They prove that a unitary has zero entanglement cost if and only if it does not scramble, and that the tripartite mutual information—a measure of scrambling—provides a quantitative lower bound on the entanglement cost. title: Fault-tolerant Quantum Processor With Minimal External Control
authors: Christopher A. Pattison, Jeongwan Haah, John Preskill
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23919v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Contemporary classical information processors integrate tens of billions of transistors printed on a chip, yet are fully controlled through comparatively few external wires. This is possible because data flows through hard-coded operations in step with a global clock and is steered by external instructions. Today's solid-state quantum processors are different -- every qubit receives instructions from outside the chip via its own dedicated control line, and error correction adds a further torrent of syndrome data that is transported off-chip. Here we show that the external control of a quantum chip can be greatly simplified. We propose a fault-tolerant architecture for universal quantum computation, inspired by modern classical processors, in which quantum information flows through a fixed, clocked device, propelled by local gates in a planar array. Our quantum processor receives an input stream of classical instructions via a small, constant number of external wires, each attached to a single qubit. Except for those few qubits coupled to external wires, all qubits evolve under a periodically-applied geometrically-local depth-3 circuit, which is fixed at the time the device is fabricated. Assuming a noiseless global clock (so that every operation is applied on schedule, though imperfectly), we establish an accuracy threshold theorem: For physical noise below a universal threshold -- afflicting every gate, measurement, and wire -- a chip with [MATH] physical qubits can run any quantum algorithm that uses~[MATH] logical qubits, where [MATH] is the error rate per logical gate. Each logical gate takes time~[MATH]; an alternative design, in which quantum operations remain strictly local and noisy, but on-chip wires broadcast noiseless classical signals instantaneously, reduces the time per logical gate to [MATH].

conclusion: External control of a quantum chip can be drastically simplified without sacrificing fault tolerance, suggesting a hardware-efficient route toward scalable, classical-processor-like quantum architectures.

title: Symmetry Classification Of Hyperfine Rovibrational Molecular Phase Space
authors: Elin Ranjan Das, Jing-Chen Zhang, Victor V. Albert, Yuan Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23406v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Symmetry-based structures have advanced molecular spectroscopy and quantum information science, yet connections between these fields remain largely unexplored. We construct a phase space theory of a molecule by jointly treating rotational, vibrational, and nuclear-spin degrees of freedom as the quotient of orientations and normal coordinates by the molecule's point group. The various combinations of how these three degrees of freedom transform under symmetries organize a molecule's states into molecular species, and we show that each species is defined by a particular absolutely maximally entangled (AME) carrier state, or, for 45 species, by a two-dimensional space of them. Up to local unitaries and the order of the sectors, molecular species realize 21 AME states across 75 point groups: a product state, four maximally entangled pairs, and 16 genuinely tripartite states. A Fourier transform on the quotient relates orientation and angular-momentum descriptions while preserving these carrier states. We propose an example experimental protocol for preparing and driving symmetry-adapted bend states of [MATH].

title: Singlet Flags: Using Native Entanglement To Restore The Circuit Distance Of Shuttled qLDPC Codes In Silicon
authors: Jonathan Baugh William Chow
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23528v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes could greatly reduce the qubit count of silicon spin-qubit processors, but their checks are long-range and of high weight. Shuttling one ancilla electron through every data qubit of a check measures such checks, but a single fault on the ancilla spreads to several data qubits, so the circuit distance can fall far below the code distance. We make the mobile ancilla one half of a spin singlet whose partner stays at home; a Bell measurement at the end of the check provides a flag for isolated bit-flip faults acquired during the walk. Using new distance-6 codes with check weights 8, 10 and 12, and exact circuit distances from two independent solvers, we show that without the flag the circuit distance falls as check weight grows, to 1 at weight 12, while with it every weight-8 and weight-10 code recovers circuit distance 5 or 6 and corrects as many faults as the code. For codes of distance 8 to 12 the flag raises the circuit distance by one to four, and the Gross code [[144,12,12]] rises from 7 to 10. In circuit-level simulations of shuttled spin qubits, the flag lowers logical error rates by typically 2-10x across bivariate-bicycle, circulant-permutation and surface codes, and the gain survives percent-level flag-readout errors and bit flips on the singlet's electrons. BP+OSD does not reach the full circuit distance of the flagged circuits, so our flagged logical error rates are upper bounds: decoding the same shots exactly raises the flag's gain on the distance-6 codes from 3-7x to 5-17x for the weight-6 BB code, and from 1-12x to 5-90x at weights 8 and 10 for p >= 2.5x10^-4.
tldr: The authors introduce 'singlet flags' — making the shuttled ancilla half of a spin singlet — to detect ancilla faults during long-range check measurement and thereby restore the circuit-level distance of high-rate qLDPC codes implemented with mobile silicon spin qubits.

conclusion: Native entanglement used as a flag is a practical, low-overhead route to recover circuit-level distance for shuttled qLDPC codes in silicon spin-qubit architectures, with the reported gains being lower bounds since BP+OSD does not saturate the flagged circuit distance.

title: Instrument Indeterminacy: Separating Uncertainty In Povm Effects And Its Neutrosophic Reading
authors: Fernando A. Otero
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23566v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neutrosophic annotation frameworks for quantum measurement attach an external triple [MATH] to each Born probability, and explicitly leave open how indeterminacy could be defined operationally. We show that indeterminacy cannot be recovered from outcome probabilities, but can be computed from the pair (state, effect). For a binary POVM [MATH] we define the instrument indeterminacy [MATH], which vanishes exactly when the state only sees the sharp part of the effect. The normalized Gini index of the outcome splits as [MATH], a law of total variance that separates the instrument contribution from the state contribution; the identity is a special case of Massar's POVM uncertainty operator, and our contribution is its neutrosophic reading. Moving the system-apparatus cut to a Naimark dilation transfers exactly [MATH] from indeterminacy to variance, which yields the missing operational definition. We extend the decomposition to [MATH]-outcome POVMs, relate the minimum indeterminacy of two incompatible unbiased qubit observables to their commutator through Busch's joint-measurability criterion, and show that [MATH] equals twice the disagreement probability of a repeated L\"uders measurement. The resulting estimator needs neither the state nor the effect and, in simulation, requires 2.5 to 6 times fewer shots than detector tomography for the same error.
tldr: The paper introduces an operational notion of instrument indeterminacy for POVM measurements, separating uncertainty due to measurement effects from state-dependent variance and giving a neutrosophic interpretation.
motivation: Neutrosophic frameworks for quantum measurement assign indeterminacy triples to Born probabilities but leave the operational meaning of indeterminacy unclear. The work aims to define and quantify indeterminacy directly from the measurement instrument rather than from outcome probabilities alone.
method: For binary POVMs, the authors define instrument indeterminacy from the state-effect pair and derive a law-of-total-variance decomposition of a normalized Gini index. They connect this to Massar's POVM uncertainty operator, Naimark dilation, n-outcome POVMs, incompatible qubit observables via Busch's joint-measurability criterion, and repeated Lúders measurements.
result: The decomposition separates instrument and state contributions to outcome uncertainty, vanishes when the state only sees the sharp part of the effect, and yields an estimator that requires neither the state nor the effect and can need 2.5 to 6 times fewer shots than detector tomography for the same error.
conclusion: Instrument indeterminacy provides an operational and experimentally accessible way to quantify POVM-induced uncertainty, connecting measurement uncertainty, incompatibility, and neutrosophic readings of quantum indeterminacy.

The authors show that indeterminacy cannot be recovered from outcome probabilities alone but can be computed from the pair (state, effect). For a binary POVM {A, I-A}, they define the instrument indeterminacy as I_ρ(A) = 4 Tr(ρ(A - A^2)), which vanishes exactly when the state only sees the sharp part of the effect. They derive a decomposition of the normalized Gini index of the outcome splits as 4TF = I_ρ(A) + 4 Var_ρ(A), a law of total variance separating instrument and state contributions. This identity is a special case of Massar's POVM uncertainty operator, and the authors present its neutrosophic reading. They further show that moving the system-apparatus cut to a Naimark dilation transfers exactly I_ρ(A) from indeterminacy to variance, providing the missing operational definition. The decomposition is extended to m-outcome POVMs, and the minimum indeterminacy of two incompatible unbiased qubit observables is related to their commutator via Busch's joint-measurability criterion. Additionally, I_ρ(A) equals twice the disagreement probability of a repeated Lüders measurement, leading to an estimator that requires neither the state nor the effect and, in simulation, needs 2.5 to 6 times fewer shots than detector tomography for the same error.

An estimator for I_ρ(A) based on the disagreement probability of repeated Lüders measurements, which requires neither state nor effect and is 2.5–6 times more shot-efficient than detector tomography in simulation.

title: Hierarchical Coupling In Tripartite Van Der Waals Cavity Magnonics For A Low-loss And Tunable Coupled-mode Hamiltonian
authors: Taehee Kim, Sunghun Park, Byoung-Moo Ann, Sung Jin An, Seung-Bo Shim, Hakseong Kim, Haydar Sahin, Zhuo Bin Siu, Mansoor B. A. Jalil, Youngwook Kim, Thomas K. M. Graham, Brian B. Zhou, Myung-Joong Hwang, Yaroslav M. Blanter, Jungpil Seo, Hee Chul Park, Minkyung Jung
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23756v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: One of the greatest merits of cavity magnonics (CM) is the ability to explore rich coupled-mode physics, driven by the large flux tunability of magnonic resonances and magnon--photon coupling. Meanwhile, van der Waals (vdW) magnets offer an ultra-compact and highly integrated implementation of CM without complex fabrication processes. Nonetheless, the substantial magnon losses significantly hinder the combination of all these advantages. Here, we realize a hierarchical anti-crossing structure in a tripartite vdW CM with CrCl3 and realize an effective coupled-dual-mode Hamiltonian. We achieve an order-of-magnitude reduction in loss while maintaining a strong coupling condition. Additionally, we theoretically confirm the feasibility of simultaneous and tuning of both loss and coupling by varying the magnetic field direction and strength. Featuring a micrometer-scale thickness and a width of a few millimeters, our device is significantly smaller than those based on bulk crystals or crystal arrays. Our results establish vdW cavity magnonics as versatile platform for investigating intriguing phenomena predicted in coupled-mode systems.

motivation: Cavity magnonics enables rich coupled-mode physics and flux tunability, and van der Waals magnets offer compact integration, but magnon losses have hindered practical implementation.
method: The authors construct a tripartite vdW cavity magnonic device using CrCl3, observe a hierarchical anti-crossing structure, and derive an effective coupled-dual-mode Hamiltonian; they also theoretically analyze tuning of loss and coupling via magnetic field direction and strength.
result: They achieve an order-of-magnitude reduction in loss while maintaining strong coupling, and demonstrate a micrometer-scale device with millimeter width, significantly smaller than bulk-crystal-based systems.
conclusion: The results establish vdW cavity magnonics as a versatile platform for exploring coupled-mode phenomena and low-loss tunable hybrid quantum systems.

title: Subsystem Evolution In The History State Formalism
authors: A. Boette, F. Lomoc, N. Canosa, R. Rossignoli
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23784v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a relational framework for characterizing the evolution of quantum composite systems, based on the correlations within a history state describing the whole evolution relative to a quantum reference clock. While total system-clock entanglement entropy consistently measures the unitary evolution of the closed global system, a different picture emerges for the reduced state of an open subsystem, whose evolution is generally non-unitary due to environmental coupling. We introduce a general formalism that quantifies open-subsystem dynamics using a subsystem-clock mutual information derived from the history state. We demonstrate that this quantity serves as a consistent quantifier of subsystem evolution with respect to a given clock basis, can be applied to arbitrary dynamics, and reduces to system-time entanglement entropy in the global limit. Furthermore, maximizing this measure over all clock bases yields a basis-independent bound on the maximum evolution achievable relative to the clock, directly linked to the difference between the subsystem's entanglement with the rest of the history state and its entanglement with the environment. Finally, we derive analytical expressions for qubit clocks, illustrate our results using spin 1/2 and spin 1 quantum walks, and present a full matrix formalism of Kraus operators for describing the most general subsystem evolution.
tldr: The paper develops a relational history-state framework for quantifying the non-unitary evolution of an open quantum subsystem relative to a quantum reference clock.
motivation: Standard history-state approaches characterize global unitary evolution via system-clock entanglement, but open subsystems require a different information-theoretic description because their reduced dynamics are generally non-unitary.
method: The authors introduce subsystem-clock mutual information derived from the history state, show it reduces to system-time entanglement entropy in the global limit, maximize it over clock bases, and derive Kraus-operator matrix expressions for general subsystem evolution.
result: The proposed mutual-information measure consistently quantifies subsystem evolution for arbitrary dynamics, yields a basis-independent bound linked to subsystem entanglement with the environment, and is illustrated analytically for qubit clocks and spin-1/2 and spin-1 quantum walks.
conclusion: Subsystem-clock correlations in history states provide a general quantifier of open-subsystem evolution and a basis-independent bound on achievable evolution relative to a quantum clock.

title: Stationary Quantum Time Series: Spectral Theory Of Process Memory And Measurement Records
authors: Hai Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23809v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical time series analysis converts temporal dependence into structure that can be learned from a single observed trajectory, through stationarity, ergodicity, spectral representation, and finite-memory models. Quantum experiments are naturally time series: every run is a sequence of interventions and outcomes, and the memory of an open system is written in its temporal statistics. However, the classical foundation cannot be translated directly: measuring a process and forgetting the outcome differs from not measuring at all, so no single family of joint probability distributions describes a quantum process. We develop a process-tensor framework for stationary quantum time series and establish its first structural theorems. For stationary combs of finite quantum Markov order l relative to a fixed informationally complete causal break, we construct a finite-dimensional causal transfer map of dimension at most d^{4l}, where d bounds the system Hilbert-space dimension at each step. ... These results supply the stationary foundation on which quantum spectral analysis, model identification, and single-trajectory inference can be built.

motivation: Classical time-series tools rely on a single joint probability family, but quantum measurement records and forgetting outcomes break this foundation, so a genuinely quantum stationary theory is needed.
method: The authors formulate stationary quantum combs relative to an informationally complete causal break and construct finite-dimensional causal transfer maps, deriving bounds on their dimension.
result: For stationary combs of finite quantum Markov order l, they obtain a causal transfer map of dimension at most d^{4l}, where d bounds the local Hilbert-space dimension.
conclusion: These results provide a stationary foundation for quantum spectral analysis, model identification, and single-trajectory inference from quantum measurement records.

title: Chirp-stabilized Charging Of A Two-level Quantum Battery
authors: Yang-Yang Yuan, Xian-Li Yin, Jin-Feng Huang, Jie-Qiao Liao
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23712v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Resonantly driven two-level quantum batteries (QBs) suffer from strong pulse-area dependence and energy backflow inherent to Rabi oscillations. To address this limitation, we propose charging of a two-level QB with chirped pulses. We investigate four charging protocols formed by pairing hyperbolic secant (sech) or Gaussian pulse envelopes with linear or hyperbolic-tangent (tanh) frequency sweeps. We show that sufficiently strong chirp modulation converts the charging mechanism from pulse-area-governed Rabi rotation to adiabatic rapid passage. We analyze the underlying adiabatic dynamics and derive the criteria for robust chirped charging, which incorporate the sweep bandwidth, nonadiabatic transitions, and dissipative effects. Under strong chirp modulation, the final stored energy and ergotropy converge to stable plateaus that are nearly insensitive to the pulse area across an extended parameter window. Of the four schemes, the sech pulse with tanh chirp delivers the widest ergotropy plateau and the weakest pulse area sensitivity. Compared with counterdiabatic driving, the sech tanh protocol attains stable charging performance without demanding an extra drive quadrature. Furthermore, this chirp-enabled charging is resilient to static detuning and weak-to-moderate dissipation. This work establishes a practical route toward robust charging of quantum batteries using chirped pulse control.

result: Strong chirp converts charging from Rabi rotation to adiabatic rapid passage, producing stable plateaus in stored energy and ergotropy; the sech-tanh protocol gives the widest ergotropy plateau and is resilient to static detuning and weak-to-moderate dissipation.
conclusion: Chirped-pulse control offers a practical route to robust quantum battery charging without the extra drive quadrature required by counterdiabatic driving.

title: Parity Push Post-Selection With Soft Parity Constraints For Quantum Ldpc Codes
authors: Hong Jun Kim, Gun Sik Min, Seok-Hyung Lee, Jun Heo
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23759v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-selection lowers the logical error rate of a quantum error-correcting code by rejecting unreliable shots. For a code with [MATH] logical observables, the logical gap, a standard post-selection criterion, involves [MATH] logical classes, and existing approximations to it suffer from a non-convergence error floor or a shielding effect. We introduce a decoder-agnostic post-selection strategy for quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes, called parity push post-selection (PPPS), which re-decodes a shot once per logical observable with a push toward the opposite parity. Each push adds one check node and one variable node to the Tanner graph of the detector error model, and we accept a shot only when every re-decoding returns a solution in the original logical class. We show that, with degenerate maximum-likelihood decoding, PPPS accepts a shot exactly when the logical gap exceeds the push strength [MATH]. Applied with the Relay-BP decoder to the [[72,12,6]] bivariate bicycle code at [MATH] and the [[144,12,12]] code at [MATH] under circuit-level depolarizing noise, PPPS lowers the logical error rate by factors of about 50 and 75, respectively, at rejection rates near 1%. We observe that PPPS rejects failures that prior post-selection strategies cannot reject, and thus shows improved performance.

conclusion: PPPS provides an effective post-selection strategy that rejects failures missed by prior methods and improves qLDPC code performance under circuit-level depolarizing noise.

title: Spectral Disks For Quantum Markov Generators
authors: Dariusz Chru\'sci\'nski, Sergey Denisov, Wojciech Tarnowski, Karol \.zyczkowski
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23556v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spectral bounds for Markov generators require a choice of time scale. In quantum dynamics, a rate read off from a jump representation, the escape rate from a pure state and the smallest spectral disk need not agree. We prove that the spectrum of every GKLS generator written without a Hamiltonian lies in a disk tangent to the imaginary axis, with radius given by the norm of the operator [MATH] built from the jump map [MATH]. This settles the first two scaling conjectures of "Corralling spectra of generators of time-continuous Markov evolution (both classical and quantum)", J. Phys. A: Math. Theor. {59}, 175202 (2026). The third, escape-rate conjecture fails for a qutrit with a single normal jump. Nevertheless, twice the escape rate bounds every decay rate of any positive trace-preserving semigroup For GKLS generators with vanishing canonical Hamiltonian, four times the escape rate always supplies a spectral disk, and the factor four is optimal uniformly in dimension. We compare these bounds with classical Cassini ovals and thermodynamic ellipses, explain the obstacles to their quantum extensions, and formulate optimization over completely positive jump-map representations as a semidefinite program.
tldr: The paper proves sharp spectral-disk bounds for GKLS generators with vanishing Hamiltonian, settling two scaling conjectures and disproving the escape-rate conjecture while giving escape-rate-based decay bounds.

method: The authors analyze GKLS generators without Hamiltonian, bound the spectrum using the norm of an operator built from the jump map, construct a qutrit counterexample with a single normal jump, and formulate optimization over completely positive jump-map representations as a semidefinite program.
result: They show the spectrum lies in a disk tangent to the imaginary axis with radius given by the jump-map operator norm; the first two scaling conjectures are settled, the third fails for a qutrit, twice the escape rate bounds all decay rates, and four times the escape rate gives an optimal dimension-independent spectral disk.
conclusion: The work provides rigorous and optimal spectral bounds for quantum Markov generators, clarifies obstacles to extending classical Cassini-oval and thermodynamic-ellipse bounds, and offers an SDP approach to optimizing jump representations.

abstract: ArXiv:2611.23861v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When a common bias reverses two bistable fields, the system can pass through either of two single-reversal configurations on its way to the favored state. We show that interference between these two orders of reversal can block the final step. In a dimer of coupled quantum Rabi cavities, the four field configurations form a loop, and a complex photon-hopping amplitude threads it with an Aharonov-Bohm flux. Near half a flux quantum, the two paths to complete reversal interfere destructively: in microscopic simulations, a slow uniform sweep reverses one field with probability 0.998, although the final bias favors reversing both. A four-state model calibrated at zero bias predicts how the window of this Aharonov-Bohm blockade narrows with sweep time. The blocked state remains coherent. A differential pulse followed by a return sweep converts the relative phase of the two single-reversal configurations into a fringe in the joint field signs, with contrast 0.95. In a trimer, a phase gradient imprinted between sweeps determines whether the next sweep adds or removes a reversed field: reversing the second of two gradients changes the most probable outcome from three reversed fields to one.

motivation: Coupled bistable quantum systems can reverse through multiple paths, and understanding whether interference can suppress the final reversal step is important for controlling such platforms.
method: The authors model a dimer of coupled quantum Rabi cavities whose four field configurations form a loop threaded by a complex photon-hopping phase, and they supplement microscopic simulations with a calibrated four-state model.
result: Near half a flux quantum, the two reversal paths interfere destructively, yielding a 0.998 probability of reversing only one field in a slow sweep; pulse sequences convert relative phase into high-contrast fringes, and trimer phase gradients control whether subsequent sweeps add or remove reversed fields.
conclusion: Aharonov-Bohm blockade provides a coherent mechanism for controlling multistable field reversal in coupled cavity systems, with potential applications in phase-sensitive quantum control of hybrid platforms.

title: General Noise Channels And Mid-Circuit Measurements For Pre-Trajectory Sampling With Batched Execution
authors: Louis Follet, Paavai Pari, Isidor Schoch, Thien Nguyen, Justin G. Lietz, Daniel Lowell, Brucek Khailany, Krysta M. Svore, Dirk R. Englund, Taylor L. Patti
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23923v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many studies of quantum protocols require fast sampling of large amounts of measurement data from noisy quantum circuits, such as for training machine-learning decoders for quantum error correction. Exact simulation of realistic noise is expensive, while stabilizer-based simulators are fast but approximate, for example through Pauli twirling, which generally alters the output statistics. Pre-trajectory sampling with batched execution (PTSBE) accelerates exact trajectory simulation by sampling noise before state evolution. This method requires the outcome probability of every stochastic event to be independent of the state, which excludes mid-circuit measurements and general Kraus channels. We present a generalization of PTSBE to measurement and Kraus operators without approximation. Each event is partially pre-sampled, while deferred outcomes are drawn during grouped execution via multinomial branching and cached-state reuse. We implement the method for GPUs as an extension of CUDA-Q. On distance-3 topological code memories under amplitude damping, it is up to 24x faster than conventional trajectory sampling in CUDA-Q. On 30-qubit random circuits with mid-circuit measurements, it is up to 83x faster and outperforms the near-Clifford simulator Clifft when more than about 25% of the gates are non-Clifford. With repeated sampling of each final state, its sampling rate per trajectory exceeds that of CUDA-Q by nearly five orders of magnitude. Our method also allows us to compare exact amplitude damping with its Pauli-twirled channel on a surface-code memory, revealing that twirling overestimates the detection rate by 21% and raises the logical error rate of a lookup decoder by 8%. This work makes exact, high-throughput simulation practical for general noisy circuits, from data generation for training decoders to studying measurement-based fault-tolerant protocols under realistic noise.

motivation: Exact noisy-circuit simulation is expensive, while stabilizer/Pauli-twirling methods are approximate and can distort statistics, which is problematic for generating data to train quantum error-correction decoders and study fault-tolerant protocols.
method: The authors extend PTSBE by partially pre-sampling stochastic events and deferring state-dependent outcomes to grouped execution using multinomial branching and cached-state reuse, implemented as a CUDA-Q GPU extension.
result: The method achieves up to 24x speedup on distance-3 topological code memories under amplitude damping, up to 83x speedup on 30-qubit random circuits with mid-circuit measurements, and reveals that Pauli twirling overestimates detection rates by 21% and raises lookup-decoder logical error rates by 8%.
conclusion: This makes exact high-throughput trajectory simulation practical for general noisy circuits, supporting decoder training and measurement-based fault-tolerant protocol studies.

title: Fe$^{2+}$:forsterite Qubit System
authors: G. M. Wysin Dishaanth S. Pillai
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23550v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum Computing uses quantum mechanical phenomena, such as superposition and entanglement of quantum bits (qubits), to represent and manipulate information in multidimensional state spaces. This approach allows complex mathematical functions to be executed simultaneously rather than sequentially, making them much more efficient than classical computers. However, current quantum computers suffer from quantum decoherence, where small changes to their environment, such as thermal fluctuations and vibrations, affect the systems' fragile states. The goal of this study is to discuss the functionality of a proposed Fe[MATH]:forsterite qubit system by solving the unitary time-evolution of a quantum state vector for the system's Hamiltonian, using known axial and traverse anisotropy terms at temperatures up to 10 K. The system can effectively transfer population between its two lowest states at rates predicted by the Rabi half-period, with 99.9% fidelity. Additionally, it can hold the population at a desired state without docohering. The results remained consistent for temperatures up to 10 K, meaning, unlike many common qubit systems, the proposed qubit system could function without a dilution fridge and is not fragile to thermal noise.
tldr: The paper proposes and theoretically simulates a Fe2+:forsterite spin qubit that can achieve high-fidelity population transfer and coherence at temperatures up to 10 K.
motivation: Solid-state qubit platforms that operate without dilution refrigeration could reduce complexity and improve scalability for quantum computing.
method: The authors solve the unitary time evolution of a quantum state vector for a Fe2+:forsterite Hamiltonian using known axial and transverse anisotropy terms at temperatures up to 10 K.
result: The system transfers population between its two lowest states with 99.9% fidelity at Rabi half-period rates and maintains population without decohering up to 10 K.
conclusion: Fe2+:forsterite is proposed as a promising thermally robust qubit platform that may not require dilution refrigeration, though experimental validation remains needed.

title: Uniformly Convergent Perturbation Theory For Open Quantum Systems At, Near, And Away From Exceptional Points
authors: Pedro Linck
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23604v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Near a Liouvillian exceptional point, spectral perturbation theory becomes ill-conditioned, yet the observable dynamics of a finite-dimensional open system remains regular in the perturbation. Using a Dyson expansion, which requires no diagonalization of the perturbed generator, we analyze the scaling, stability, and convergence of the perturbative corrections at, near and away from exceptional points. We derive scaling laws showing that nonperipheral Jordan blocks raise the degree of the polynomial-in-time factors multiplying decaying exponentials, which are present for any generator as resonances, and we quantify this excess. We further establish a uniform-in-time error estimate for the perturbative series, valid for any relaxing finite-dimensional Lindbladian and controlled by a parameter [MATH], where [MATH] is the perturbation strength and [MATH] is a constant built from unperturbed data. All constants of the bound remain continuous through an exceptional point when the coalescing eigenvalues are kept in one spectral cluster. The estimate extends to the frequency domain via the Laplace transform, and to time-dependent perturbations. We test it in a driven two-level system with a Liouvillian exceptional point, including perturbations that break its symmetry.
tldr: The paper develops a uniformly convergent Dyson-expansion perturbation theory for finite-dimensional open quantum systems governed by Lindbladians, including regimes at, near, and away from exceptional points.
motivation: Spectral perturbation theory near Liouvillian exceptional points is ill-conditioned, even though the observable dynamics remains regular, so a diagonalization-free perturbative framework is needed.
method: The author uses a Dyson expansion that avoids diagonalizing the perturbed generator, derives scaling laws for nonperipheral Jordan blocks, and establishes uniform-in-time error estimates controlled by the perturbation strength and constants from unperturbed data.
result: The analysis yields scaling laws showing how nonperipheral Jordan blocks increase polynomial-in-time prefactors, a uniform-in-time error bound that remains continuous through an exceptional point when coalescing eigenvalues are grouped in one spectral cluster, and extensions to the Laplace domain and time-dependent perturbations.
conclusion: The framework provides a stable and convergent perturbative treatment of Lindbladian dynamics across exceptional points, demonstrated on a driven two-level system with a Liouvillian exceptional point.

title: Covering The Pauli Observables: Sampling Thresholds And The Design Effect Of A Measurement Setting
authors: Kausthubh Chandramouli, Noah Siekierski, Bojko N. Bakalov, Dror Baron
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23827v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum state tomography and shadow-based estimation rely on measuring Pauli observables. An experiment does not measure them one at a time: it chooses a measurement setting that assigns one of the bases X, Y or Z to each qubit, and a single run in that setting yields estimates of every Pauli observable compatible with it. We say that the setting covers those observables. We determine how many random settings cover a prescribed fraction of all Pauli observables. As the number of settings grows exponentially with the number of qubits, the covered fraction has a sharp threshold at a growth rate of [MATH] per qubit, set by the rate-distortion function of covering at zero distortion. We give an explicit expression for the number of settings needed to reach a target fraction, accurate up to a remainder that reduces to a small oscillation for many qubits, and show that random sampling is asymptotically optimal up to a factor of less than 1.69. Coverage does not determine what a setting contributes to an estimator. Observables covered by one setting are estimated from the same outcomes, so their estimates are correlated. We quantify this correlation through the design effect of a setting, which equals the squared Pauli expectation that the setting captures and depends on the target state. We derive its mean over settings in closed form for every state and show that it can be estimated without bias from the measurement data. title: Finite-time Stochastic Resetting In Bounded Domains: Competing Targets, Energetic Cost, And Optimal Search Strategies
authors: Hanshuang Chen, Chongyao Tang, Guofeng Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23790v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the first-passage dynamics and energetic cost of a Brownian particle subject to finite-time stochastic resetting in a bounded one-dimensional domain with two absorbing boundaries. Unlike conventional instantaneous resetting, the particle is returned to a prescribed resetting position through a finite-duration process driven by a linear trapping potential. By solving the corresponding backward equations, we derive analytical expressions for the mean global first-passage time and the splitting probabilities. Our results show that the finite duration of the return process can substantially modify the dependence of the mean global first-passage time on the resetting rate. In particular, we identify a critical trapping strength above which resetting can accelerate the search process, and characterize how the range of favorable resetting positions depends on the trapping strength. We further characterize the energetic cost of resetting by deriving the generating function of the total work and obtaining an analytical expression for its mean value. For the linear trapping potential considered here, we establish an exact relation between the mean total work and the mean cumulative return time. This relation allows us to establish a quantitative trade-off between the mean global first-passage time and the energetic expenditure, revealing how the finite duration of the return process affects search efficiency. Brownian dynamics simulations confirm our theoretical predictions.
tldr: The paper analyzes finite-time stochastic resetting for a Brownian particle searching a bounded domain, deriving first-passage statistics and the energetic cost of resetting.
motivation: Conventional resetting models assume instantaneous returns, but finite-duration resetting via a trapping potential can substantially alter search efficiency and thermodynamic expenditure.
method: The authors solve backward equations for the mean global first-passage time and splitting probabilities, and derive the work generating function and mean total work for a linear trapping-potential reset protocol, confirming results with Brownian dynamics simulations.
result: They identify a critical trapping strength above which resetting accelerates the search, characterize favorable resetting positions, and establish an exact relation between mean total work and mean cumulative return time that yields a first-passage-time versus energetic-cost trade-off.
conclusion: Finite-duration return processes qualitatively modify stochastic-resetting search behavior and impose a quantitative energetic trade-off, informing optimal search strategies in bounded domains.

title: QCCDCert: Formally Verified Compilation For Qccd Co-Design
authors: John Zhuoyang Ye, Jens Palsberg, Ke Sun, Hartmut Haeffner
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23469v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) architectures enable scalable trapped-ion quantum computing by dynamically shuttling ions between specialized processing and storage zones. A QCCD can be built with many trap sizes and layouts. Comparing them requires compiling every program under each design's transport, capacity and control constraints, and trusting the target code of each compilation. We present a co-design framework built on one Lean-verified compiler. The hardware description and its operating rules are compiler inputs, so a single theorem covers every candidate design: the target code of every compilation preserves its program's behavior and obeys the hardware rules. Across 75 benchmark programs of 11 to 130 qubits, the best design found takes 66% less modeled execution time on average than the worst design of equal capacity. An AI agent that proposes devices based on our compiler's checked results beats the fastest of these designs on 71 of 75 programs. Our verified compiler provably avoids the 11 defects that we report in three previous compilers. It scales to hundreds of qubits, compiling 512-qubit programs for a 38-trap device in 1 to 29 minutes.
tldr: A Lean-verified compiler framework for quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) trapped-ion architectures that enables sound co-design comparison of trap layouts and programs.
motivation: QCCD designs vary widely in trap size and layout, but comparing them requires compiling every program under each design's transport, capacity, and control constraints while trusting each compiled target code.
method: The hardware description and operating rules are made compiler inputs, so a single machine-checked theorem guarantees that any compilation preserves program behavior and obeys hardware rules; the framework is benchmarked on 75 programs of 11-130 qubits and coupled to an AI design-proposal agent.
result: Across benchmarks, the best design uses 66% less modeled execution time on average than the worst design of equal capacity, the AI agent beats the fastest baseline design on 71 of 75 programs, the compiler provably avoids 11 defects found in three prior compilers, and it compiles 512-qubit programs for a 38-trap device in 1-29 minutes.
conclusion: Formally verified compilation provides a trustworthy substrate for QCCD co-design at scale, though the work is primarily a compiler/verification engineering contribution rather than a quantum-information or thermodynamic result.

title: Quantum Monge-Kantorovich Optimal Transport In Spacetime Through Spatiotemporal Kirkwood-Dirac Distributions And Spatiotemporal States
authors: Zhian Jia
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23462v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Monge-Kantorovich optimal transport is a mathematical framework that determines the most efficient way to transform one probability distribution into another while minimizing a given cost function. Its central constructions include the Wasserstein distances, which quantify the space of probability distributions, and dual formulations that link to convex analysis. Its standard quantum generalization replaces probability distributions with density operators and cost function with positive semidefinite cost operator, which should be regarded as spatial quantum optimal transport. In this work, we propose the quantum optimal transport problem in spacetime through the spatiotemporal phase-space Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobability distribution and spatiotemporal states and through spatiotemporal state. We show that the two formalisms are equivalent and related via spatiotemporal operator frames. In the Kirkwood-Dirac phase-space formalism, the spatiotemporal distribution and the cost function are complex-valued, and the spatiotemporal couplings are Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobability distributions that yield the correct marginals for the local states. In the spatiotemporal state formalism, the cost operators are generally non-Hermitian, and the spatiotemporal couplings are generally non-Hermitian and yield the correct reduced local states. The Margenau-Hill phase-space distribution gives rise to a real-valued optimal transport in spatiotemporal phase space; in the spatiotemporal state formalism, this corresponds to a Hermitian spatiotemporal coupling state. We give a rigorous definitions and a careful discussion of its duality. We also introduce a spatiotemporal quantum Wasserstein metric based on a metric in spatiotemporal phase spaces and show that it satisfies the metric axioms.
tldr: The paper extends quantum Monge-Kantorovich optimal transport to spacetime using spatiotemporal Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobability distributions and spatiotemporal states.
motivation: Standard quantum optimal transport generalizes classical transport by replacing probability distributions with density operators, but it is primarily spatial; this work aims to formulate transport in spacetime to capture temporal correlations.
method: The authors define spacetime quantum optimal transport via complex-valued Kirkwood-Dirac phase-space distributions and via non-Hermitian spatiotemporal states, showing equivalence through operator frames, and analyze duality and a quantum Wasserstein metric.
result: The two formalisms are shown to be equivalent; the Margenau-Hill distribution yields a real-valued phase-space transport corresponding to Hermitian couplings, and the proposed spatiotemporal Wasserstein metric satisfies the metric axioms.
conclusion: This provides a rigorous mathematical framework for spacetime quantum optimal transport and quasiprobability-based transport, though its direct connection to mainstream quantum information tasks is not established.

title: Compute Before You Digitize: ADC-less Mixed-Signal Processing For Scalable Cryogenic Qubit Readout
authors: Qirui Zhang, Ben Toby, He Wang, Benjamin Lienhard, David Blaauw, Dennis Sylvester
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23448v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce DIRAC, an ADC-less in-cryostat qubit readout architecture that uses analog computing to redraw the analog-digital boundary. Directly operating on the front-end's analog output, passive complex mixers perform the equivalent of digital demodulation, ping-pong active-RC integrators average their outputs into down-sampled per-qubit traces, and a time-domain stage digitizes them, eliminating Nyquist-rate ADCs. A TX-RX co-design derives the mixers' local oscillators from the readout transmitter's baseband rather than per-tone PLLs. A per-line calibration flow trains the matched filter jointly with the neural network, improving fidelity and enabling low-bit-width, low-voltage digital processing. Designed in 22 nm FD-SOI and evaluated at 4 K on 1.12M experimental shots, DIRAC matches the fidelity of a floating-point (FP32) digital pipeline for readout windows down to 750 ns, at 31.6[MATH] and 238[MATH] lower energy than the fixed-point (FxP) and FP32 pipelines. It cuts the total 4 K power per physical qubit by 50.4% and 68.6% relative to FxP and room-temperature flex cables, respectively. At a fixed logical-qubit count and 4 K budget, this yields, against FxP, a code distance larger by 2 to 6 and a 1.6-7.3[MATH] (Willow) and 4.9-204[MATH] (SI1000, [MATH]) lower logical error rate.
tldr: DIRAC is an ADC-less cryogenic mixed-signal readout architecture that uses analog computing to demodulate and integrate qubit signals before digitization, reducing 4 K power and improving logical error rates.
motivation: Scalable superconducting qubit readout is limited by the power and wiring overhead of Nyquist-rate ADCs and room-temperature electronics, motivating in-cryostat analog processing to move the analog-digital boundary.
method: The architecture uses passive complex mixers for analog demodulation, ping-pong active-RC integrators for down-sampled traces, and a time-domain digitization stage, with TX-RX co-design and joint matched-filter/neural-network calibration; it is implemented in 22 nm FD-SOI and evaluated at 4 K on 1.12M shots.
result: DIRAC matches FP32 digital readout fidelity for windows down to 750 ns while using 31.6x and 238x less energy than fixed-point and FP32 pipelines, respectively, cutting 4 K power per qubit by 50.4-68.6% and enabling larger code distances and lower logical error rates.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that analog mixed-signal processing can substantially reduce cryogenic readout power and improve scalable superconducting-qubit system performance, though it is primarily an electronics/architecture contribution rather than a quantum-information or thermodynamic result.

title: Qubit-qumode Simulation Of Molecular Torsion In Photoisomerization
authors: Dimitrios Athanasakos, Florian Hechenberger, Tommaso Rainaldi, Felix Ringer, George Siopsis
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23408v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photochemical reactions driven by large nuclear motion, such as the photoisomerization of retinal, depend strongly on both the global anharmonic forces of the potential and the periodic topology of molecular torsion. In this work, we develop a hybrid discrete (qubit) and continuous variable (qumode) quantum simulation framework for photochemical reactions that maps electronic states to qubits, vibrations to qumodes, and the periodic torsion to a compact qumode encoding. Applying this approach to the two-mode Hahn-Stock and three-mode PSB3 models of retinal photoisomerization, we compare i) local vibronic approximations, ii) the full trigonometric potential on the noncompact line, and iii) the same potential on the compact circle, which matches the molecular torsion topology. We numerically show that the topological description can significantly alter relevant observables. We realize the compact torsion via both a wrapped Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) encoding and a two-qumode circle encoding and introduce two methods that reduce the hardware resources of both encodings. Spreading an encoded coordinate over several qumodes lowers the average occupation number of each mode, and adding counterterms to the Hamiltonian reduces the required squeezing amount. We expect that these methods make percent-level simulations of the considered molecules promising targets for hybrid qubit-qumode hardware. For more complex molecules, each additional nuclear coordinate is represented directly as a single qumode or an encoded register using the same native operations, so the framework extends naturally to larger systems.
tldr: The paper proposes a hybrid qubit-qumode quantum simulation framework for molecular photoisomerization, using GKP and circle encodings to represent periodic torsion and reduce hardware resources.
motivation: Photochemical reactions such as retinal photoisomerization depend on anharmonic potentials and periodic molecular torsion, which are challenging to simulate; hybrid discrete-continuous-variable quantum hardware may capture these features efficiently.
method: The authors map electronic states to qubits and vibrations to qumodes, encode periodic torsion compactly via wrapped GKP or two-qumode circle encodings, and compare local vibronic approximations, noncompact trigonometric potentials, and compact-circle potentials for the Hahn-Stock and PSB3 retinal models.
result: They show that the topological compact description can significantly alter observables, and introduce two resource-reduction methods: spreading an encoded coordinate over several qumodes to lower average occupation and adding counterterms to reduce required squeezing.
conclusion: The framework makes percent-level simulations of the considered molecules promising for hybrid qubit-qumode hardware and extends naturally to larger molecules by representing each additional nuclear coordinate as a qumode or encoded register.

title: From Powers--Stormer To Loewner Inertia: Weighted Trace Functionals And Orthogonal Perturbations
authors: Trung Hoa Dinh, Cong Trinh Le, Minh Toan Ho
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23814v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the weighted trace functional [MATH], where [MATH]. The Jordan decomposition of [MATH] yields exact common-roof decompositions for operator monotone and operator convex functions, including the Powers--St\o rmer and Ricard trace comparisons. The orthogonal cross term gives a finite rank-one realization of the classical conditional L\"owner-matrix criterion for operator convexity. For powers, resolvent squares yield a coupling-dependent Mellin strip, endpoint identities, and quantitative bounds on off-sector spectral interactions. Linearization produces positive and inverse moment subspaces of power L\"owner matrices. A confluent determinant calculation provides the remaining sign data in the known inertia classification. We give explicit equality conditions and a finite-copy application of the Powers--St\o rmer equality case.

method: The authors use Jordan decompositions of weighted trace functionals, orthogonal cross terms, resolvent squares, Mellin strip analysis, linearization, and confluent determinant computations.

title: Optimal Joint Bounds For Sparse Ground-State Energy Estimation And Ground-State Preparation
authors: Dhrumil Patel
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23387v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ground-state energy estimation (GSEE) and ground-state preparation (GSP) are fundamental problems in quantum computing. Given a Hamiltonian [MATH] with [MATH] and a guiding state [MATH] with overlap at least [MATH] with the ground space of [MATH], the goal in GSEE is to estimate the ground-state energy of [MATH] to additive error [MATH] with failure probability at most [MATH], while in GSP it is to prepare a state with ground-space weight at least [MATH], given a gap lower bound [MATH]. Their costs are measured by quantum query complexity, i.e., the number of oracle calls needed to access [MATH]. Recent work proved optimal bounds [MATH] for GSEE and [MATH] for GSP in the time-evolution and block-encoding models. However, these models do not directly account for the sparsity of [MATH], measured by the maximum number [MATH] of nonzero entries in any row or column. In the sparse-access model, oracles instead return the locations and values of these entries. This introduces the additional parameter [MATH], and it remained open how query complexity depends jointly on [MATH], [MATH], [MATH] or [MATH], and [MATH]. We resolve this by proving sparse-query lower bounds [MATH] for GSEE and [MATH] for GSP, even for stoquastic Hamiltonians. We also show that these constructions recover the earlier time-evolution and block-encoding lower-bound scalings. We then give matching upper-bound algorithms in the reversible in-place sparse-location model. Thus, we obtain [MATH] for GSEE and [MATH] for GSP, showing that [MATH] is necessary and sufficient and completing the joint dependence on all problem parameters.
tldr: The paper proves optimal joint quantum query bounds for sparse ground-state energy estimation and ground-state preparation, completing the dependence on sparsity, precision, and related parameters.
motivation: Ground-state energy estimation and preparation are fundamental quantum computing problems, but prior optimal bounds did not directly account for Hamiltonian sparsity in the sparse-access model.
method: The author proves sparse-query lower bounds for both GSEE and GSP, including for stoquastic Hamiltonians, and gives matching upper-bound algorithms in the reversible in-place sparse-location model.
result: The paper establishes necessary and sufficient joint query complexity scalings for sparse GSEE and GSP, recovering earlier time-evolution and block-encoding lower bounds as special cases.
conclusion: The results complete the joint parameter dependence for sparse ground-state estimation and preparation, but the contribution is a quantum algorithms/query-complexity result rather than one aligned with the listed core research interests.

title: Perspectives On The Hidden Subgroup Problem Over Unitriangular Groups
authors: Damien Poquillon
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23590v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the quantum Hidden Subgroup Problem (HSP) over the upper unitriangular group [MATH]. While efficient quantum algorithms were discovered for some families of non abelian groups and nil-2 [MATH]-groups, no efficient algorithms are known for groups of nilpotency class higher than 2. The only techniques known for such groups scale exponentially in the size of the input. We first study the group [MATH], the smallest upper unitriangular group exhibiting nilpotency class three. We analyze the application of the Pretty Good Measurement approach used for Heisenberg groups and show its limits. We then focus on the more general case [MATH] to adapt existing techniques to this particular structure. In particular, we derive an algorithm for cyclic subgroups as a subroutine for a general algorithm, although it is not efficient in the size of the group. Our results highlight the difficulties introduced by the increasing nilpotency class and suggests some directions for an efficient quantum algorithm for the HSP over [MATH].
tldr: An analysis of the quantum Hidden Subgroup Problem over upper unitriangular groups of nilpotency class three, showing why existing techniques fail and giving an inefficient cyclic-subgroup subroutine.
motivation: Efficient quantum algorithms for the HSP are known for abelian, certain non-abelian, and nil-2 groups, but nothing efficient exists for nilpotency class above two; the paper probes the smallest such case to understand the obstruction.
method: The paper studies the group of upper unitriangular matrices of small size, applies the Pretty Good Measurement approach previously used for Heisenberg groups to expose its limitations, and then generalizes to larger unitriangular groups by adapting existing techniques to the cyclic-subgroup case.
result: PGM is shown to be insufficient at nilpotency class three, and a cyclic-subgroup algorithm is derived as a subroutine for a general algorithm, though it scales exponentially in the input size.
conclusion: Increasing nilpotency class introduces genuine difficulty for HSP algorithms, and the authors suggest directions that might lead to an efficient quantum algorithm for this family.

title: Separating Qma From The Qcma Hierarchy Via A Switching Lemma For Polynomials
authors: Yiming Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23693v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct a classical oracle relative to which QMA is not contained in the QCMA hierarchy. Our main technical contribution is a switching lemma for bounded polynomials, which provides a new conceptual viewpoint on earlier sampler-based arguments separating QMA and QCMA. Crucially, the parameters of this switching lemma are independent of the number of input variables. The separation builds on the code intersection subset size problem of Bostanci, Huang, and Vaikuntanathan (FOCS 2026). We also construct a classical oracle relative to which QCMA collapses to P but QMA does not, and another relative to which QMA collapses to P but PP does not.
tldr: The paper constructs a classical oracle separating QMA from the QCMA hierarchy using a new switching lemma for bounded polynomials whose parameters are independent of the number of variables.
motivation: Separating QMA from QCMA (and its hierarchy) remains a central open problem in quantum complexity theory; oracle separations provide evidence and conceptual insight into the structure of quantum proof systems.
method: The authors prove a switching lemma for bounded polynomials that yields a new viewpoint on earlier sampler-based separation arguments, and build on the code intersection subset size problem of Bostanci, Huang, and Vaikuntanathan to construct classical oracles.
result: Relative to a classical oracle, QMA is not contained in the QCMA hierarchy; further oracles are given where QCMA collapses to P but QMA does not, and where QMA collapses to P but PP does not.
conclusion: The work sharpens the landscape of quantum complexity classes via a parameter-efficient switching lemma, though it lies outside the researcher's information-theoretic, thermodynamic, networking, and hybrid-platform focus areas.

title: Imaging Chiral Snake States In A Qubit Array With Programmable Gauge Fields
authors: Hanyi Wang, Lijun Sun, Bihao Guo, Weizhi Tao, Jian Ding, Shengbin Wang, Xinfang Zhang, Wei-Yong Zhang, Hantao Sun
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23888v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spatially varying magnetic fields steer charged particles along directed paths. Where a field reverses sign, particles follow snake-like orbits along the reversal line, in a direction set by both the field orientation and the sign of their energy. Transport measurements have detected such snake states, but imaging their dynamics in a reprogrammable field landscape remains challenging. Here we digitally simulate the Harper--Hofstadter model with programmable synthetic magnetic fields on a 49-qubit superconducting processor. In each Trotter step, every hopping term is one native fractional-iSWAP gate, and single-qubit [MATH] rotations set all 36 plaquette fluxes independently, without additional entangling gates. Uniform, random, and stepped flux landscapes reveal Aharonov--Bohm suppression of diagonal propagation, disorder-induced slowing, and magnetic reflection. At a field reversal, bonding and antibonding initial states, which carry opposite energy biases, propagate in opposite directions, and both directions reverse when the field is inverted. A symmetry analysis of these reversals yields a chiral displacement of nearly one lattice spacing after ten Trotter rounds, with symmetry-breaking residuals below 0.05 lattice spacings. Bond-resolved flux programming with site-resolved imaging thus provides a quantitative tool for synthetic gauge fields and a route to time-dependent gauge fields and interacting particles.
tldr: A 49-qubit superconducting processor digitally simulates the Harper-Hofstadter model with programmable synthetic magnetic fields to image chiral snake states at field-reversal lines.
motivation: Snake states arising where a magnetic field reverses sign have only been inferred from transport measurements; a reprogrammable synthetic-field platform would allow direct, site-resolved imaging of their dynamics.
method: Each Trotter step implements every hopping term as a single native fractional-iSWAP gate, while single-qubit Z rotations independently set all 36 plaquette fluxes without extra entangling gates; uniform, random, and stepped flux landscapes are programmed and bond-resolved readout is used.
result: The experiment observes Aharonov-Bohm suppression of diagonal propagation, disorder-induced slowing, magnetic reflection, and opposite-directional propagation of bonding/antibonding states at a field reversal, with chiral displacement of nearly one lattice spacing after ten Trotter rounds and symmetry-breaking residuals below 0.05 lattice spacings.
conclusion: Bond-resolved flux programming with site-resolved imaging offers a quantitative tool for synthetic gauge fields and a route toward time-dependent gauge fields and interacting lattice models.

title: Sub-Doppler Cooling Of Potassium-41 In A Hybrid Quadrupole-Octupole Symmetry Magneto-Optical Trap
authors: Khoa Nguyen, Benjamin Foulks, Jonathan Wrubel
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23466v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sub-Doppler cooling processes rely on the near-degeneracy of the Zeeman sub-levels of the atom. Effective sub-Doppler cooling is only achieved when the ac-Stark shift of the molasses light is significantly larger than the Zeeman shift. This condition is typically achieved by switching off all magnetic gradients, and using Helmholtz coils to cancel Earth's magnetic field. Another way to achieve a nearly zero magnetic field gradient is to superimpose a second pair of oppositely oriented quadrupole coils with a different spatial geometry. At the ideal current ratio, this creates an octupole-symmetry magnetic field for the atoms. The resulting octupole magnetic field has a gradient increasing quadratically from zero at the center. In this work, the effectiveness of sub-Doppler cooling and trapping using D2 and D1 light is evaluated in such a hybrid trap for [MATH]K. The temperature, lifetime, and phase-space density of the atoms are measured. For both D2 and D1 light, the octupole MOT is found to have a longer lifetime, while maintaining a similar temperature to the zero-field case. D1 gray-molasses temperatures down to [MATH]K and phase-space density up to [MATH] are measured for [MATH] [MATH] atoms. The effectiveness of the hybrid quadrupole-octupole trap suggests the possibility of increasing the loading time for atoms into an optical dipole trap with active sub-Doppler cooling.
tldr: The paper evaluates sub-Doppler cooling and trapping of 41K atoms in a hybrid quadrupole-octupole magneto-optical trap that produces a near-zero-field region without switching off magnetic gradients.
motivation: Sub-Doppler cooling requires a near-degenerate Zeeman structure, normally obtained by extinguishing all magnetic gradients and nulling Earth's field; the authors seek a simpler geometry that maintains low temperatures while prolonging trap lifetime and improving phase-space density.
