This operator-theoretic setting gives a continuum analogue of the spectral/SVD-based framework used for finite networks: the eigenfunctions provide the reduction basis, and the decay of the corresponding singular values quantifies the effect of discarded modes. For finite-rank graphons, we prove exact reduction results for two classes of graphon dynamical systems. We also show that, for finite-rank graphons, the reduced system preserves equilibria, linear stability, and local bifurcations. For infinite-rank graphons, we derive error bounds for the spectral reduction. Numerical examples using finite-rank and infinite-rank graphons illustrate the exact and approximate regimes of the theory.
tldr: The paper develops a graphon-based spectral dimension reduction framework for dynamical systems on dense graph limits.
motivation: Spectral dimension reduction works well for large finite networks when the interaction matrix has low-rank structure, and the authors seek a continuum analogue for graphon dynamical systems.
method: The reduction is formulated using the compact self-adjoint integral operator associated with the graphon, with eigenfunctions as reduction basis and singular-value decay quantifying discarded modes.
result: For finite-rank graphons the authors prove exact reduction and preservation of equilibria, linear stability, and local bifurcations; for infinite-rank graphons they derive error bounds, illustrated numerically.
conclusion: The work provides an operator-theoretic continuum extension of spectral reduction for network dynamics, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Kernel Design In Particle Mesh Ewald Methods: Splitting, Interpolation, And Upsampling
authors: Shidong Jiang, Jiuyang Liang, Libin Lu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23737v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For more than thirty years, particle mesh Ewald (PME) methods have dominated the computation of electrostatic interactions in molecular dynamics. A PME method uses a splitting kernel to divide the interaction into a local part, summed within a cutoff, and a smooth part, computed on a grid with a spreading and interpolation (SI) kernel. The established methods use Ewald's Gaussian split with B-spline SI kernels, and the recent Ewald summation with prolates accelerates them severalfold by using a prolate spheroidal wave function (PSWF) for both kernels. Neither choice meets two needs of molecular dynamics: a smooth energy, which long simulations need in order to conserve it, and a low-order SI kernel that stays accurate on coarse grids and gains accuracy as the grid is refined. We present a framework for designing both kernels to meet these needs. For inverse powers from the Coulomb to the dispersion interaction, our splits make the local part smooth at the cutoff to any order while keeping the Fourier concentration of the smooth part close to optimal. We show that with analytic differentiation, the force error of a continuous SI kernel of fixed shape vanishes under grid refinement only if every particle, wherever it lies, gives the grid its exact charge and dipole moment. Our SI kernel for the Coulomb interaction ensures this by construction and is twice continuously differentiable. Compared with the B-spline of the same order, it needs fewer grid points by a factor of up to nearly five; on coarse grids, it mostly needs a lower order than the PSWF kernel. In simulations of liquid water over 100 million time steps, the new kernels reduce the energy drift of both the established and the PSWF kernels by about three orders of magnitude, with a smaller force error than either. Existing PME codes can adopt them by replacing only the two kernels and the Fourier multiplier.
tldr: The paper introduces a framework for designing splitting and spreading-interpolation kernels in particle mesh Ewald methods, achieving smoother energies, lower force error, and dramatically reduced energy drift in molecular dynamics simulations.
motivation: Established PME kernels (Ewald Gaussian splits with B-splines, or PSWF-based schemes) fail to simultaneously provide smooth energies needed for long-time energy conservation and low-order SI kernels that remain accurate on coarse grids while converging under refinement.
method: The authors design splitting kernels for inverse-power interactions (Coulomb through dispersion) that are smooth at the cutoff to arbitrary order while keeping near-optimal Fourier concentration, and derive an analytic-differentiation condition requiring exact charge and dipole assignment for vanishing force error, yielding a twice continuously differentiable SI kernel.
result: The new SI kernel requires up to nearly five times fewer grid points than a B-spline of the same order, often needs lower order than the PSWF kernel on coarse grids, and in 100-million-step liquid water simulations reduces energy drift by about three orders of magnitude with smaller force error.
conclusion: The proposed kernels offer a drop-in improvement for existing PME codes, requiring only replacement of the two kernels and the Fourier multiplier to obtain markedly better long-time energy conservation in molecular dynamics.

title: Optical Neural Networks Should Be Evaluated By Function, Not Only Physics
authors: Shi-Yuan Ma, Xingjian Bai, Ryan Hamerly, Mahmoud Jalali Mehrabad
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23610v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical neural networks (ONNs) are attracting significant attention as alternative platforms for machine learning (ML). In an ONN, an optical module often takes over part of the computation inside a digital ML pipeline. How much of the task does the optical module itself perform, and how much does it contribute to any claimed system-level advantages, such as throughput or energy? This paper offers a simple, function-oriented evaluation methodology. Whatever its internal physics, the optical module appears to the surrounding digital pipeline as a mapping between real-valued tensors. We therefore evaluate it in three steps: (i) define its boundary in the pipeline, as real-valued tensors in and out; (ii) replace it with standard digital modules to identify those that match the optical system's performance on the same task and metric; and (iii) state system-level claims, such as speed or energy, per inference against the performance-matched digital module. We summarize steps (i) and (ii) in an Expressivity Card and demonstrate its use on published ONN systems. This helps isolate the optical module's contribution and provides a concrete digital reference for assessing its claimed system-level advantages, without the need to understand the physics. While we focus on optical systems as the most prominent example, the same approach applies to any physical analog computing platform used in ML, wherever a physical module takes over part of a digital pipeline.
tldr: The paper proposes a function-oriented benchmarking methodology, summarized in an 'Expressivity Card', for evaluating optical neural networks against performance-matched digital modules inside hybrid digital-ML pipelines.
motivation: Optical neural networks are increasingly claimed to offer throughput or energy advantages, but there is no systematic way to isolate how much of the task the optical module actually performs and how much of the system-level benefit it truly delivers.
method: The optical module is treated as a black-box mapping between real-valued tensors: its boundary in the pipeline is defined, it is replaced by standard digital modules that match its task performance, and system-level claims (speed, energy per inference) are then stated relative to that performance-matched digital reference.
result: The authors formalize steps (i) and (ii) as an Expressivity Card and demonstrate its application to several published ONN systems, showing how the optical contribution can be separated from the surrounding digital pipeline.
conclusion: Evaluating analog/optical computing platforms by function rather than internal physics gives a fair, physics-agnostic benchmark; the approach generalizes to any physical analog module embedded in a machine-learning pipeline.

title: Retinal Arterial Velocity-proxy Waveforms From Differential Spectral Broadening In Laser Doppler Holography
authors: Zacharie Auray, Yann Fischer, Olivier Martinache, Michael Atlan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23599v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Laser Doppler holography (LDH) records pulsatile spectral broadening in retinal arteries. We compare vessel and local-background measurements to extract a signed differential-broadening waveform, [MATH]. A minimal Gaussian convolution model motivates quadratic subtraction, and Doppler scaling relates the added width to a characteristic blood velocity. Real arteries show pulsatile waveforms, whereas identically processed imaginary arteries show only low-amplitude fluctuations around zero. We interpret the empirically scaled signal as a velocity proxy for waveform shape and within-vessel changes during a single acquisition under stable conditions.
tldr: The paper extracts retinal arterial velocity-proxy waveforms from differential spectral broadening in laser Doppler holography.
motivation: Laser Doppler holography can record pulsatile spectral broadening in retinal arteries, but isolating a signed velocity-related waveform from vessel and background measurements requires a differential approach.
method: The authors compare vessel and local-background measurements and use a minimal Gaussian convolution model to motivate quadratic subtraction of spectral widths, with Doppler scaling relating added broadening to a characteristic blood velocity.
result: Real arteries show pulsatile waveforms, while identically processed imaginary arteries show only low-amplitude fluctuations around zero, supporting the interpretation of the scaled signal as a velocity proxy.
conclusion: The empirically scaled differential-broadening signal provides a velocity-proxy waveform for characterizing within-vessel pulsatile changes during a single stable acquisition.

title: Localized Active Phase In The Coevolving Voter Model With Fixed Links
authors: Hoseung Jang, Maxi San Miguel, Byungjoon Min
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23870v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The coevolving voter model (CVM) describes the evolution of node states and network topology through copying and rewiring dynamics. It traditionally assumes that all ties can be rewired, overlooking unbreakable real-world relationships like family or close friendships. To address this, we introduce fixed links that cannot be rewired and study how these structural constraints modify the collective dynamics of the CVM. In addition to the active and frozen phases of the CVM, we find a new localized active phase in which activity is sustained, beyond a percolation transition, by a giant component of fixed links. The existence of this new phase is predicted by a moment-closure approximation that goes beyond the standard pair approximation. The finite-size manifestation of this phase is an asymmetric fragmented phase. In addition, the active-frozen transition of the CVM, manifested as a fragmentation transition for finite systems, is delayed by the existence of fixed links to larger values of the rewiring rate.
tldr: The paper studies a coevolving voter model with unrewirable fixed links and identifies a new localized active phase sustained by a giant component of fixed links.
motivation: The standard coevolving voter model assumes all ties can be rewired, which overlooks real-world unbreakable relationships such as family or close friendships. The authors aim to understand how such structural constraints alter collective dynamics.
method: They introduce fixed links into the coevolving voter model and analyze the resulting phases using a moment-closure approximation beyond the standard pair approximation, supported by finite-size analysis.
result: Beyond the usual active and frozen phases, they find a localized active phase in which activity persists beyond a percolation transition due to a giant component of fixed links; finite systems show an asymmetric fragmented phase, and the active-frozen transition is delayed to larger rewiring rates.
conclusion: Fixed links qualitatively modify the phase behavior of the coevolving voter model, producing a new localized active phase and shifting the fragmentation transition, with implications for models of social and network dynamics under unbreakable ties.

title: Strong Structural Stability Of Scalar-Plus-Compact Operators On Banach Spaces
authors: Xinxing Wu, Mengjuan Wang, Xu Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23290v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that every strongly structurally stable operator of the form \(\lambda I+K\) on a real or complex Banach space, where \(\lambda\) is a scalar and \(K\) is compact, is hyperbolic. Applying this result to the real Banach space constructed by Argyros and Haydon and its complexification, both of which are infinite-dimensional separable Banach spaces with the scalar-plus-compact property, we show that neither space supports a nonhyperbolic and strongly structurally stable operator, thereby giving a negative answer to the part of the open problem of Bernardes and Messaoudi concerning strong structural stability.
tldr: The paper proves that any strongly structurally stable operator of the form λI+K (scalar plus compact) on a Banach space must be hyperbolic, and uses this to resolve part of an open problem of Bernardes and Messaoudi on the Argyros–Haydon space.
motivation: Strong structural stability of operators is a notion from linear dynamics and operator theory, and its relation to hyperbolicity for the scalar-plus-compact class on the Argyros–Haydon hereditarily indecomposable Banach space was left open.
method: Pure functional-analytic arguments establishing hyperbolicity of strongly structurally stable operators of the form λI+K, then specializing to the Argyros–Haydon space and its complexification.
result: Neither the Argyros–Haydon space nor its complexification supports a nonhyperbolic strongly structurally stable operator, giving a negative answer to the corresponding part of the open problem.
conclusion: The results settle a piece of the Bernardes–Messaoudi problem and clarify the interplay between strong structural stability and hyperbolicity in scalar-plus-compact operator theory.

title: Condorcet's Nontransitive Dice: A Minimal Realization Of A Complete Ranking Profile
authors: S\'andor Boz\'oki, L\'aszl\'o Csat\'o, J\'ozsef Temesi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct three independent finite-support random variables whose six strict ordering probabilities reproduce the complete ranking-frequency profile in a classical example of Condorcet's paradox. The construction has total support size seven, and we prove that no realization of this profile has smaller total support size. Here dice are allowed to be weighted: different outcomes need not have equal probabilities. We then formulate the realization problem for an arbitrary vector of six ordering probabilities. We distinguish constraints on the pairwise comparison probabilities from constraints on the full ranking distribution and give an example showing that pairwise feasibility is not sufficient. For the fixed interlaced supports [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH], we derive the polynomial realization system. On the branch where the smallest outcome of the second variable has probability zero, we give a compact polynomial characterization for profiles with their first two ordering probabilities positive. This yields an explicit semialgebraic sufficient condition for the general realization problem and a rational construction, both with elementary proofs.
tldr: The paper constructs a minimal realization of Condorcet's nontransitive dice profile using three weighted random variables with total support size seven and studies the general realization problem for ranking probabilities.
motivation: Condorcet's nontransitive dice provide a classical example of cyclic pairwise preferences, and the authors aim to characterize when such ranking-frequency profiles can be realized by independent random variables.
method: The authors prove a minimal total support-size bound for the six strict ordering probabilities of Condorcet's example and derive polynomial and semialgebraic conditions for the realization problem on fixed interlaced supports.
result: They obtain a support-size-seven construction that is proven minimal, distinguish pairwise feasibility from full ranking-distribution feasibility, and give explicit semialgebraic sufficient conditions plus a rational construction.
conclusion: The work solves a combinatorial probability realization problem related to Condorcet's paradox but has no direct connection to quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Sharp Error Estimates For Lagrange Interpolation And Kantorovich-type Operators In Weighted $L_p$-spaces
authors: L. Angeloni, D. Costarelli, Yu. Kolomoitsev
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23326v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we establish sharp direct and inverse approximation estimates for algebraic Lagrange interpolation polynomials and Kantorovich-type operators in weighted [MATH] spaces on [MATH]. A well-known limitation in the theory of approximation by interpolation polynomials states that for small rates of convergence [MATH], classical moduli of smoothness fail to provide matching direct and inverse estimates due to the insufficiency of integral metrics to determine pointwise values at the interpolation nodes. To overcome this difficulty, we introduce new special semi-discrete measures of smoothness based on Steklov averaging operators, which combine global [MATH]-smoothness with discrete deviations from Steklov averages at the interpolation nodes. By using these measures, we establish fully matching direct and inverse approximation theorems for Lagrange interpolation polynomials, thereby providing complete two-sided characterizations of the rate of convergence for an arbitrary rate [MATH]. As a natural application of the developed approach, we also obtain corresponding direct and inverse estimates, as well as strong converse inequalities, for Kantorovich-type operators constructed via Lagrange polynomials.
tldr: The paper derives sharp direct and inverse approximation estimates for algebraic Lagrange interpolation polynomials and Kantorovich-type operators in weighted Lp spaces on an interval, using new Steklov-average-based semi-discrete moduli of smoothness.
motivation: Classical integral moduli of smoothness cannot yield matching direct and inverse theorems for interpolation at small convergence rates, because integral metrics do not control pointwise values at interpolation nodes.
method: The authors introduce special semi-discrete measures of smoothness built on Steklov averaging operators, which combine global Lp-smoothness with discrete deviations from Steklov averages at the nodes, and use them to prove matching two-sided estimates.
result: Fully matching direct and inverse approximation theorems are obtained for Lagrange interpolation at arbitrary rates, plus corresponding estimates and strong converse inequalities for Kantorovich-type operators constructed from Lagrange polynomials.
conclusion: The new semi-discrete smoothness functionals give a complete two-sided characterization of convergence rates, resolving a long-standing limitation of classical moduli in weighted Lp settings.

title: Theta-Eta Mellin Transforms, Shifted Reflections, And Rigorous Approximation Theory For A Variant Theta Construction
authors: Darrell Cox Sourangshu Ghosh
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23356v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a rigorous analytic framework for investigating a proposed functional equation associated with a variant theta construction. We prove the classical Mellin identity connecting the Jacobi kernel [MATH] to the completed Dirichlet eta function, and extend its Mellin transform meromorphically to the whole plane with a single simple pole at the origin. Mellin uniqueness identifies [MATH] as the unique kernel in a natural weighted [MATH] class whose Mellin transform is the shifted completed eta function. We distinguish this Gaussian kernel from the weighted exponential series [MATH], whose Mellin transform is [MATH] and obeys a different, explicitly derived reflection relation. We show that every affine reflection [MATH] can be generated for a shifted completed eta or zeta function by choosing the shift appropriately; consequently, the occurrence of [MATH] alone cannot identify the original variant with a shifted eta function. The corrected analytic product defined here is an elementary meromorphic multiplier of the completed zeta function and therefore has a precise [MATH] functional equation. We prove an explicit eta-tail bound, a sharper alternating-tail asymptotic, a uniformly convergent Euler-transformed eta series with a geometric error bound, a uniform zeta-approximation bound away from the line [MATH], and a combined truncation estimate when both the zeta and weighted-exponential factors are truncated. We also determine the principal Laurent data and the cancellation of the gamma poles at the trivial zeta zeros for the corrected product. Reproducible high-precision experiments verify the stated error scales. The exact identification of the original variant with a shifted completed eta function remains open.
tldr: The paper develops rigorous Mellin-transform and approximation-theory results for a variant theta construction related to the completed Dirichlet eta and zeta functions.
motivation: It aims to investigate a proposed functional equation for a theta-type kernel and clarify whether the original variant can be identified with a shifted completed eta function.
method: The authors prove Mellin identities, meromorphic extensions, uniqueness results, reflection relations, tail bounds, Euler-transformed series, and truncation estimates, supported by high-precision numerical experiments.
result: They establish rigorous analytic approximation bounds and show that affine reflections for shifted completed eta or zeta functions can arise from choosing the shift appropriately, so the appearance of a specific reflection alone is insufficient for identification.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous analytic framework and error estimates, but the exact identification of the original variant with a shifted completed eta function remains open.

title: Beyond Area: Perimeter Optimization In The Planar Skorokhod Embedding Problem
authors: Maher Boudabra
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23461v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The planar Skorokhod embedding problem asks for a simply connected planar domain whose Brownian exit distribution has a prescribed real marginal [MATH]. We investigate the minimization of conformal perimeter over the class of all such embeddings. We first establish the main existence theorem showing that whenever a finite-perimeter embedding exists, the infimum is attained (and vice versa). We derive necessary conditions for finiteness and sufficient conditions based on logarithmic integrability of the density. In particular, we demonstrate that finite area does not guarantee the existence of an embedding with finite perimeter. Although Gross's canonical embedding minimizes area, we construct an explicit family of domains for which Brownian symmetrization strictly increases perimeter, disproving its universal perimeter minimality. On the positive side, using Pruss's containment theorem and inequalities from convex geometry, we establish a general lower bound in terms of the convex hull of the Gross domain. Consequently, whenever the Gross embedding is bounded and convex, it is the unique perimeter minimizer. Finally, we formulate an open problem concerning the relationship between the existence of finite-perimeter embeddings and the regularity of Gross's canonical embedding.
tldr: The paper studies minimization of conformal perimeter over planar Skorokhod embeddings, i.e. simply connected domains whose Brownian exit distribution has a prescribed marginal.
motivation: Gross's canonical embedding minimizes area, but whether it also minimizes perimeter was open; the authors ask whether area minimality implies perimeter minimality for Brownian exit-distribution embeddings.
method: They prove an existence theorem for finite-perimeter embeddings, derive necessary and sufficient conditions via logarithmic integrability of the density, construct explicit counterexample families, and use Pruss's containment theorem plus convex-geometry inequalities to bound perimeter below by the convex hull of the Gross domain.
result: Finite area does not guarantee a finite-perimeter embedding; Brownian symmetrization can strictly increase perimeter, disproving universal perimeter minimality of Gross's embedding, while bounded convex Gross domains are shown to be the unique perimeter minimizer.
conclusion: Perimeter and area optimization for Skorokhod embeddings are genuinely distinct problems, and the regularity of Gross's canonical embedding is left as an open problem connecting finite-perimeter existence to it.

title: An Explicit Domain-preserving Projection Scheme For Scalar Stochastic Differential Equations
authors: Xingwei Hu, Yaozhong Hu, Aiguo Xiao
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23522v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop an explicit domain-preserving projection scheme for scalar stochastic differential equations whose solutions evolve in a prescribed interval. A Lamperti-type transformation converts the original equation into one with additive noise, whose drift may be singular near finite boundaries or grow polynomially at infinity. The proposed domain-preserving projected Euler-Maruyama (DPPEM) scheme combines an explicit Euler-Maruyama step with projection onto a step-size-dependent interior interval. Under one-sided Lipschitz, boundary, and weighted growth assumptions, with projection parameters chosen according to the coefficient growth and available moment orders, we establish strong order one convergence for admissible moment orders. The analysis combines local consistency and stability estimates with moment and boundary negative moment bounds for the exact solution. Numerical moment bounds follow from the convergence estimate, while numerical negative moment bounds are obtained under additional conditions. Estimates for the inverse Lamperti map yield strong order one convergence for the original equations in the CIR, Heston 3/2, CEV, Ait-Sahalia, and bounded interest-rate models under the stated model conditions. Numerical experiments illustrate the predicted convergence rates and compare computational costs with the Lamperti backward Euler-Maruyama scheme.
tldr: The paper introduces a domain-preserving projected Euler-Maruyama scheme for scalar stochastic differential equations constrained to an interval, proving strong order-one convergence under one-sided Lipschitz and growth conditions.
motivation: Numerical solutions of SDEs with state-dependent boundaries (e.g., interest-rate models) can leave the admissible domain or blow up near singular boundaries, so a scheme that provably stays inside the domain with high convergence order is needed.
method: A Lamperti-type transformation converts the equation to additive noise with possibly singular drift; an explicit Euler-Maruyama step is combined with projection onto a step-size-dependent interior interval, analyzed via local consistency, stability, and moment/negative-moment bounds.
result: Strong order one convergence is established for admissible moment orders, and inverse-Lamperti estimates extend the guarantee to CIR, Heston 3/2, CEV, Ait-Sahlia, and bounded interest-rate models, confirmed numerically and compared to a Lamperti backward Euler-Maruyama scheme.
conclusion: The DPPEM scheme provides a practical, explicit, domain-preserving integrator with provable strong order-one accuracy for a broad class of scalar SDE models.

title: Federated Differential Privacy With Batch Contamination
authors: Jason K. C. Ng, Thomas B. Berrett, Yi Yu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23551v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study mean estimation under federated differential privacy (FDP) constraints and batch contamination, considering both Gaussian and heavy-tailed distributions. In the homogeneous setting, where sample sizes and privacy budgets are constant across servers, we show that the costs of privacy and contamination disentangle. Under a bounded [MATH]th moment condition, with [MATH], the cost of batch contamination is of order [MATH], where [MATH] is the contamination level and [MATH] is the per-batch sample size. This reveals a phase transition at [MATH], for [MATH], which is the first of its kind in the literature. We develop a two-stage procedure that achieves the minimax rate up to poly-logarithmic factors. A key component is a private smoothed voting procedure tailored to the FDP setting that provides optimal sensitivity control. For heterogeneous batch sample sizes and privacy budgets, we introduce a batch partitioning framework that groups batches with comparable per-batch sample sizes and privacy budgets. Surprisingly, the minimax rate is determined, up to poly-logarithmic factors, by the most informative group of batches. Consequently, in some regimes, it is minimax optimal to use only an arbitrarily small proportion of the data set. Heterogeneity also introduces interactions between the costs of privacy and contamination, in contrast to their disentanglement in the homogeneous setting. For unknown contamination level, we propose an adaptive, near-minimax optimal Lepski-type extension for the heterogeneous Gaussian setting, designed specifically to prevent privacy leakage by ensuring no repeated use of data points.
tldr: The paper studies mean estimation under federated differential privacy and batch contamination, deriving minimax rates and adaptive procedures for homogeneous and heterogeneous settings.
motivation: Federated differential privacy with contaminated batches is a practical statistical setting, but the costs of privacy and contamination and the effects of heterogeneity are not fully understood.
method: The authors analyze minimax estimation under bounded moment assumptions, develop a two-stage private smoothed voting procedure, and introduce batch partitioning and Lepski-type adaptation for heterogeneous settings.
result: They show privacy and contamination costs disentangle in the homogeneous case with a phase transition at a contamination threshold, while heterogeneity can make it optimal to use only a small proportion of data and introduces interactions between privacy and contamination.
conclusion: The work provides near-minimax optimal procedures and new theoretical insights for federated differentially private estimation under batch contamination, but it is a classical privacy/statistics paper with no quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems content.

title: Drift-Aware Adaptive Semantic Codec Update Strategy For Dynamic Semantic Communications
authors: Bizhu Wang, Manqi Li, Shujun Han, Mengying Sun, Xiaodong Xu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23722v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Semantic communication reduces transmission overhead by conveying task-relevant semantic features, but its performance depends on the consistency between training and target-domain data distributions. In dynamic environments, distribution drift can make offline-trained semantic codec models stale and degrade transmission performance. Frequent updates alleviate this degradation but increase communication, computation, and queueing costs, whereas infrequent updates delay model adaptation. To address this tradeoff, we propose a drift-aware adaptive update strategy for dynamic semantic communication systems. Drift intensity is quantified in the semantic feature space, and Drift-Aware Age of Model (DA-AoM) is introduced to jointly capture drift-induced performance degradation, drift-dependent update service delay, and conventional update latency. Closed-form average DA-AoM expressions are derived for edge-layer M/M/1 and cloud-layer D/M/1 update scenarios, based on which the update frequency is optimized under the queueing-stability constraint. Simulations show that DA-AoM captures the joint effects of drift intensity, computing rate, bandwidth, and update frequency on model freshness beyond conventional Age of Information (AoI). The proposed strategy reduces average DA-AoM by 9.2\%--42.4\% compared with representative baselines under the same resource constraints.
tldr: The paper proposes a drift-aware adaptive semantic codec update strategy for dynamic semantic communication systems using a new metric called Drift-Aware Age of Model.
motivation: Semantic communication performance degrades when target-domain data distributions drift from offline training distributions, but frequent codec updates incur communication, computation, and queueing costs.
method: The authors quantify drift in semantic feature space, introduce Drift-Aware Age of Model (DA-AoM), derive closed-form average DA-AoM expressions for M/M/1 and D/M/1 update scenarios, and optimize update frequency under queueing stability constraints.
result: Simulations show DA-AoM captures joint effects of drift intensity, computing rate, bandwidth, and update frequency better than conventional AoI, reducing average DA-AoM by 9.2%–42.4% versus baselines.
conclusion: The proposed drift-aware update strategy balances model freshness and resource costs in dynamic semantic communication systems, but the work is outside the quantum information research directions.

title: Split-and-Learn: Decoupled Learning For Reactive Transport In Heterogeneous Marine Sediments
authors: Maria Vasilyeva, Siu Wun Cheung, Jihoon Kim, Richard B. Coffin, Ingo Pecher
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23748v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reactive transport in heterogeneous marine sediments couples flow and multicomponent transport with nonlinear chemistry and evolving porosity and permeability, and its simulation over thousands of years is computationally expensive, especially when uncertain heterogeneity requires many simulations. We develop Split-and-Learn, a framework that keeps the sequential operator-splitting scheme of the full-order model and replaces each stage by a data-driven surrogate with its own structure. Transport is learned on a local data-driven multiscale space, either as a compressed reduced solution map (global inverse atoms) or as coarse-block pieces of the forward operator assembled into a Galerkin or least-squares Petrov-Galerkin system (local atoms). Chemistry is learned through bounded reaction extents with stoichiometric reconstruction, which preserves reaction invariants and nonnegativity. Flow uses learned interface traces and a reduced mixed multiscale solve that enforces coarse-block mass balance. We prove the stability of the split scheme with the evolving medium and bound the error of the learned solver by the accumulated one-step errors of its stages. Numerical experiments in two- and three-dimensional heterogeneous sediment domains show the accuracy and computational cost of the individual and combined learned stages against the full order split solver.
tldr: Split-and-Learn develops decoupled data-driven surrogates for reactive transport in heterogeneous marine sediments while preserving operator-splitting structure and stability.
motivation: Simulating coupled flow, multicomponent transport, and nonlinear chemistry over thousands of years in uncertain heterogeneous sediments is computationally expensive, motivating efficient surrogates.
method: The framework retains sequential operator splitting and replaces transport, chemistry, and flow stages with structure-preserving learned surrogates, including multiscale transport spaces, bounded reaction extents, and reduced mixed multiscale flow solves.
result: The authors prove stability of the split scheme with evolving media and bound learned-solver error by accumulated one-step stage errors; numerical experiments in 2D and 3D show accuracy and cost relative to the full-order solver.
conclusion: The work provides a computationally efficient, stability-aware learned solver for reactive transport in heterogeneous marine sediments, but it has no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Fixed And Periodic Points Of Bi-dual Intersection Operators
authors: Youjiang Lin
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23812v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We classify the fixed and periodic points, up to positive dilation, of the operators [MATH] in the indexed bi-dual intersection family associated with centro-section integrals. For [MATH] and [MATH], a star body satisfies [MATH] for some [MATH] and an integer [MATH] if and only if it is an origin-centered Euclidean ball. No convexity, origin symmetry, or initial differentiability is assumed. An exact Grassmannian graph representation gives a decreasing weight and yields a strictly positive linear increment under continuous Steiner symmetrization unless the body is already symmetric. At a fixed point, a uniform radial Taylor estimate makes the same volume-preserving increment quadratic. Sobolev estimates for the spherical Radon transform and its adjoint supply the required regularity. Independently, a strict Lyapunov inequality reduces every periodic point up to dilation to a fixed point. We also prove automatic positivity and smoothness for bounded nonnegative solutions and local geometric convergence of normalized iterates near the ball.
tldr: The paper classifies fixed and periodic points of bi-dual intersection operators associated with centro-section integrals on star bodies.
motivation: The work studies geometric operator dynamics arising from centro-section integrals and seeks to characterize bodies invariant under these operators up to dilation.
method: It uses an exact Grassmannian graph representation, Steiner symmetrization, Sobolev estimates for the spherical Radon transform and its adjoint, and Lyapunov inequalities.
result: The main result shows that fixed points up to positive dilation are origin-centered Euclidean balls, and every periodic point reduces to a fixed point; additional regularity and convergence results are proved.
conclusion: The paper establishes a rigidity/classification theorem for centro-section integral operators, with no apparent connection to quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Asymmetric Optical Image Watermarking
authors: Guang Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23350v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Watermark detectors held by a provider cannot be checked by third parties, and a party that can detect a mark can usually also forge it. We study a two-layer image watermark in which the Fourier transform at the core of the pipeline is performed by a coherent optical 4F unit. Layer 1 carries an Ed25519 signature bound to the image content in Fourier magnitudes, so anyone with the public key verifies offline. Layer 2 is a key-defined carrier written by a secret phase hologram and read by a matched-filter correlator. The optics is a scalar-diffraction simulation with finite modulator bits, pixel aperture, pupil, defocus, misalignment, and sensor noise. No hardware is built. All criteria were fixed in a hashed specification before any optical result. The simulated optical signer reproduces the digital pipeline (field error 1.7e-15, bit agreement 99.997%), verifies at least 99.5% of 877 images under each of 8 post-sensor settings, one unattacked, and accepts none of 40,670 unmarked images. The optical carrier is key-selective: the matched key detects it on 99.8% of the unattacked images, and detection falls to 0% under a scale error of 1% and to 0% under a mask shift of 1 bin. Security rests on the signature and the content binding, for which we separate what is provable from what is measured.
tldr: A two-layer optical image watermarking scheme combining an Ed25519 content-bound signature with a key-selective phase-hologram carrier, evaluated entirely through scalar-diffraction simulation.
motivation: Watermark detectors held by providers cannot be independently audited, and parties able to detect a mark can often forge it, so the authors seek asymmetric, publicly verifiable and key-selective marking.
method: Layer 1 embeds an Ed25519 signature bound to image content via Fourier magnitudes; Layer 2 encodes a secret carrier in a phase hologram read by a matched-filter correlator, with the 4F Fourier transform simulated including finite modulator bits, pupil, defocus, misalignment and sensor noise.
result: The simulated optical signer matches the digital pipeline (field error 1.7e-15, 99.997% bit agreement), verifies ≥99.5% of 877 images across 8 post-sensor settings while rejecting all 40,670 unmarked images, and carrier detection collapses to 0% under 1% scale error or 1-bin mask shift.
conclusion: The scheme offers practical asymmetric, publicly verifiable watermarking with strong key selectivity, though security claims are largely based on the signature and content binding rather than fully proven optical properties.

title: Lossless Reversible Watermarking For Aigc With Applications In Authentication
authors: Yupeng Qiu, Han Fang, Ee-Chien Chang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23395v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AIGC watermarking is commonly used for tracing, but it can also support applications such as authentication and tampering detection. We study lossless reversible watermarking, which enables exact recovery of the original watermarked image after permissible distortions. By exploiting the relatively low entropy of the information required for image generation, together with robust latent-space watermarking, we design a framework that preserves sufficient information for lossless recovery. We then apply the framework to AIGC authentication, which generally faces two key challenges. First, the authentication mechanism must resist adaptive adversaries. Second, the content relevant to authentication, such as visual designs or expressed messages, may depend on application requirements that are not known at generation time. To solve these difficulties, we incorporate cryptographic message authentication to provide unforgeability against adaptive attacks. Lossless recovery provides the original image as reference evidence, after which a suitable analyzer can be selected to make the authentication decision. Experiments on Stable Diffusion demonstrate exact recovery under a wide range of distortions.
tldr: The paper proposes a lossless reversible watermarking framework for AIGC images that supports authentication and tamper detection via cryptographic message authentication and robust latent-space watermarking.
motivation: AIGC watermarking is typically used for tracing, but authentication requires resistance to adaptive adversaries and flexibility for application-dependent content unknown at generation time.
method: The framework exploits low-entropy generation information and robust latent-space watermarking to enable exact recovery after permissible distortions, and incorporates cryptographic message authentication for unforgeability.
result: Experiments on Stable Diffusion demonstrate exact recovery of the original watermarked image under a wide range of distortions.
conclusion: Lossless reversible watermarking combined with cryptographic authentication provides a practical approach for AIGC authentication and tamper detection.

title: A-Tag: Cryptographic File Tagging With Enforced Live Human Presence
authors: Mohammed Gharib, Sam Burns, Martin Zizi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23602v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The increasing autonomy of software agents and the proliferation of AI-generated content have weakened the reliability of digital actions as evidence of human involvement. Existing mechanisms, such as digital signatures and authentication protocols, verify identity and integrity, but do not establish whether a live human was present at the time an action was performed. In this paper, we introduce A-Tag, a system for verifiable human-in-the-loop tagging of digital artifacts. A-Tag cryptographically binds a file to a verified instance of live human presence at the moment of tagging. The resulting tag serves as a persistent and transferable proof that the action was triggered by a live human, without making claims about the origin, identity of the actor, or semantic content of the file. A-Tag is a modular framework combining liveness verification based on micro-motion signals shaped by human motor control, a secure cryptographic binding between the verified event and the artifact, and a publicly verifiable logging mechanism enabling independent validation. We formalize security properties of human presence signals, define an adversarial model capturing automated and relay attacks, and analyze the system's guarantees and limitations. We implement A-Tag on commodity devices and evaluate it under realistic conditions. Our evaluation shows that A-Tag provides cryptographically sound artifact binding with deterministic verification, while enabling robust recovery under real-world transformations, achieving over 99 percent success for image-based artifacts, and maintaining sub-second verification and practical tagging latency.
tldr: A-Tag is a cryptographic system that binds digital artifacts to verified live human presence using micro-motion liveness signals and secure logging.
motivation: Digital signatures and authentication verify identity and integrity but cannot establish that a live human was present when an action occurred, a gap made salient by autonomous software agents and AI-generated content.
method: The framework combines liveness verification from human motor-control micro-motion signals, cryptographic binding between the verified presence event and the artifact, and a publicly verifiable logging mechanism, with formal security properties and an adversarial model.
result: Implemented on commodity devices, A-Tag achieves over 99% success for image-based artifacts, sub-second verification, practical tagging latency, and robust recovery under real-world transformations.
conclusion: A-Tag provides cryptographically sound, transferable proof of human-in-the-loop tagging without claiming actor identity or semantic content, though it falls outside quantum information science.

title: Expanding And Evaluating The Applicability Of Safe Pareto Improvements
authors: Caspar Oesterheld Nathaniel Sauerberg
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23614v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Even when players can make credible joint commitments in games, disagreement about the game's default outcome (e.g., about equilibrium selection) can prevent them from agreeing on any particular payoff profile. We study safe Pareto improvements (SPIs): commitments that sidestep this obstacle by inducing a new game that is isomorphic to the original (after iteratively removing strictly dominated actions) but entrywise Pareto better. We do so by constructing token games: cheap-talk games rendered meaningful by commitments to take payoff-relevant actions (in prior work, strategies in the original game) as a function of the token outcome. Since these token games preserve the original game's strategic structure, players should expect them to be played isomorphically and hence agree that they Pareto improve on the original. In this work, we study token game SPIs under three additional commitment abilities: (1) burning utility, (2) transferring utility between players, and (3) transferring utility with an outside party conditional on the token outcome (e.g., via insurance-like contracts). We characterize when SPIs exist in each case and give efficient algorithms for optimizing over them. Finally, we propose evaluating SPI frameworks by how often they enable SPIs in randomly generated games. In such experiments, our methods substantially outperform prior work.
tldr: The paper studies safe Pareto improvements in game theory via token games and characterizes when such improvements exist under additional commitment abilities.
motivation: Players with credible joint commitments may still disagree about the default outcome or equilibrium selection, preventing agreement on a Pareto-better payoff profile.
method: The authors analyze token games under utility burning, utility transfer between players, and conditional utility transfer with an outside party, providing existence characterizations and efficient optimization algorithms.
result: They characterize when safe Pareto improvements exist in each setting and show that their methods substantially outperform prior work in random-game experiments.
conclusion: The work expands the applicability of safe Pareto improvement frameworks and proposes empirical evaluation by frequency of SPIs in randomly generated games.

title: Plug-and-Play Multi-Licensee Robust Watermarking For Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
authors: Jianshuo Liu, Kang G. Shin, Haining Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23838v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures enable high-capacity large language models (LLMs) with high sparse computation, making them attractive for deployment on private hardware. However, distributing model weights exposes valuable intellectual property (IP) to leakage and unauthorized redistribution, creating an urgent need to both verify model ownership and trace leaked copies to individual licensees. Existing model-watermarking techniques are ill-suited for meeting this need because they are fragile under MoE's dynamic routing or require costly retraining to embed a distinct watermark for each licensee, thus making scalable distribution difficult. To address these challenges, we present PPMoE, the first plug-and-play multi-licensee watermarking framework for MoE LLMs. Rather than training a separate model per user, PPMoE trains a compact set of mergeable incremental weight modules that steer the MoE router toward distinct, mutually compatible routing patterns. During model distribution, the model owner selectively merges unique combinations of these pre-trained, mutually compatible modules into the base model on the fly, embedding a licensee-specific watermark without additional training. PPMoE supports reliable multi-licensee attribution under both white- and black-box threat models. In the white-box setting, attribution is done by inspecting triggered routing decisions or the merged weight modules responsible for these decisions, whereas in the black-box setting, attribution relies on analyzing output token likelihood ratios. Extensive experiments across five state-of-the-art MoE models, seven benchmark datasets, and varying number of licensees show that PPMoE achieves very high attribution accuracy while preserving base model utility and maintaining strong robustness to various adaptive watermark-removal attacks.
tldr: The paper introduces PPMoE, a plug-and-play multi-licensee watermarking framework for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs using mergeable incremental weight modules that steer routing patterns for ownership attribution.
motivation: Distributing MoE LLM weights exposes intellectual property to leakage and unauthorized redistribution, requiring scalable ownership verification and licensee tracing that existing watermarking methods do not provide.
method: PPMoE trains a compact set of mutually compatible modules that induce distinct MoE routing patterns, then merges unique module combinations into the base model at distribution time to embed licensee-specific watermarks without retraining.
result: Experiments on five MoE models and seven datasets show high attribution accuracy under white-box and black-box threat models while preserving model utility and resisting adaptive watermark-removal attacks.
conclusion: PPMoE enables scalable multi-licensee watermarking for MoE LLMs, but the work is in AI model security and IP protection rather than quantum information science.

title: Weighing The Envelope: Component Weight And Arbitration In Envelope-Layer Defenses For A Single Llm Agent
authors: Yuelin Han
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23844v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The envelope layer is the channel through which malicious content enters an LLM agent. Prior work established label and memory effects on multi-agent A2A envelopes, but the weight structure when MCP tools and memory coexist in a single agent remains unclear. Our threat model assumes an attacker pre-plants a malicious tool and poisons long-term memory; a benign user request inadvertently triggers it, and the attacker never enters the conversation. Following GDA Measurement and A/B/C/D, we measure how labels, memory, tool roles, and the backend shape invocation decisions across label-memory conflict, tool roles, robustness, and tool generalization. A tool-side forced-verification label substantially reduces semantic breach, but strong success memory pulls it back; a memory-side downgrade statement returns the outcome to the level of the label alone. The label works through mandatory implementation inspection plus default denial, not length or format; memory authorization wording erodes it with dose, while position and multi-turn pressure do not change the defense direction. Tool roles divide label effects into substitution, suppression, and boundary failure: low penetration is not safety, local leakage is the main residual risk, and a second malicious tool shows the same direction. Envelope labels are not a switch but a measurable, reversible weight constrained by backend and tool role, acting as a soft gate and risk signal within a broader defense rather than a substitute for permissions, sandboxing, or human review.
tldr: The paper empirically measures how envelope-layer labels, memory content, tool roles, and backend choices influence an LLM agent's susceptibility to pre-planted malicious tools and poisoned memory.
motivation: The envelope layer is the entry channel for malicious content in LLM agents, yet how label and memory signals interact when MCP tools and memory coexist in a single agent is not understood.
method: Using a GDA measurement and A/B/C/D design, the authors vary labels, memory, tool roles, and backend to probe invocation decisions under label-memory conflict, robustness, and tool-generalization settings.
result: A forced-verification tool-side label substantially reduces semantic breach but strong success memory pulls it back, while a memory-side downgrade statement restores label-only performance; tool roles split label effects into substitution, suppression, and boundary failure.
conclusion: Envelope labels act as a measurable, reversible soft gate and risk signal within a broader defense, not a substitute for permissions, sandboxing, or human review.

title: Mimo Channel Extrapolation To Unobserved Radiation Modes Via Learned Path Refinement
authors: Chongwen Huang Shaoyang Sun
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23904v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A pattern-reconfigurable multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) receiver can sample every antenna element and still leave entire radiation modes unobserved. The calibrated patterns weight a common set of propagation paths, which links these missing channels to the measured rows. Our estimator learns to correct the complex gains and spatial frequencies of those paths, so a correction inferred from measured rows updates every unmeasured mode. Each stage combines a damped least-squares proposal with a learned correction scaled by noise power and local array sensitivity. Training on complete simulated channels rewards corrections that reduce prediction error across modes, including those with no measured rows. The learned rule transfers from pursuit-based training estimates to a ridge variable-projection initializer without retraining. In matched simulations, refinement reduces error on wholly unobserved modes as well as across the full channel. Coefficient updates account for most of the gain, and the learned rule further improves on adaptive ridge shrinkage at fixed angles. Individual channel trajectories show that extrapolation can improve even as the residual on the measured rows increases.
tldr: The paper proposes a learned path-refinement method to extrapolate unobserved radiation-mode MIMO channels from measured antenna rows.
motivation: Pattern-reconfigurable MIMO receivers can leave entire radiation modes unobserved, so methods are needed to infer missing channels from calibrated measurements.
method: The estimator corrects complex gains and spatial frequencies of common propagation paths, combining damped least-squares proposals with learned noise- and sensitivity-scaled corrections.
result: In matched simulations, refinement reduces prediction error on wholly unobserved modes and across the full channel, with coefficient updates providing most of the gain.
conclusion: Learned path refinement enables MIMO channel extrapolation to unobserved radiation modes and can improve even when measured-row residual increases.

title: Construction Of Ternary Minimal Linear Codes With Dimension $n+r$ Via Index Codes And The Access Structures Of Their Dual Codes
authors: Qunying Liao Haibo Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.24072v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recently, minimal linear codes have been extensively studied due to their applications in secret sharing schemes, secure two-party computations, and so on. Constructing minimal linear codes violating the Ashikhmin-Barg condition and then determining their weight distributions have been interesting in coding theory and cryptography. In this paper, we present a general construction of ternary linear codes of dimension [MATH], where [MATH] and [MATH] are positive integers, and derive a necessary and sufficient condition for the resulting codes to be minimal. We first specialize the construction using index codes arising from spreads, with three classes of index codes satisfying the minimality condition, we obtain the parameters and weight enumerators of the corresponding minimal codes, and determine the access structures type of the secret-sharing schemes based on their dual codes. By the index codes from Krawtchouk polynomials, we then give a second specialization of the construction, with a class of index codes satisfying the minimality condition, we obtain the parameters of the resulting minimal codes, and determine the access-structure type of the secret-sharing scheme based on each dual code. Several constructed families of minimal codes violate the Ashikhmin-Barg condition.
tldr: The paper constructs ternary minimal linear codes of dimension n+r using index codes and analyzes the access structures of their dual codes for secret-sharing schemes.
motivation: Minimal linear codes are important for secret sharing and secure computation, and constructing codes that violate the Ashikhmin-Barg condition is a central coding-theory problem.
method: The authors give a general construction of ternary linear codes, derive a minimality condition, and specialize it using spread-based index codes and Krawtchouk-polynomial index codes.
result: They obtain parameters and weight enumerators for several minimal-code families, determine secret-sharing access-structure types from dual codes, and identify families violating the Ashikhmin-Barg condition.
conclusion: The work advances classical coding theory and cryptographic secret sharing but has no direct connection to quantum information, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Pulsar-v: I/O-Aware Post-Update Attestation For Risc-v
authors: Niccol\`o Lentini, Stefano Di Carlo, Alessandro Savino
abstract: ArXiv:2611.24135v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-update attestation proves that a device installed the intended firmware, not that the image stayed protected until the report was signed. In a multi-master SoC, a master outside the attested processor can corrupt update-critical memory. In contrast, the firmware identity, lifecycle state, and the CPU's protection evidence remain byte-identical to a healthy device's. We present PULSAR-V, a post-update attestation architecture which binds the authenticated update commit to the effective permissions and immutability of both gates (PMP/EPMP on the CPU, the I/O policy mediating DMA), sampled at the commit and at attestation, the I/O gate latching its own commit-time state in hardware. In a RISC-V SoC prototyped on a ZCU102 FPGA (CV32E40S core with 16 PMP regions, IOPMP-style unit, AXI write guard), a 256-byte write from the board's Arm DMA engine bypasses PMP and corrupts the committed image: every conventional claim stays true, and PULSAR-V rejects the device on its I/O-policy evidence alone. It also rejects an intact device whose policy left the image writable, a verdict no integrity check can reach. The gate and its commit latch cost 436 LUTs, 4.6% of the SoC, and evidence collection takes 43.1k cycles independent of image size, 41x less than re-hashing 16 KiB.
tldr: PULSAR-V is a post-update attestation architecture for RISC-V SoCs that binds firmware-commit evidence to the effective permissions of both the CPU's PMP/EPMP and the I/O DMA policy gate, catching corruption that bypasses the attested processor.
motivation: Conventional attestation proves a device installed the intended firmware but not that the image stayed protected until the report was signed; in multi-master SoCs, a non-attested master can silently corrupt update-critical memory while all standard claims remain valid.
method: The authors prototype a RISC-V SoC (CV32E40S core, 16 PMP regions, IOPMP-style unit, AXI write guard) on a ZCU102 FPGA, hardware-latching the I/O gate's commit-time policy state and sampling both gates at commit and at attestation.
result: A 256-byte DMA write from the board's Arm engine bypasses PMP and corrupts the committed image while conventional claims stay true; PULSAR-V rejects the device on I/O-policy evidence alone, and also rejects an intact-but-writable device. The gate and latch cost 436 LUTs (4.6% of SoC) and evidence collection takes 43.1k cycles, 41x cheaper than re-hashing 16 KiB.
conclusion: Extending attestation to I/O-side memory protection closes a real gap in firmware integrity verification, at modest hardware and timing cost, though the work is a classical hardware-security contribution unrelated to quantum information science.

title: On The Complexity Of Envy Cycle Elimination
authors: Warut Suksompong
abstract: ArXiv:2611.24167v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The envy cycle elimination (ECE) algorithm is a fundamental algorithm for the fair allocation of indivisible goods, guaranteeing an allocation that is envy-free up to one good under arbitrary monotone utilities. We show that the ECE algorithm can be implemented in [MATH] time for [MATH] agents and [MATH] goods, and establish the tightness of this bound.
tldr: The paper analyzes the computational complexity of the envy cycle elimination algorithm for fair allocation of indivisible goods.
motivation: Envy cycle elimination is a fundamental algorithm guaranteeing envy-free-up-to-one-good allocations under monotone utilities, but its computational complexity was not tightly characterized.
method: The author provides an algorithmic implementation and a matching lower bound for the running time of envy cycle elimination with multiple agents and goods.
result: The ECE algorithm can be implemented in the stated time bound, and the bound is shown to be tight.
conclusion: The work settles the complexity of envy cycle elimination, contributing to algorithmic fair division rather than quantum information science.

title: What Survives The Shift From Text To Pixels? Conditional Protection Against Prompt Injection In Image-Rendered Documents
authors: Haoyang Liu, Yinong Xu, Zhe Lang, Zhenyu Guan, Qianyun Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.24231v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal language models increasingly answer questions over external documents, exposing them to indirect prompt injection: commands planted in untrusted content to hijack the response. Rendering untrusted content as page images lowers attack success on average, leaving open which injected operations survive rendering, at what utility cost, and whether failed image attacks reflect unread commands or commands read but not followed. We pair text and page-image versions of 191 English question-answering sources across six models, measuring marker appending, answer formatting, and answer replacement alongside clean Question-Answering utility. Rendering reduces append and format execution for every model, yet Qwen3-VL-8B still executes image-borne replacement at 77.96\%. Protection also depends on target type, rendering settings, wording, and repetition, and a search over eight fixed attack candidates largely closes the image deficit in appending and formatting for Qwen and Gemini, though not for GPT-5-nano. Utility ratios on original questions range from 93.31\% to 101.61\%, but Qwen falls to 61.99\% when answers combine two evidence spans. Illegibility cannot explain all failed attacks: models often transcribe and identify image-borne commands they do not execute, and trusted user authorization raises execution on unchanged pages. Inside Qwen, patching early attack-region states induces all three operations, more weakly in images. Attention blocking suggests why: a text command acts through its own positions, whereas visual encoding spreads an image command and its target across the instruction page. Rendering thus offers conditional protection, motivating evaluations that report security by model, operation, and attack budget alongside utility.
tldr: The paper studies which indirect prompt-injection attacks survive when untrusted content is rendered as page images in multimodal LLM document question-answering, and at what utility cost.
motivation: Multimodal models answering questions over external documents are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection, and rendering untrusted content as images is sometimes assumed to mitigate such attacks; the authors ask which injected operations actually survive rendering and why.
method: They pair text and page-image versions of 191 English QA sources across six models, measuring marker appending, answer formatting, and answer replacement along with clean QA utility, plus attention/activation patching analyses inside Qwen.
result: Rendering reduces append and format execution for all models, but Qwen3-VL-8B still executes image-borne answer replacement 77.96% of the time; utility ratios range from 93.31% to 101.61%, dropping to 61.99% for two-span answers in Qwen, and models often transcribe image commands without executing them.
conclusion: Rendering provides only conditional protection that depends on model, operation, target type, wording, and attack budget, motivating security evaluations that report all of these factors.

title: Real-space Electrostatic Sums Through Truncation Error Analysis
authors: Chuin Wei Tan, William C. Witt, Boris Kozinsky
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23510v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Methods that treat electrostatics in real space, without explicit reciprocal-space evaluation, are appealing for large-scale atomistic simulations. They typically employ local charge-neutralization schemes, but their relationship to the underlying error contributions of the full Ewald sum has not been fully characterized. A principled basis for parameter selection is also lacking. In this work, we show that the correction terms of Wolf's and Pickard's real-space methods approximate the truncation error of real-space electrostatic sums. This perspective motivates simplified fixed-radii and force-shifted Pickard variants that preserve the truncation-error compensation behavior while enforcing continuity of pair energy and force at the cutoff. We derive a nonempirical scaling relation for the optimal path in the parameter space of the cutoff radius and screening distance, generalizing Pickard's empirical heuristic and explaining when and why it can fail. A systematic scheme for restoring omitted reciprocal contributions is introduced, which accelerates convergence to the full Ewald energy.
tldr: The paper reinterprets Wolf's and Pickard's real-space electrostatic correction schemes as approximations to the truncation error of real-space Coulomb sums, yielding simplified variants and a nonempirical scaling relation for optimal cutoff/screening parameters.
motivation: Real-space electrostatics methods avoid reciprocal-space evaluation and suit large-scale atomistic simulations, but their connection to the full Ewald error structure and a principled basis for parameter choice have been unclear.
method: The authors analyze truncation error of real-space electrostatic sums, show that Wolf and Pickard correction terms compensate for it, construct fixed-radii and force-shifted Pickard variants with continuous energy and force at the cutoff, and derive a nonempirical scaling relation plus a scheme for restoring omitted reciprocal contributions.
result: The derived scaling relation generalizes Pickard's empirical heuristic and identifies when it fails; the proposed variants preserve error-compensation behavior while ensuring continuity, and the recovery scheme accelerates convergence to the full Ewald energy.
conclusion: A truncation-error perspective provides a principled, nonempirical framework for parameter selection in real-space electrostatic methods for atomistic simulation.

title: Octahedrally And Icosahedrally Symmetric Solutions Of The N-Vortex Problem On The Sphere
authors: Pietro Pomaro
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the octahedrally and icosahedrally symmetric solutions of the N-vortex problem on the sphere, for N = 24 and N = 60 respectively, in the case of equal vorticities. Exploiting the symmetries arising from rotations and permutations of the vortices, the problem is reduced to the analysis of a one-degree-of-freedom Hamiltonian system on the sphere. The original contributions of this article concern the analysis of this reduced system yielding in particular a classification of the equilibrium and collision configurations with the prescribed symmetries. The computational complexity of the analysis is overcome by exploiting the associated discrete symmetries through the invariant theory of reflection groups and Palais' principle of symmetric criticality, and, in some cases, by resorting to numerical approximations.
tldr: The paper classifies octahedrally and icosahedrally symmetric equilibrium and collision configurations for the N-vortex problem on the sphere at N=24 and N=60.
motivation: The N-vortex problem on the sphere is a classical Hamiltonian fluid-dynamics model, and highly symmetric configurations provide tractable windows into its equilibrium structure.
method: The authors reduce the dynamics using rotation and permutation symmetries to a one-degree-of-freedom Hamiltonian system, then apply invariant theory of reflection groups and Palais' symmetric criticality principle, with some numerical approximations.
result: They obtain a classification of equilibrium and collision configurations with the prescribed octahedral and icosahedral symmetries for equal vorticities.
conclusion: The work advances the mathematical theory of point vortices on the sphere but has no direct connection to quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Large Entropy Implies H\"older Regularity On Large Sets
authors: Yan Mary He Fabrizio Bianchi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23490v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be a holomorphic endomorphism of [MATH] of algebraic degree [MATH], with [MATH]. We prove that every ergodic [MATH]-invariant probability measure [MATH] of entropy strictly greater than [MATH] admits compact sets of [MATH]-measure arbitrarily close to one on which the restrictions of [MATH] have H\"older continuous super-potentials. Consequently, [MATH] gives zero mass to every Borel pluripolar set.
tldr: The paper proves that ergodic invariant measures of sufficiently large entropy for holomorphic endomorphisms of projective space admit large compact subsets on which the super-potentials are Hölder continuous, and hence such measures give zero mass to pluripolar sets.
motivation: In complex dynamics, entropy of invariant measures and regularity of the associated (super-)potentials are central to understanding the structure of equilibrium and other natural measures; the authors aim to connect a purely measure-theoretic quantity (entropy) with analytic regularity properties of the dynamics.
method: Using tools from pluripotential theory and ergodic theory for holomorphic endomorphisms of P^k of algebraic degree d ≥ 2, the authors construct compact sets of measure arbitrarily close to one and establish Hölder continuity of the restrictions of the super-potentials there.
result: Every ergodic invariant probability measure with entropy strictly above a threshold admits compact sets of measure arbitrarily close to 1 on which super-potentials are Hölder continuous, which implies the measure vanishes on all Borel pluripolar sets.
conclusion: Large entropy forces strong analytic regularity on large sets, yielding a sharp dichotomy between high-entropy measures and pluripolar (analytically small) sets in complex dynamics.

title: SFiD: Self-Supervised Fitness-Driven Optimization For Next-Generation Networking
authors: Kalpesh K. Patel, Ekant Sharma, Sandeep Kumar Singh, Lajos Hanzo
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23802v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Next-generation (NG) wireless networks face increasingly complex and dynamic optimization challenges driven by data-intensive applications and massive device connectivity. Existing methods suffer from one or more limitations, including high computational complexity, poor scalability and adaptability, reliance on large labeled datasets, or weak generalization in dynamic and non-convex wireless environments. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a self-supervised fitness-driven diffusion (SFiD) method that autonomously generates its own training data and iteratively learns from it. It also exhibits strong generalization capabilities and the ability to effectively tackle challenging optimization problems. We validate the convergence of our proposed method to the global optimum on both analytical convex and non-convex optimization problems. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, we consider reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) phaseshift optimization in cell-free massive multiple-input multipleoutput (CF-mMIMO) systems with imperfect channel state information and spatial correlation at the RIS as a case study. Specifically, we develop SFiD-C for continuous variable optimization and apply it to optimize continuous RIS phase shifts in CF-mMIMO systems. We also develop SFiD-D for discrete variable optimization and apply it to optimize discrete RIS phase shifts in CF-mMIMO systems. Furthermore, we develop a binary neural network (BNN) based version of SFiDD for reducing its computational complexity, referred to as SFiD-D (BNN). Finally, our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed methods markedly improve computational efficiency and achieve comparable or superior performance compared to meta-heuristic and DRL benchmarks for both continuous and discrete RIS phase-shift optimization.
tldr: The paper proposes a self-supervised fitness-driven diffusion optimization method for next-generation wireless networking, with a case study on RIS phase-shift optimization in cell-free massive MIMO.
motivation: Next-generation wireless networks require scalable, adaptive optimization methods that avoid high complexity and large labeled datasets in dynamic non-convex environments.
method: SFiD autonomously generates training data and iteratively learns from it; continuous and discrete variants are developed for RIS phase-shift optimization, including a binary neural network version for reduced complexity.
result: The proposed methods converge on analytical convex and non-convex problems and improve computational efficiency while achieving comparable or superior performance to meta-heuristic and DRL benchmarks.
conclusion: SFiD offers an effective self-supervised optimization framework for complex wireless network design, demonstrated on RIS-assisted cell-free massive MIMO systems.

title: Securing And Auditing Long-Horizon Llm Agents: State-Transfer Auditing And Controls In The Agent Harness
authors: Nehal Kathrotia Deep Shah
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23346v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents across codebases, web browsers, and enterprise infrastructure rely on an execution harness to move state between the working context, session history, persistent memory, and external environment. While conventional execution traces log model prompts and tool calls, critical security and reliability failures occur during state transfers: a transfer can admit unchecked content (indirect prompt injections, unverified memory writes), rewrite state lossily (context compaction dropping user constraints, memory consolidation stripping source authority), or restore state incompletely (workspace rollbacks leaving aborted KV state active on the inference server). Because current traces omit what crosses these boundaries, failure attribution and runtime monitors fail on multi-step trajectories. We present a state-transfer audit architecture for the agent harness. At each transfer boundary, we define an audit point specifying the minimal hash-chained record the harness emits, separating low-overhead deterministic checks from model-based semantic checks and binding internal context, memory, and inference-server cache state to external actions. We show that the same transfer records required for causal failure attribution supply the durable state needed by runtime security controls, including least-privilege capabilities, replay-resistant authorization outside the prompt, information flow control, obligation monitors, and transactional recovery across multi-agent and infrastructure pipelines. Finally, we analyze multimodal GUI adaptations and implement and evaluate a reference harness middleware across 240 multi-step fault-injection trajectories, showing that transfer records localize root causes and catch cross-transfer violations missed by lifecycle and tool-only logs at microsecond deterministic overhead.
tldr: The paper proposes a state-transfer auditing architecture for securing and debugging long-horizon LLM agents by recording hash-chained audit points at state boundaries.
motivation: Long-horizon LLM agents can fail or be compromised during transfers between working context, memory, and external environments, but existing execution traces do not capture these boundary crossings.
method: The authors define audit points at each transfer boundary, separating deterministic low-overhead checks from model-based semantic checks, and evaluate a reference harness middleware on 240 fault-injection trajectories.
result: Transfer records localize root causes and catch cross-transfer violations missed by lifecycle and tool-only logs, with microsecond deterministic overhead.
conclusion: The same state-transfer records needed for causal failure attribution also support runtime security controls such as least-privilege capabilities, replay-resistant authorization, and transactional recovery.
