title: Depth Hierarchies For Symmetric Algebraic Circuits
authors: Anuj Dawar, Prateek Dwivedi, Benedikt Pago, Tim Seppelt
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23541v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Algebraic complexity studies the cost of computing families of polynomials by algebraic circuits, with the central goal of proving super-polynomial circuit lower bounds and separations between different models of algebraic computation. Since such lower bounds remain elusive for general circuits, a common strategy is to focus on restricted models. A recent line of work (ICALP 2020, ITCS & STOC 2026) introduces and studies symmetry as a syntactic circuit restriction, showing exponential symmetric lower bounds for the permanent, as well as separations between symmetric analogues of algebraic formulas ([MATH]), skew circuits ([MATH]), and circuits ([MATH]). We investigate the role of depth as a complexity parameter in symmetric circuits. For every fixed [MATH], we exhibit a family of polynomials computable by symmetric circuits of polynomial size and depth [MATH], but requiring size [MATH] at depth [MATH]. We also define symmetric versions of the bounded-depth algebraic complexity classes [MATH], for all [MATH], that we call [MATH], and establish two strict hierarchies: Firstly, a hierarchy within [MATH], and secondly, a hierarchy of the form [MATH] for all [MATH]. The latter shows that symmetric circuits of depth [MATH] are strictly more powerful than depth-[MATH] circuits. Moreover, we place the bounded-depth classes within the landscape of symmetric algebraic complexity developed by Dwivedi, Pago and Seppelt (STOC 2026). We complement this picture by introducing [MATH], a symmetric analogue of [MATH], and establishing [MATH]-completeness of the permanent under symmetric projections.
tldr: The paper establishes depth hierarchies for symmetric algebraic circuits, showing that bounded-depth symmetric circuits form strict hierarchies in size and depth.
motivation: Algebraic circuit lower bounds for general circuits remain elusive, so restricted models such as syntactically symmetric circuits are studied; the role of depth as a complexity parameter in this symmetric setting was previously unexamined.
method: The authors construct, for each fixed depth, families of polynomials computable by polynomial-size symmetric circuits of that depth but requiring superpolynomial size at shallower depth, and define symmetric analogues of bounded-depth algebraic classes (including a symmetric version of VP-like classes).
result: Two strict hierarchies are proven — one within bounded-depth symmetric classes and one showing depth-(d+1) symmetric circuits strictly exceed depth-d circuits — and the permanent is shown complete for the new symmetric class under symmetric projections.
conclusion: Depth is a genuine complexity resource in symmetric algebraic circuits, and the new bounded-depth classes fit coherently into the existing landscape of symmetric algebraic complexity.

title: On Regularity-free Characterization Of Bisymmetric Means
authors: Kazuki Okamura Gergely Kiss
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23300v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that every reflexive, bisymmetric binary operation on a non-degenerate real interval that is strictly increasing in each variable is automatically continuous and is a weighted quasi-arithmetic mean. This settles the reflexive, strictly increasing case of the automatic-continuity problem without assuming symmetry. The proof constructs a symmetric mean as the unique fixed point of a natural increasing operation and then applies the known symmetric automatic-continuity theorem. Maksa's method, combined with an interpolation argument on a countable dense set, yields an exact characterization of operations of arbitrary finite arity, with uniquely determined positive weights.
tldr: The paper proves that reflexive, bisymmetric, strictly increasing binary operations on real intervals are continuous weighted quasi-arithmetic means, without assuming symmetry.
motivation: It addresses the automatic-continuity problem for bisymmetric means and seeks a regularity-free characterization of such operations.
method: The authors construct a symmetric mean as the unique fixed point of an increasing operation, apply the known symmetric automatic-continuity theorem, and use Maksa's method with interpolation on a countable dense set.
result: Every reflexive, bisymmetric binary operation on a non-degenerate real interval that is strictly increasing in each variable is continuous and is a weighted quasi-arithmetic mean; the characterization extends to arbitrary finite arity with uniquely determined positive weights.
conclusion: The reflexive, strictly increasing case of the automatic-continuity problem is settled without symmetry assumptions, yielding an exact arity-general characterization of weighted quasi-arithmetic means.

title: Conjugate Power Series Of Ultralogarithm Branches
authors: Sergey V. Berezin
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23317v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate multivalued solutions of the transcendental ultralogarithm equation [MATH] for arbitrary real parameters [MATH]. A sector-based conjugation criterion is formulated and rigorously proved, reducing the technical two-dimensional indexing of conjugate master-series expansions inside ([MATH]) and outside ([MATH]) the disk of convergence to a unified one-dimensional branch index [MATH]. For integer exponents, a logarithmic analog of Vieta's theorem is established. Using multi-channel phase hodographs, we analyze branch evolution across integer, fractional, and transcendental incommensurable ([MATH], [MATH]) exponents. It is demonstrated that logarithmic stratification eliminates branch cuts of fractional powers, ensuring global stability of iterative root refinement near branch points without auxiliary sheet-selection parameters. Finally, using the Sagdeev pseudopotential method in plasma physics, we confirm the continuous preservation of branch numbering in the Lambert [MATH] limit and the physical invariance of the indices [MATH] (subsonic regime) and [MATH] (supersonic regime).
tldr: This paper develops a branch-indexing theory for multivalued solutions of the transcendental ultralogarithm equation, including a logarithmic analogue of Vieta's theorem and a plasma-physics check via the Sagdeev pseudopotential method.
motivation: Multivalued special functions such as the ultralogarithm and Lambert W have awkward two-dimensional sheet/branch indexing; the authors seek a unified, sheet-parameter-free description of conjugate power-series expansions.
method: A sector-based conjugation criterion is formulated and proved, reducing two-dimensional master-series indexing inside and outside the convergence disk to a single branch index; multi-channel phase hodographs track branch evolution for integer, fractional and incommensurable exponents, with a Sagdeev pseudopotential analysis in plasmas.
result: Logarithmic stratification is shown to remove branch cuts of fractional powers, giving globally stable iterative root refinement near branch points, and branch numbering is confirmed continuous in the Lambert W limit with physical invariance of the subsonic/supersonic indices.
conclusion: The framework yields a clean one-dimensional branch taxonomy for ultralogarithmic functions with practical implications for root-finding and for soliton-type plasma problems, but has no bearing on quantum information, thermodynamics, networks or hybrid quantum platforms.

title: Reflections On Thiele, Schur, And Continued Fractions
authors: Maxim Derevyagin
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23325v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We survey several classical continued-fraction constructions from a common point of view centered on linear-fractional transformations, interpolation, and the recurrence relations they generate. Beginning with Thiele's interpolation algorithm, we trace how similar mechanisms reappear in the Schur algorithm, Wall's continued fractions, and multipoint Nevanlinna--Pick interpolation. Particular attention is paid to the emergence of [MATH]-type continued fractions, which arise naturally as even parts of Thiele continued fractions, and to the associated pencils of tridiagonal matrices. A detour through Euler's continued-fraction formula illustrates how rational Nevanlinna functions lead naturally to finite [MATH]-pencils, while the Schur algorithm is related to Wall pencils and, through a different reorganization, to CMV matrices. We also discuss a modified Schur transformation that removes an interpolation condition at a pair of symmetric points, which leads to a linear pencil of two Hermitian tridiagonal matrices. Finally, we indicate how periodically occurring interpolation nodes at infinity convert [MATH]-pencils into ordinary banded matrices, suggesting a connection with GMP matrices.
tldr: This is a classical mathematical survey of continued-fraction constructions, interpolation algorithms, and associated matrix pencils, with no apparent quantum information, thermodynamics, networking, or hybrid-systems content.
motivation: The paper aims to unify several classical continued-fraction constructions—Thiele interpolation, the Schur algorithm, Wall continued fractions, and multipoint Nevanlinna–Pick interpolation—under a common viewpoint based on linear-fractional transformations and recurrence relations.
method: It surveys and connects continued-fraction algorithms via linear-fractional transformations, interpolation conditions, recurrence relations, M-type continued fractions, tridiagonal matrix pencils, Wall pencils, CMV matrices, and a modified Schur transformation.
result: The survey traces how related structures reappear across these classical algorithms, highlights the emergence of M-type continued fractions and associated tridiagonal pencils, and indicates connections to banded and GMP matrices through periodically occurring interpolation nodes at infinity.
conclusion: The work is a classical analysis/survey of continued fractions and interpolation theory, suggesting matrix-theoretic connections but not addressing quantum information theory or any of the user's quantum-focused research directions.

title: Quadratically Regularized Medians In Metric And Wasserstein Spaces
authors: Beno\^it Bonnet-Weill, Matteo Tacchi-B\'enard, Nicola Zaupa
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23545v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we introduce a new class of robust aggregators in Wasserstein spaces. After proving that all the commonly used Wasserstein barycenters are manipulable by one single corrupted input through a novel first-order optimality condition, we generalize both to the metric setting and to fractional exponents the concept of Lipschitz resilience introduced recently by Allouah, Guerraoui, Hoang and Villemaud. We proceed to show that adding a quadratic regularization to Wasserstein medians defined either in terms of the [MATH]-metric or linearized [MATH]-metric are resilient in that sense, by leveraging fine convexity estimates along generalized geodesics and flat interpolations. We finally show that iteratively solving the latter problem amounts to performing a Majorization-Minimization approximation of [MATH]-medians.
tldr: The paper introduces quadratically regularized Wasserstein medians as robust aggregators that are provably resilient to corrupted inputs, extending Lipschitz resilience from the metric setting to fractional exponents.
motivation: Commonly used Wasserstein barycenters can be manipulated by a single corrupted input, so principled robust aggregation procedures are needed for statistical learning on probability distributions.
method: The authors derive a first-order optimality condition showing manipulability of Wasserstein barycenters, generalize Lipschitz resilience to metric spaces and fractional exponents, and prove resilience of quadratically regularized Wasserstein medians via convexity estimates along generalized geodesics.
result: Quadratic regularization of Wasserstein medians (under both the metric and linearized metric formulations) yields resilience guarantees, and solving the regularized problem is shown to be equivalent to a Majorization-Minimization approximation of Wasserstein medians.
conclusion: Regularized median-based aggregation offers a robust alternative to barycenters in Wasserstein geometry, with theoretical resilience guarantees and a practical MM algorithm.

title: Irreducible $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$-action On Projective $k$-lattices And Frobenius Numbers
authors: Michael Bersudsky, Seongmin Kim, Seonhee Lim
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23579v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The irreducible representation of [MATH] on [MATH] induces an action on the space [MATH] of projective classes of rank [MATH]-discrete subgroups in [MATH]. For every lattice subgroup of [MATH] and every starting point in [MATH] and [MATH], we prove convergence of the orbit averages over expanding norm balls and give a complete, explicit description of their limits. In an overview, every limit is supported on the subbundle over the unique compact [MATH]-orbit in the Grassmannian. The conditional measures on the fibers are either uniform on finite sets or convex combinations of at most two homogeneous measures associated with split simple subgroups of [MATH] containing the principal [MATH]. Another objective of our work is to relate weak-[MATH] limits of probability measures on [MATH] supported on the projective classes of lattices orthogonal to integer vectors with limiting distributions of the corresponding normalized Frobenius numbers. This correspondence gives limit laws for vectors sampled from certain proper subvarieties, extending J. Marklof's work on sampling from full-dimensional domains. Specifically, together with our results for [MATH] orbits in [MATH], this correspondence gives limit laws for primitive integer vectors sampled from [MATH]-orbits. Using an earlier result of the first author and Shapira, we obtain analogous laws for integer vectors sampled on level sets of certain quadratic forms, as the level tends to infinity.
tldr: The paper proves convergence and explicit limit descriptions for orbit averages of an irreducible SL_2(R) action on projective k-lattices, and connects these homogeneous-dynamics limits to limit laws for normalized Frobenius numbers of integer vectors.
motivation: The authors aim to understand the ergodic-theoretic behavior of the SL_2(R) representation on projective classes of rank-k discrete subgroups and to link such equidistribution results with probabilistic number theory, extending Marklof's sampling limit laws beyond full-dimensional domains.
method: They analyze orbit averages over expanding norm balls for arbitrary lattice subgroups and starting points, describing the limiting measures as supported on the subbundle over the unique compact SL_2(R)-orbit in the Grassmannian, with fiber measures that are uniform on finite sets or convex combinations of at most two homogeneous measures from split simple subgroups.
result: A complete explicit classification of all possible limits of the orbit averages is obtained, and a correspondence between weak-* limits of probability measures on projective lattice classes and limiting distributions of normalized Frobenius numbers yields new limit laws for primitive integer vectors sampled from SL_2(Z)-orbits, quadratic-form level sets, and proper subvarieties.
conclusion: The work provides a detailed equidistribution theorem for SL_2(R) actions on projective k-lattices and derives novel probabilistic number-theoretic limit laws, generalizing earlier results of Marklof and of the first author with Shapira.

title: Statistical Robustness And Time Consistency In Risk Averse Optimization
authors: Yan Li Alexander Shapiro
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23640v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The aim of this manuscript is to investigate risk measures which are not necessarily convex. We show that law invariant coherent risk measures are not robust with respect to contamination of the probability measure, in the sense that an arbitrarily small contamination can change their values by an arbitrary amount. This contrasts with the Value-at-Risk, which is robust against such contamination. In addition, we show that for a given law invariant risk measure and a given policy, one can construct, under mild conditions, conditional risk measures with respect to which this policy is time consistent, in the frameworks of both Markov Decision Processes and Stochastic Optimal Control.
tldr: The paper studies non-convex risk measures, showing that law-invariant coherent risk measures are statistically non-robust while Value-at-Risk is robust, and constructs conditional risk measures that make a given policy time-consistent.
motivation: Risk measures used in optimization and decision-making may be sensitive to small probability-measure contamination and may fail time consistency, so the authors investigate robustness and time-consistency properties beyond convex risk measures.
method: The authors analyze law-invariant coherent risk measures under probability-measure contamination and compare their behavior with Value-at-Risk; they also construct conditional risk measures for a given policy in Markov Decision Processes and Stochastic Optimal Control frameworks.
result: They show that arbitrarily small contamination can change law-invariant coherent risk measures by an arbitrary amount, whereas Value-at-Risk is robust, and that under mild conditions one can construct conditional risk measures ensuring time consistency for a specified policy.
conclusion: The work highlights limitations of coherent risk measures in statistical robustness and provides a framework for enforcing time consistency in risk-averse optimization, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Theorems Of The Alternative And Nonnegativity Certificates For Systems Of Jensen-type Polynomials With Universal Quantifiers
authors: Feng Guo, Yuhang Guo, Guoyin Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23656v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Jensen-type polynomials, a class of possibly nonconvex polynomials that extends the Jensen inequality for SOS-convex polynomials while retaining natural sums of squares (SOS) certificates for nonnegativity. We show that polynomials with essentially nonpositive coefficients belong to this class and establish a composition principle that yields further examples, including componentwise univariate compositions and compositions with structured quadratic maps motivated by source-localization loss functions. We then derive theorems of the alternative that provide SOS certificates for infeasibility of systems of strict inequalities involving Jensen-type polynomials and universally quantified variables. We illustrate our results through two applications, with numerical examples. First, we show that source-localization problems admit an exact SOS reformulation under a simple dimension condition, and that an optimal solution can be recovered by solving a semidefinite program (SDP) and applying the explicit Jensen map. Second, our SOS certificates yield two {\it convergent} SDP hierarchies for semi-infinite optimization with Jensen-type polynomials, providing upper and lower bounds on the optimal value. We also establish finite-convergence and solution-extraction results, under flat truncation rank condition and the associated Jensen maps.
tldr: The paper introduces Jensen-type polynomials and derives theorems of the alternative giving sums-of-squares certificates for infeasibility of systems of strict polynomial inequalities with universally quantified variables, with applications to source localization and semi-infinite optimization.
motivation: Nonnegativity certification for nonconvex polynomials with quantifiers is hard; the authors seek a tractable class extending SOS-convexity while preserving SOS certificates.
method: They define Jensen-type polynomials, prove closure under composition (componentwise univariate and structured quadratic maps), and derive theorems of the alternative yielding exact SDP reformulations and convergent SDP hierarchies with flat-truncation convergence guarantees.
result: Source-localization problems admit an exact SOS reformulation under a dimension condition, and two convergent SDP hierarchies give upper and lower bounds for semi-infinite optimization with finite convergence under flat truncation.
conclusion: The framework extends SOS-convexity to a broader nonconvex setting with practical SDP-based certificates, but remains a purely mathematical optimization contribution.

title: Slice Isolation-as-a-Service: An Isolation Mechanism To Proactively Defend Cross-Slice Attacks In 5G-Advanced And Beyond
authors: Ashraf Matrawy Abdulaziz Abdulghaffar
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23826v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As cellular networks transition toward 5G-Advanced and Sixth Generation (6G) architectures, Network Slicing (NS) remains essential for multiplexing heterogeneous services over shared physical infrastructure. However, deploying critical Ultra-Reliable Low Latency Communications (URLLC) alongside standard broadband introduces severe cross-slice vulnerabilities. The implicit assumption that logical slicing inherently guarantees security fails against data plane exploits, as shared User Plane Functions (UPFs) remain susceptible to resource starvation and protocol tunneling. To address this, we propose the Slice Isolation-as-a-Service framework, which treats topological data plane isolation as an on-demand, monetizable capability. We formulate the multi-UPF resource allocation problem as a Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Programming (MINLP) model to strictly enforce physical and virtual isolation boundaries based on tenant security tiers, minimizing provisioning costs and end-to-end latency. To validate the framework, we engineered a novel containerized Fifth Generation (5G) testbed integrating Free5GC with Nokia Containerlab. Empirical evaluations under active volumetric flooding and the recently discovered GTP-in-GTP reflection attacks reveal that shared and Virtualized Network Function (VNF)-only isolation fail catastrophically, suffering up to 30% packet loss and complete bandwidth starvation. Our results prove that MINLP-driven strict physical isolation successfully neutralizes cross-slice injection and preserves 99.999% reliability for mission-critical slices, confirming our isolation framework as a crucial proactive defense for next-generation core networks.
tldr: The paper proposes a Slice Isolation-as-a-Service framework that uses MINLP-based multi-UPF resource allocation and strict physical isolation to defend against cross-slice attacks in 5G-Advanced and 6G core networks.
motivation: Network slicing in 5G-Advanced/6G is assumed to be inherently secure, but shared User Plane Functions remain vulnerable to data-plane exploits such as resource starvation and GTP-in-GTP tunneling, threatening URLLC services.
method: The authors formulate multi-UPF resource allocation as a Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Programming problem enforcing physical and virtual isolation per tenant security tier, and build a containerized 5G testbed combining Free5GC with Nokia Containerlab for evaluation.
result: Under volumetric flooding and GTP-in-GTP reflection attacks, shared and VNF-only isolation suffer up to 30% packet loss and bandwidth starvation, while MINLP-driven strict physical isolation neutralizes cross-slice injection and preserves 99.999% reliability.
conclusion: Topological data-plane isolation offered as a monetizable on-demand service is argued to be a crucial proactive defense for next-generation cellular core networks.

title: Smoothing And Learning For Movement-Robust RSS-Based Spoofing Detection
authors: Usama Mir
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23854v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physical-layer spoofing detection identifies an attacker who impersonates a legitimate wireless user by checking whether transmissions claiming the same identity originate from different locations, using the received signal strength (RSS) measured at several receivers. A recent scheme by Romero et al. makes this approach robust to user movement by combining a neural-network position-change detector (PCD) with community detection on a graph of frames and a fixed threshold on a hand-crafted test statistic. I study two modifications to this scheme. First, I smooth the sequence of PCD scores with a median or Gaussian temporal filter before thresholding. Second, I replace the fixed decision threshold with a supervised classifier operating on six statistical features of the region sequence produced by community detection. On real indoor RSS measurements from 52 transmitter locations, Gaussian filtering raises PCD accuracy from 0.870 to 0.921 when the PCD is trained on 10 locations and from 0.905 to 0.925 when trained on 40. On synthetic attack and no-attack sequences built from the same measurements, evaluated on a held-out test set of 1,679 sequences, the best classifier (XGBoost) reaches an accuracy of 0.949 and an F1 score of 0.940, and random forests reach an AUC of 0.99. The detector separates static attackers almost perfectly but misses about a third of attacks in which two transmitters move simultaneously, which produce region sequences similar to those of a single moving user.
tldr: This paper improves a physical-layer spoofing-detection scheme for wireless networks by temporally smoothing neural-network position-change scores and replacing a fixed threshold with a supervised classifier over community-detection region sequences.
motivation: RSS-based spoofing detection that checks whether transmissions claiming one identity arrive from different locations is fragile when legitimate users move, so the authors seek to make the position-change detector and decision rule more robust.
method: Median and Gaussian temporal filters are applied to the sequence of neural-network PCD scores before thresholding, and six statistical features of the community-detection region sequence are fed to supervised classifiers (XGBoost, random forest) in place of the fixed threshold.
result: Gaussian filtering raises PCD accuracy from 0.870 to 0.921 (10 training locations) and 0.905 to 0.925 (40 locations); the best classifier reaches 0.949 accuracy and 0.940 F1 on 1,679 held-out synthetic sequences, though about a third of two-simultaneous-mover attacks are missed.
conclusion: Lightweight temporal smoothing and learned decision rules measurably improve movement-robust RSS spoofing detection, but distinguishing multiple concurrently moving transmitters remains an open weakness.

title: Matching-Logic-Based Understanding Of Polynomial Functors And Their Initial/Final Models Revisited
authors: Dorel Lucanu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.24169v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many data types used in programming are initial algebras or final coalgebras of polynomial functors. We show how to specify them uniformly in matching logic, using the representation of polynomial functors as unary container functors [MATH]. For each container functor, we give a matching logic theory of its initial algebra and one of its final coalgebra. Besides the no-junk and no-confusion axioms and their duals, these theories include axioms about the elements that represent functions, for the initial algebra, and a bisimilarity axiom and a realisation axiom, for the final coalgebra; the existence axioms use free set variables to range over all subsets of a model. We prove that, in every model, the algebra extracted from the model is an initial algebra (a W-type) and the extracted coalgebra is a final coalgebra (an M-type) of the container extracted from the model, i.e., the one given by the model's interpretation of the shapes and positions, and that such models exist. So the data types are captured relative to the interpretation of the sorts of shapes and positions, and absolutely whenever these sorts are fixed by auxiliary specifications, which we show for finite sets, products, dependent sums, and (co)inductive sorts built from them. We derive the induction, coinduction, and bisimulation principles as theorems, and illustrate the approach on lists and on Moore machines. This paper revises and substantially extends a paper published in EPTCS 389 (FROM 2023): several axioms are corrected, and the adequacy and satisfiability proofs are new.
tldr: The paper presents a uniform matching-logic specification of initial algebras (W-types) and final coalgebras (M-types) of polynomial/container functors, proving adequacy and existence of models that realize these data types.
motivation: Many programming data types arise as initial algebras or final coalgebras of polynomial functors, but a uniform logical framework for specifying both, with correct no-junk/no-confusion and bisimilarity axioms, was lacking.
method: Polynomial functors are represented as unary container functors; for each, matching logic theories are given for the initial algebra and final coalgebra, using free set variables for existence axioms, with new adequacy and satisfiability proofs.
result: In every model the extracted algebra is an initial algebra and the extracted coalgebra a final coalgebra of the container interpreted by the model, and such models exist; induction, coinduction, and bisimulation principles are derived as theorems, illustrated on lists and Moore machines.
conclusion: The approach captures data types relative to interpretations of shape and position sorts, and absolutely when those sorts are fixed by auxiliary specifications (finite sets, products, dependent sums, (co)inductive sorts).

title: Canonical Proof Nets For Intuitionistic Multiplicative Linear Logic
authors: Matteo Acclavio, Willem Heijltjes, Dominic J. D. Hughes
abstract: ArXiv:2611.24235v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of finding canonical representations of proofs in the multiplicative fragment of intuitionistic linear logic with units. We show that, contrary to the classical case, it is possible to define a notion of proof nets for this fragment which is provided with a polynomial-time sequentialization procedure and is both canonical and efficient. In particular, we show that sequent calculus derivations differing only by a permutation of independent rule applications are translated to the same proof net, and that the translations between sequent calculus and proof nets are inverse to each other.
tldr: The paper introduces canonical proof nets for intuitionistic multiplicative linear logic with units, together with a polynomial-time sequentialization procedure.
motivation: Proof nets are meant to quotient out irrelevant permutations between independent sequent-calculus inferences, but for intuitionistic multiplicative linear logic with units a canonical, efficient representation has remained elusive, in contrast with the classical case.
method: The authors define a notion of proof net for the multiplicative intuitionistic fragment with units and construct mutual translations between sequent-calculus derivations and proof nets, proving that permutation-equivalent derivations map to the same net.
result: The translations are shown to be mutually inverse, yielding a canonical representation, and the sequentialization procedure is proved to run in polynomial time.
conclusion: Canonical and efficient proof nets exist for intuitionistic multiplicative linear logic with units, giving a clean syntactic representation of proofs modulo permutation equivalence.

title: When Shuffling Fails: Token Recovery From Obfuscated Kv Caches
authors: Chengzhi Yi, Xiao Cheng, Wei Song, Haoyu Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.24276v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM serving systems store, offload, and share KV caches, exposing token-level representations to infrastructure operators and co-tenants. Shuffled obfuscation combines secret linear transforms with fresh permutations, claiming security from b! possible shufflings. We show that input symmetry invalidates this counting argument: security depends on distinguishable outputs under chosen inputs. Repeated tokens produce identical first-layer Value rows, making every row permutation leave the data unchanged. Only auxiliary structures such as a single-row recovery marker vary, reducing the effective state space from b! to b. We construct Repeat-to-Reveal. The attacker collects the b distinguishable states from its own probes and exploits their rank-one differences to recover an equivalent denoiser without knowing the defender's secret parameters. A one-time calibration transfers across requests sharing the same secret epoch, enabling passive token-multiset recovery from subsequently observed cache blocks through public-model dictionary matching. We instantiate the attack on official KV-Cloak and evaluate 3,000 real WildChat user prompts across nine models and eleven configurations. The attack recovers the secret parameters with high accuracy and achieves 100 percent token-multiset recovery on GPU. Refreshing row-level secrets between epochs interrupts cross-request transfer, confirming secret reuse scope as the operative vulnerability. We further confirm orbit collapse on two other open-source defenses: the sequence-permutation implementation of Thomas et al. and PermLLM. The KV-Cloak developers invited a detailed report through their private vulnerability reporting channel.
tldr: The paper shows that shuffled obfuscation of LLM KV caches is insecure because repeated tokens collapse the effective permutation space, enabling token-multiset recovery.
motivation: LLM serving systems expose KV caches to infrastructure operators, and shuffled obfuscation claims security from a factorial number of permutations. The authors argue that input symmetry invalidates this counting-based security argument.
method: They construct the Repeat-to-Reveal attack, using repeated tokens to reduce distinguishable states from b! to b, then exploit rank-one differences and one-time calibration to recover an equivalent denoiser and perform passive token-multiset recovery via public-model dictionary matching.
result: The attack is evaluated on KV-Cloak with 3,000 WildChat prompts across nine models and eleven configurations, achieving high secret-parameter recovery and 100% token-multiset recovery on GPU; orbit collapse is also confirmed for two other defenses.
conclusion: Secret reuse across requests is the operative vulnerability, and refreshing row-level secrets between epochs interrupts cross-request transfer.

title: Numerical Approximation Of Benjamin-Ono Type Models For Two-dimensional Internal Waves
authors: Angel Dur\'an
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23327v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper we analyze the numerical approximation with spectral methods of two asymptotic models for the two-dimensional propagation of internal waves in a two-layer system of fluids with rigid-lid condition. The semidiscretization in space of the periodic initial-value problem with the spectral Fourier-Galerkin method is introduced and some error estimates are derived. Then the semidiscrete system is integrated in time with the Implicit Midpoint Rule and several numerical experiments illustrate the performance of the corresponding full discretization.
tldr: The paper develops and analyzes spectral numerical methods for Benjamin-Ono-type asymptotic models of two-dimensional internal waves in a two-layer fluid.
motivation: Internal wave propagation in stratified fluids is modeled by Benjamin-Ono-type equations, and accurate numerical approximation is needed for the two-dimensional periodic initial-value problem.
method: The author uses a Fourier-Galerkin spectral semidiscretization in space, derives error estimates, and integrates the semidiscrete system in time with the implicit midpoint rule.
result: Numerical experiments illustrate the performance of the full discretization and support the theoretical error analysis.
conclusion: The proposed spectral method provides an effective numerical approach for Benjamin-Ono-type models of two-dimensional internal waves.

title: A Feasible-Domain Reduction Approach With Objective-Loss Guarantees For Multilevel Multiobjective Linear Programming
authors: Mustapha Kaci
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23548v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In some approaches to decentralized multilevel multiobjective programming, each decision-maker selects a compromise and restricts the feasible region before passing the decision to the next level. However, these restrictions do not necessarily limit the deterioration of objective values at preceding levels. This paper studies how to choose variable bounds that keep such losses within prescribed tolerances. We establish exact conditions using linear programming duality and derive simpler bounds based on objective coefficients. We also examine the choice of restriction widths and establish guarantees for successive reductions. A two-level numerical example illustrates the results and the influence of tolerances on the final compromise.
tldr: The paper develops a feasible-domain reduction method for multilevel multiobjective linear programming with guarantees on objective-value loss at preceding decision levels.
motivation: Decentralized multilevel multiobjective programming can suffer from uncontrolled deterioration of higher-level objectives when lower-level decision-makers restrict the feasible region, so bounds are needed to keep such losses within tolerances.
method: Using linear programming duality, the author derives exact conditions and simpler coefficient-based bounds for choosing variable restrictions, and analyzes successive reductions.
result: The paper establishes conditions and guarantees for keeping objective losses within prescribed tolerances, illustrated by a two-level numerical example.
conclusion: The approach provides a practical way to constrain feasible-region reductions in multilevel multiobjective linear programming while maintaining objective-loss tolerances.

title: Optimal Production Scheduling For Multi-Product Mineral Manufacturing
authors: Joshua L. Pulsipher Stefan Mazzadi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23699v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Short-term scheduling in multi-product mineral manufacturing requires coordinating material movement and production across interconnected processing stages while addressing confirmed customer orders and longer-term production requirements. This work develops a generalized network-based, lexicographic multi-objective optimization (MOO) scheduling framework for these systems. The formulation represents the progression of material from raw-material supply through production and inventory to customer fulfillment. A sequential objective hierarchy first prioritizes fulfillment of confirmed customer orders and then progressively directs feasible production capacity toward cumulative targets supplied by the facility's demand-planning process. This approach ensures that the performance achieved for each higher-priority objective is preserved before subsequent targets are considered. Selected product-line activation decisions are represented using generalized disjunctive programming (GDP). An industrial mineral-manufacturing case study demonstrates the proposed framework's ability to generate feasible shift-level schedules and preserve the intended operational priorities with practical computational performance.
tldr: The paper develops a generalized network-based lexicographic multi-objective optimization framework for short-term production scheduling in multi-product mineral manufacturing.
motivation: Short-term scheduling in multi-product mineral manufacturing must coordinate material movement across interconnected processing stages while balancing confirmed customer orders against longer-term demand targets.
method: A network-flow formulation traces material from raw supply through production and inventory to customer fulfillment, with a sequential objective hierarchy and generalized disjunctive programming (GDP) for product-line activation decisions.
result: An industrial mineral-manufacturing case study shows the framework generates feasible shift-level schedules that preserve operational priorities with practical computational performance.
conclusion: Lexicographic MOO with GDP modeling is effective for priority-preserving scheduling in multi-product mineral production systems.

title: Apply All, Prove Once: Embedding Parameterized Lemmas In Drat
authors: Randal E. Bryant, Zachary Battleman, Marijn J. H. Heule
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23574v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The deletion-resolution-asymmetric-tautology (DRAT) proof format is widely used to express unsatisfiability proofs of Boolean formulas. Our DRATL format extends DRAT with parameterized lemmas, allowing a single proof to succinctly capture the common case where multiple instances of a pattern occur in a formula, differing in the identities and phases of the variables. Proofs expressed in DRATL can be hierarchical, with the proof of one lemma containing instantiations of others. Our elaborator program expands a DRATL proof containing multiple, nested lemmas into a standard DRAT proof. Most significantly, the elaboration yields compact proofs, where a single sequencing of the proof steps for each lemma covers all of its instantiations. Several case studies demonstrate that lemmas can provide a powerful method to generate short proofs for challenging problems.
tldr: The paper introduces DRATL, an extension of the DRAT proof format that supports parameterized lemmas, enabling compact unsatisfiability proofs for Boolean formulas with repeated patterns via hierarchical lemma instantiation and elaboration back to standard DRAT.
motivation: DRAT proofs of unsatisfiable Boolean formulas can grow unwieldy when a formula contains many instances of the same structural pattern differing only in variable identity and phase; the authors aim to make such proofs succinct and human-manageable.
method: They define DRATL, a format adding parameterized, nestable lemmas to DRAT, and implement an elaborator that expands a DRATL proof with multiple nested lemmas into an equivalent standard DRAT proof, with a single proof-step sequence per lemma covering all instantiations.
result: Case studies show that parameterized lemmas yield substantially shorter proofs and provide a powerful method for generating compact proofs of challenging problems, while the elaboration remains verifiable in standard DRAT.
conclusion: Embedding parameterized lemmas in DRAT offers a practical route to compact, hierarchical machine-checkable proofs, improving proof authoring and proof-size efficiency for SAT-based verification.

title: Authenticating IoT Data On Ethereum After Pectra And Fusaka: A Cost Study Of Signature Schemes, Batching And Anchoring For Agricultural Supply Chain Finance
authors: Ming-Fong Sie, Jian-Hong Chen, Gwan-Yen Lin, Yen-Shuo Chen, Shih-Wei Liao
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23764v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Blockchain-based supply chain finance can turn the sensor-recorded production history of smallholder farms into verifiable credit evidence, but only if every record is authenticated and anchored at a cost that scales to large device fleets. Ethereum's 2025 Pectra and Fusaka upgrades changed this cost landscape: they added precompiles for BLS12-381 and P-256, repriced calldata and MODEXP, and capped transaction gas at [MATH]. We organize the authentication and anchoring of IoT records into three trust levels, from posting a Merkle root through a trusted aggregator to verifying every device signature on-chain, and implement four replay-protected signature designs: ECDSA over secp256k1 and P-256, BLS aggregate signatures with on-chain hash-to-curve, and a pseudonymous identity-based signature with batch verification. Measured as signed transactions under the rules before and after both upgrades, the upgrades mainly changed which designs are feasible, not their cost. Batching and Merkle anchoring cut the cost of ECDSA authentication sixfold, to 8,963 gas per record, and secp256k1 ECDSA remains the cheapest authenticated design: P-256 costs 1.6 times as much, the identity-based design 2.7 times and BLS aggregation 3.9 times, dominated by on-chain hashing to the curve. One transaction carries at most 1,754 ECDSA-authenticated records but only 411 BLS-aggregated ones. On a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, pairing-based signing takes 5.7 ms against 0.29 ms for ECDSA. Pairing-based designs pay off only when the application needs their additional properties, and the identity-based design adds key escrow at the key generation centre. The benchmark harness is released for reproducibility.
tldr: This paper benchmarks authentication and anchoring costs for IoT data on Ethereum after the Pectra and Fusaka upgrades, comparing ECDSA, P-256, BLS aggregate signatures, and an identity-based scheme under batching and Merkle anchoring.
motivation: Blockchain-based agricultural supply chain finance requires authenticating sensor records from many smallholder devices at scale, and recent Ethereum upgrades changed the cost landscape for signature verification and data anchoring.
method: The authors organize IoT record authentication into three trust levels and implement four replay-protected signature designs, measuring gas costs as signed transactions before and after the upgrades on a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W.
result: Batching and Merkle anchoring reduce ECDSA authentication cost sixfold to 8,963 gas per record, with secp256k1 ECDSA remaining cheapest; P-256 costs 1.6x, identity-based signatures 2.7x, and BLS aggregation 3.9x, with a transaction carrying at most 1,754 ECDSA records versus 411 BLS records.
conclusion: Pairing-based designs are only worthwhile when their additional properties are needed, and the identity-based design introduces key escrow at the key generation center; the benchmark harness is released for reproducibility.

title: Temporal Fair Division: Simultaneous Guarantees For Goods And Chores
authors: Tianqi Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23782v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study temporal fair division of indivisible items in both the goods and chores settings, with [MATH] agents and nonnegative additive values or costs. Items arrive one at a time and must be assigned immediately and irrevocably. The arrival order and all agents' values or costs are known in advance, and the cumulative allocation must satisfy the fairness requirements after each arrival. For goods, we give a polynomial-time algorithm that simultaneously achieves exact temporal proportionality up to one item (TPROP1), a [MATH] approximation to temporal maximin share (TMMS), and a [MATH] approximation to temporal envy-freeness up to one item (TEF1). The TMMS factor is optimal. For chores, we give a polynomial-time algorithm that simultaneously achieves exact TPROP1 and a [MATH] approximation to TMMS. Classical scheduling lower bounds based on fixed sequences carry over to chores TMMS, establishing the optimality of this factor for [MATH]. For every [MATH], we further show that [MATH] is the optimal TMMS factor subject to exact TPROP1. For every fixed [MATH] and every finite [MATH], we construct an instance of chores admitting no [MATH]-TEF1 allocation.
tldr: This paper studies temporal fair division of indivisible goods and chores that arrive one at a time, giving polynomial-time algorithms that simultaneously satisfy temporal proportionality, maximin share, and envy-freeness guarantees.
motivation: Fair division has traditionally been studied for static allocations, but many real settings require irrevocable online assignment with fairness maintained after every arrival, a setting that lacks simultaneous guarantees across goods and chores.
method: The author designs polynomial-time online allocation algorithms achieving TPROP1 together with approximations to TMMS and TEF1 for goods, and TPROP1 with an optimal TMMS approximation for chores, using scheduling lower bounds and impossibility constructions.
result: For goods the algorithm attains exact TPROP1, an optimal TMMS factor, and a TEF1 approximation; for chores exact TPROP1 with the optimal TMMS factor is achieved, and no finite TEF1 guarantee exists for fixed agent counts.
conclusion: The work establishes tight, optimal simultaneous fairness guarantees for temporal fair division across both goods and chores, and shows a sharp impossibility for temporal envy-freeness in the chores setting.

title: AutoPI: Taxonomy-Guided Adaptive Red Teaming For Prompt Injection In Llm Agents
authors: Konstantinos Psounis Stavros Damianakis
abstract: ArXiv:2611.24313v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prompt injection is the dominant unsolved security risk for LLM agents, and the community now agrees that robustness must be measured against adaptive attackers rather than fixed benchmark injections. Many adaptive red teamers exist, and most are built to maximize attack success rate (ASR). Yet ASR counts how often a target breaks, not in how many different ways. A red teamer can achieve a high ASR by reusing a few techniques that work, leaving the others untested and absent from the attacks used to harden models. We present AutoPI, an adaptive red teamer designed to find many different ways to break a target, not just to break it often. AutoPI uses PIAtlas, a taxonomy of prompt-injection techniques, both to guide its search and to measure coverage. For each scenario, an attacker LLM writes an injection for every sub-technique in the taxonomy and then reworks the ones that fail using feedback from an LLM judge. The method is black-box and training-free, it plugs into existing benchmarks in place of their fixed attack templates, and it stays up to date as the taxonomy evolves. We evaluate AutoPI on AgentDojo and IPI Arena against open-weight and proprietary target models. Alongside ASR, we report technique coverage, the fraction of taxonomy classes, techniques, and sub-techniques that yield at least one successful injection. On AgentDojo, AutoPI finds a successful injection against Qwen3.6-35B in all six classes of the taxonomy and for more than 90% of its techniques. Against Claude Haiku 5.5, the most robust target we evaluate, it achieves between 20% and 50% higher ASR and between 25% and 400% higher class-level coverage than recent state-of-the-art adaptive red teamers, while requiring no training. We release our code and the generated attacks to support reproducible, coverage-aware evaluation.
tldr: AutoPI is an adaptive, black-box red teamer that uses the PIAtlas taxonomy of prompt-injection techniques to generate diverse attacks against LLM agents and to measure technique coverage rather than only attack success rate.
motivation: Existing adaptive red teamers optimize attack success rate (ASR), which rewards reusing a few effective techniques and leaves most of the attack space untested, so benchmarks and model hardening miss many failure modes.
method: For each scenario an attacker LLM writes an injection for every sub-technique in the PIAtlas taxonomy, then iteratively rewrites failed attempts using feedback from an LLM judge; the approach is training-free and plugs into existing benchmarks in place of fixed attack templates.
result: On AgentDojo and IPI Arena, AutoPI succeeds in all six taxonomy classes against Qwen3.6-35B and in over 90% of its techniques, and against Claude Haiku 5.5 it achieves 20–50% higher ASR and 25–400% higher class-level coverage than recent state-of-the-art adaptive red teamers without training.
conclusion: Coverage-aware, taxonomy-guided red teaming exposes more diverse vulnerabilities than ASR-maximizing attackers, and the released code and attacks support reproducible security evaluation of LLM agents.

title: A Topologist's Proof Of Krasnosel'skii's Bifurcation Theorem
authors: Nils Waterstraat Robert Skiba
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23262v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This note offers a proof of Krasnosel'skii's bifurcation theorem that bypasses the traditional machinery of nonlinear analysis: neither the Leray-Schauder degree nor the Lyapunov-Schmidt reduction is used. The argument rests only on elementary operator theory and straightforward vector-bundle topology, providing a topologist's perspective on a classical result in nonlinear functional analysis.
tldr: The note gives a new proof of Krasnosel'skii's bifurcation theorem using only elementary operator theory and vector-bundle topology, avoiding Leray-Schauder degree and Lyapunov-Schmidt reduction.
motivation: Classical proofs of Krasnosel'skii's bifurcation theorem rely on heavy machinery from nonlinear functional analysis, and the authors aim to provide a more transparent, topologically motivated argument.
method: The proof combines elementary operator theory with straightforward vector-bundle topology, replacing the standard degree-theoretic and Lyapunov-Schmidt techniques.
result: A self-contained topological proof of Krasnosel'skii's bifurcation theorem is established without Leray-Schauder degree or Lyapunov-Schmidt reduction.
conclusion: The work offers a topologist's perspective on a classical nonlinear analysis result, potentially simplifying its exposition and accessibility.

title: Structure-Preserving Universal Differential Equations For Epidemic Dynamics
authors: Maia Martcheva Abdallah Alsammani
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23291v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Universal differential equations (UDEs) combine mechanistic epidemic models with learned neural closures, but generic additive corrections may violate essential epidemiological properties. We introduce a class of structure-preserving epidemic UDEs in which learned closures parameterize intercompartmental fluxes and the force of infection factorizes through infected compartments. This architecture guarantees positivity, population boundedness, and invariance of the disease-free set. We derive a rank-one next-generation matrix and a closed-form basic reproduction number determined by the learned rates at the disease-free equilibrium. Under explicit conditions, we establish results on threshold dynamics, disease-free and endemic equilibria, stability, and uniform persistence. For a neural SEIR model, center manifold analysis characterizes the direction of bifurcation through derivatives of the learned transmission rate. We further establish fundamental identifiability limitations: closures that agree on observed epidemic trajectories can yield different reproduction numbers and bifurcation types. Quantitative bounds relate uncertainty in the reproduction number to closure regularity and the distance of observations from the disease-free equilibrium, while monotonicity provides one-sided bounds. A numerical example involving three closures illustrates these results. Our findings provide a rigorous framework for epidemiologically consistent scientific machine learning and clarify which dynamical properties can be recovered from epidemic data.
tldr: The paper develops structure-preserving universal differential equations for epidemic modeling with guaranteed epidemiological properties and analyzes identifiability and threshold dynamics.
motivation: Generic neural closures in universal differential equations can violate basic epidemiological constraints such as positivity and boundedness, motivating a structure-preserving formulation.
method: Learned closures parameterize intercompartmental fluxes and the force of infection factorizes through infected compartments, enabling derivation of a rank-one next-generation matrix and closed-form reproduction number.
result: The authors establish positivity, boundedness, invariance, threshold dynamics, stability, persistence, and identifiability limitations linking closure agreement on observed trajectories to differing reproduction numbers and bifurcation types.
conclusion: The framework provides rigorous epidemiological consistency for scientific machine learning in epidemic dynamics and clarifies which dynamical properties are recoverable from data.

title: Taylor Coefficients And Duality For Finite Multiple T-values
authors: K. Srinivasa Raghava
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23315v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We express every normalized finite multiple [MATH]-value of positive even depth as the coefficient of [MATH] in an explicit iterated integral built from [MATH] and [MATH]. An analogous formula for odd-depth [MATH]-values, combined with reversal, gives a coefficient representation of [MATH] for every nonempty index [MATH]. The coefficients involved are [MATH]-integral without a restriction on the weight. For indices [MATH] with [MATH] odd, we obtain an explicit Bernoulli convolution. It yields a prime-by-prime proof of [MATH] for odd [MATH], and the corresponding identity with an [MATH]-value for even [MATH], whenever [MATH] and [MATH]. This proves the finite assertion of the first family in Cheng and Zhao's duality conjecture. We also establish uniform depth-two identities, evaluate the boundary cases, and explain the obstruction to the same termwise argument for [MATH].
tldr: Pure number theory paper expressing normalized finite multiple t-values as Taylor coefficients of explicit iterated integrals and proving a case of Cheng–Zhao's duality conjecture.
motivation: Multiple t-values and their finite (level-one) analogues are central objects in modern multiple zeta value theory, and duality conjectures relating them remain largely open.
method: Constructs explicit iterated integrals in terms of two generating functions, extracts Taylor coefficients to represent finite multiple t-values of even and odd depth, and uses Bernoulli convolutions to obtain prime-by-prime identities.
result: Derives coefficient representations for all nonempty indices, an explicit Bernoulli convolution for odd weights, and proves the finite assertion of the first family in Cheng and Zhao's duality conjecture, plus uniform depth-two identities.
conclusion: The work advances the algebraic/analytic theory of finite multiple t-values and duality, but is purely mathematical with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Error Analysis Of Deep Learning
authors: Yuling Jiao, Peiying Wu, Jerry Zhijian Yang, Pingwen Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23321v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This review examines deep learning theory through the lens of error decomposition, systematically addressing approximation, statistical, and optimization errors. We trace the development of error analyses from bounds on individual error components to frameworks that account for all three. Using nonparametric regression and the Deep Ritz Method as dual running examples, we demonstrate how these analyses apply across fundamentally different loss structures. We then review representative analyses in scientific machine learning, generative learning, reinforcement learning, representation learning, and large language models, showing how learning errors affect solutions, distributions, and predictions through problem-specific arguments. Throughout, we clarify which error components are controlled, how they are combined, and what assumptions are needed to obtain guarantees for trained networks.
tldr: This review organizes deep learning theory through approximation, statistical, and optimization error decomposition across several learning settings.
motivation: The paper aims to clarify how theoretical guarantees for deep neural networks are built from different error components and what assumptions underlie them.
method: It surveys error-analysis frameworks using nonparametric regression and the Deep Ritz Method as running examples, then reviews representative analyses in scientific machine learning, generative learning, reinforcement learning, representation learning, and large language models.
result: The review shows how controlled error components are combined in problem-specific ways to yield guarantees for trained networks across different loss structures.
conclusion: It provides a structured overview of deep learning error analysis but does not address quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Computing With Orientation-Dependent Vector Fields In Crystallographic Texture Analysis
authors: Erik W\"unsche Ralf Hielscher
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23328v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a computational framework for representing orientation-dependent vector fields. Building on (arXiv:2608.21235), we translate the differential-geometric formulation into crystallographic notation and focus on its computational use in crystallographic texture analysis. In crystallographic applications, small orientation changes are commonly described by rotation vectors, spin tensors, or infinitesimal misorientations. By contrast, vector fields in harmonic computations are usually represented by components with respect to Euler-angle derivatives, following the classical formulation of generalized spherical harmonics. This representation is convenient but numerically unfavorable. We instead use rotation-vector components, extending a familiar description of individual orientation changes to orientation-dependent vector fields. In this representation, vector fields are described by three scalar component functions, which can be expanded into generalized spherical harmonics. We derive frequency-domain formulas for gradient, divergence, and curl, enabling their evaluation directly on harmonic coefficients. In particular, the gradient of a band-limited scalar function remains band-limited with the same bandwidth.
tldr: The paper presents a computational framework for representing orientation-dependent vector fields in rotation-vector components and expands them in generalized spherical harmonics for crystallographic texture analysis.
motivation: Crystallographic texture analysis requires numerically stable representations of orientation-dependent vector fields; the classical Euler-angle-derivative component representation is convenient but numerically unfavorable.
method: Building on a prior differential-geometric formulation, the authors recast vector fields in crystallographic notation using rotation-vector components, express them as three scalar functions expanded in generalized spherical harmonics, and derive frequency-domain formulas for gradient, divergence, and curl acting directly on harmonic coefficients.
result: The framework yields explicit frequency-domain operators for gradient, divergence, and curl on harmonic coefficients, and shows that the gradient of a band-limited scalar function remains band-limited with unchanged bandwidth.
conclusion: The rotation-vector-based harmonic framework provides a numerically favorable and computationally practical tool for texture analysis, though it lies entirely outside quantum information science.

title: Gram's Law For Moving Targets Of The Riemann Zeta-function
authors: Ryan Goulden
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23332v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the solutions of [MATH] for targets [MATH] that grow with [MATH], and Gram's law for them: the statement that each shifted Gram interval contains exactly one solution. The deviation from Gram's law is an integer phase-slip counter, equal up to rounding to [MATH], where [MATH] and [MATH] is a balance abscissa determined by the target. If [MATH] with [MATH], where [MATH], and [MATH] converges, then every sufficiently high shifted Gram interval contains exactly one solution, which is simple; this localises the fixed points of [MATH]. The threshold is sharp: for [MATH] with [MATH], Gram's law fails in [MATH] intervals up to height [MATH], and for [MATH] it fails infinitely often but with density zero. In both ranges the counter has an explicit limiting distribution. For targets growing more slowly than any power, such as [MATH], the solutions lie on average [MATH] to the left of the critical line. If [MATH], the proportion of solutions to the right of the line tends to [MATH], whereas for fixed targets Selberg conjectured a quarter, and the counting error at the shifted Gram points is asymptotically Gaussian with variance [MATH]. For [MATH] the solutions follow neither [MATH] nor the zeros of [MATH]. All results are unconditional; numerical computations for [MATH] illustrate how slowly they take effect.
tldr: An unconditional analytic number theory study of Gram's law for moving targets of the Riemann zeta-function, characterizing when shifted Gram intervals contain exactly one solution.
motivation: Gram's law and the distribution of zeta zeros relative to the critical line are classical questions in analytic number theory, and the author extends them to targets that grow with height rather than fixed targets.
method: Analytic estimates of the argument of the zeta-function, an integer phase-slip counter quantifying deviations from Gram's law, and sharp threshold analysis on the growth rate of the target, supplemented by numerical computation.
result: Sharp thresholds are established: for sufficiently convergent targets every high shifted Gram interval contains exactly one simple solution, while for faster-growing targets Gram's law fails with an explicit limiting distribution of the counter; slow-growing targets yield solutions displaced on average to the left of the critical line.
conclusion: The results localize fixed points of the zeta-function and reveal a transition in the statistics of zeros for moving targets, with all results unconditional.

title: A Study Of Fixed Versus Adaptive Step Sizes For Phasor Dynamics Simulations
authors: Steven B. Roberts, Luke Lowery, Slaven Peles, Adam Birchfield, Carol S. Woodward
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23424v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transient phasor dynamics simulations model the response of power systems to disturbances using differential-algebraic equations (DAEs). Fixed-step integration is widely used to solve these DAEs numerically, but a step size suitable for resolving a fault transient may be unnecessarily small during the rest of a simulation. In this work, we provide a quantitative comparison of fixed and adaptive backward differentiation formulas on a suite of seven grid test cases ranging from 200 to 70,000 buses. Adaptive step sizes automatically shrink near faults, perturbations, and controller limits, and grow during less active portions of the simulation. At the global error achieved by a fixed quarter-cycle step size, adaptive results give 1.8 to 2.6 times speedups. Local error distributions, step size profiles, and work-precision plots show how accuracy, nonlinear solver, and step selection contribute to these differences. The results establish adaptive integration as the preferred approach for these simulations.
tldr: A quantitative comparison of fixed-step versus adaptive-step backward differentiation formula integrators for transient phasor-domain power grid simulations, showing 1.8–2.6x speedups with adaptive stepping.
motivation: Fixed-step integration of power-system differential-algebraic equations is forced to use small steps to resolve fault transients, wasting computation during quiet periods of the simulation.
method: Adaptive BDF integrators are benchmarked against fixed-step integration on seven grid test cases from 200 to 70,000 buses, with local error distributions, step-size profiles, and work-precision plots used to attribute performance differences.
result: At the global error level of a fixed quarter-cycle step size, adaptive stepping yields speedups of 1.8 to 2.6 times while automatically shrinking steps near faults and controller limits and enlarging them elsewhere.
conclusion: Adaptive integration is established as the preferred numerical approach for transient phasor dynamics simulations of power systems.

title: A Graph-Theoretic Framework For Identifying Mathematical Programming Decompositions
authors: Nicholas N. Kalamaris (department Of Chemical And Biological Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA), Christos T. Maravelias
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23472v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a framework for identifying combinations of complicating variables and/or constraints that can be used to formulate mathematical programming decompositions. A mathematical program is represented by a graph which accounts for the structural and functional relationship between variables and constraints. Graph projections are used to focus on variable- or constraint-based decompositions. A series of coarsening operations is used to generate a reduced graph based on the original or projected graph. On the reduced graph, we use integer programming to identify different combinations of complicating variables and/or constraints. Specifically, variables and constraints are identified as complicating based on their structural role and/or their functionality (contribution to nonlinearity) in the mathematical program. The framework allows us to assess the viability of different decomposition types (variable, constraint, cross) and identify multiple potential decomposition formulations of the same type (e.g. different combinations of complicating variables for Benders decomposition). The systematic nature of our framework facilitates broader studies into the efficacy of different decompositions across a range of problems including energy markets, process design, and machine learning.
tldr: This paper introduces a graph-theoretic framework for automatically identifying complicating variables and constraints that enable mathematical programming decompositions such as Benders or Lagrangian decomposition.
motivation: Selecting which variables or constraints to designate as complicating is largely done heuristically; the authors aim to systematize this choice so that different decomposition types and alternative formulations can be compared rigorously.
method: A mathematical program is represented as a graph capturing structural and functional relations between variables and constraints; graph projections isolate variable- or constraint-based views, coarsening reduces the graph, and integer programming then selects sets of complicating variables/constraints based on structural role and nonlinearity contribution.
result: The framework evaluates the viability of variable, constraint, and cross decompositions and enumerates multiple candidate decomposition formulations of the same type for a given problem instance.
conclusion: The approach provides a systematic tool for decomposition design, enabling broader empirical studies of decomposition efficacy in domains such as energy markets, process design, and machine learning.

title: Optimal Control Of Rkhs Diffeomorphic Flows For Classification And Generative Modeling
authors: Andreas Mang Christopher Chukwuemeka
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23497v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a unified optimal-control framework that solves supervised classification and likelihood-based density estimation with a single diffeomorphic flow whose velocity lives in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS); the two tasks share all structure except the objective. Variable projection eliminates the terminal model (a classifier, or a Gaussian-mixture (GMM) reference), leaving a reduced control problem whose gradient comes from an analytic discrete adjoint. The RKHS parameterization makes the flow's divergence exact and deterministic at the cost of one kernel matrix-vector product, avoiding the stochastic trace estimators and potential-flow restrictions of existing continuous normalizing flows. Because the objective and gradient are deterministic, matrix-free reduced Gauss-Newton (GN) and related second-order solvers are practical for both tasks, which we benchmark against a range of first- and second-order optimizers; the learned map is a diffeomorphism with explicitly controlled regularity. In experiments from dimension 2 to 256, the reduced GN solvers use the fewest iterations of any optimizer tested and, together with joint L-BFGS, the least work; a multiscale kernel improves the density fit, and a trainable GMM reference reduces the deformation needed for multimodal transport at comparable likelihood while lowering the likelihood on real data. The full-model solve is quadratic in the particle count and sub-linear in dimension; a control-point reduction makes the particle-count scaling linear at near-lossless accuracy.
tldr: A unified optimal-control framework learns a single RKHS-parameterized diffeomorphic flow for both supervised classification and density estimation, with exact divergence and matrix-free Gauss-Newton solvers.
motivation: Continuous normalizing flows typically rely on stochastic trace estimators and potential-flow restrictions; the authors seek a deterministic, exact-divergence formulation amenable to second-order optimization and shared across classification and generative tasks.
method: The velocity field lives in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, making the flow divergence exact via one kernel matrix-vector product; variable projection eliminates the terminal classifier or GMM reference, yielding a reduced control problem with analytic discrete-adjoint gradients solved by reduced Gauss-Newton.
result: In dimensions 2 to 256 the reduced GN solvers need the fewest iterations (with joint L-BFGS the least work), multiscale kernels improve density fit, and a control-point reduction makes particle-count scaling linear at near-lossless accuracy.
conclusion: RKHS-based diffeomorphic flows with deterministic objectives enable practical second-order optimal control for both classification and generative modeling, though trainable GMM references can lower likelihood on real data.

title: Spectral Stability And Convergence Of The Unnormalized Graph Laplacian On Noisy Point Clouds
authors: Yariv Aizenbud Daniel Ageev
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23573v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The first eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the unnormalized graph Laplacian of clean samples from a manifold, suitably scaled, approximate those of a weighted Laplace-Beltrami operator. However, the samples are usually observed with noise and therefore need not lie on the manifold. We build the clean and noisy graph Laplacians, with bandwidth [MATH], on the clean samples and on the noisy observations, where the noise is arbitrary but bounded by [MATH]. We show that, with high probability, the first eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the noisy graph Laplacian are close to those of the clean one: the eigenvalues within [MATH], and the subspaces spanned by the first eigenvectors within [MATH], whether or not the eigenvalues are simple. Consequently, if [MATH] is small enough relative to [MATH], the noisy graph Laplacian approximates the weighted Laplace-Beltrami operator at the same rate as the clean one. We also show that, for large noise, we can get the same rate as the clean graph Laplacian by first using a denoiser, and then building the graph Laplacian on the denoised observations.
tldr: The paper proves spectral stability of the unnormalized graph Laplacian built on noisy point clouds, showing eigenvalues and eigenvector subspaces approximate those of the clean Laplacian and the weighted Laplace-Beltrami operator.
motivation: Graph Laplacians on manifold samples are known to approximate Laplace-Beltrami operators, but real data is noisy and may leave the manifold, so stability under bounded noise needs theoretical guarantees.
method: Clean and noisy graph Laplacians with bandwidth are constructed from clean samples and observations with arbitrary noise bounded by a parameter; high-probability perturbation bounds on eigenvalues and eigenspaces are derived, plus a denoising preprocessing step for large noise.
result: Eigenvalues are close within explicit tolerance and spans of leading eigenvectors are close whether or not eigenvalues are simple; when noise is small relative to bandwidth, the noisy Laplacian matches the clean convergence rate to the Laplace-Beltrami operator, and denoising recovers this rate for large noise.
conclusion: Noisy graph Laplacians remain spectrally faithful to their clean counterparts, justifying manifold-learning spectral methods on noisy data and providing a principled denoising strategy.

title: Benchmarking Traditional And Learning-Based Reference-Free Compressors For Long-Read Sequencing Data
authors: Huidong Ma, Hui Sun, Xinyan Shi, Cheng Zhong, Xiaoguang Liu, Gang Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23794v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-read sequencing technologies generate large volumes of data, creating substantial storage and transmission demands. Although reference-based compressors can achieve high compression, their reliance on an appropriate reference genome limits their use. We present LRCBench, a benchmark and survey of reference-free lossless compressors for long-read sequencing data. We review traditional and learning-based general-purpose and sequencing-specific methods, then evaluate 35 compressors on 16 real-world datasets from Oxford Nanopore and PacBio platforms. We compare compression ratio, storage savings, runtime, peak memory use, and robustness across datasets. Learning-based compressors are evaluated on six MinION datasets because of their high computational costs. CoLoRd achieves the best overall compression ratios in our experiments, while other methods offer trade-offs in speed, memory use, and robustness. We also examine multithreaded speedup and discuss future directions in parallel acceleration, privacy protection, adaptive parameter tuning, and hardware-algorithm co-design.
tldr: LRCBench benchmarks 35 traditional and learning-based reference-free lossless compressors on 16 long-read sequencing datasets from Oxford Nanopore and PacBio platforms.
motivation: Long-read sequencing produces massive data volumes and reference-based compressors depend on a suitable reference genome, so a systematic assessment of reference-free alternatives is needed.
method: The authors survey general-purpose and sequencing-specific compressors and evaluate them on real datasets, comparing compression ratio, storage savings, runtime, peak memory, and robustness, with learning-based methods tested on six MinION datasets and multithreaded speedup also examined.
result: CoLoRd achieves the best overall compression ratios, while other compressors trade off speed, memory use, and robustness across datasets.
conclusion: The benchmark identifies practical trade-offs among reference-free compressors and outlines future directions in parallel acceleration, privacy protection, adaptive parameter tuning, and hardware-algorithm co-design.

title: Image Watermarking With Memory Across Reissuance
authors: Xinyuan Li, Yi Nian, Xiaoqin Feng, Tiankai Yang, Yue Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23363v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Publishers often revise and reissue images, yet valid watermarks may persist on superseded releases or unapproved edits. Even a current release can contain regions last authorized at different revisions. We introduce and formalize reissuable provenance: determining an image's current, superseded, or unissued status and recovering each region's last authorized revision (its generation), with abstention when evidence is insufficient. Generational Stratigraphy Fields (GSF) combine watermark evidence with an authenticated live reference to the current release, enabling replacement or retirement without rewriting circulated copies. Each reissue freshly embeds new generation labels in approved regions and inherited labels elsewhere, preserving history without requiring old watermarks to survive successive edits.
