Our complete-output reissuance evaluation follows 480 histories through four releases, retaining each AI editor's entire output. GSF achieves 99.67% accuracy in classifying issued images as current or superseded and 94.09% recall of unissued edits. After three reissues, one generation map provides time and location: it recovers regional labels with 93.13% median accuracy and localizes the latest approved revision with 92.86% IoU. Regional labels remain readable under tested delivery transformations that impair issued-state recognition. Watermarks can thus express who issued an image, which release is authoritative now, and when each region was last authorized.
tldr: The paper introduces 'reissuable provenance' and Generational Stratigraphy Fields (GSF) for tracking which revision of a reissued image is authoritative and when each region was last authorized.
motivation: Publishers revise and reissue images, so valid watermarks can persist on superseded or unapproved edits, and a single current release may contain regions authorized at different revisions — a provenance gap current watermarking does not address.
method: GSF combines watermark evidence with an authenticated live reference to the current release, freshly embedding new generation labels in approved regions on each reissue while inheriting labels elsewhere, and evaluates complete-output reissuance over 480 histories across four releases.
result: GSF classifies issued images as current vs. superseded with 99.67% accuracy and recalls unissued edits at 94.09%; after three reissues it recovers regional labels at 93.13% median accuracy and localizes the latest approved revision at 92.86% IoU, with labels readable under tested delivery transformations.
conclusion: Watermarks can encode who issued an image, which release is authoritative, and when each region was last authorized, without requiring old watermarks to survive successive edits.

title: ACaM: Automated Capability Modeling For Agentic Ai Security
authors: Monika Santra, Dhilung Kirat, Qiushi Wu, Kevin Eykholt, Xiaokui Shu, Ian Molloy
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23507v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In agentic AI systems, an LLM invokes tools that hold standing access to credentials, private data, filesystems, and external services. Such agents are increasingly deployed without an answer to a basic question: what can an agent access, exfiltrate, and propagate, independent of what it is designed for or is observed to do? The question goes unanswered because existing approaches trust a tool's natural-language description as a proxy for its behavior. But nothing enforces that the description and its implementation agree. This gap is known as Description-Code Inconsistency (DCI). DCI enables a threat class called capability laundering, in which a tool's implementation contains dangerous behavior that its description omits. The behavior may come from incidental drift or a supply-chain compromise. It runs silently whenever an LLM invokes the tool for its stated, benign purpose. We present ACaM, a neurosymbolic approach to capability modeling that derives each tool's capabilities from its code, so a laundered capability cannot hide behind a benign description. In ACaM, static analysis grounds an LLM in code-derived facts, and no LLM output can override a fact that static analysis has established. The LLM supplies only the behavioral meaning that those facts cannot express. ACaM compiles agent source code into the Agent Capability Property Graph (ACPG) and uses it to reconstruct threat chains that span multiple tool calls. We evaluate ACaM on 43 real-world agents, including 9 multi-agent systems. On 24 manually annotated agents, it recovers capability properties with 98.3% macro-F1 and reconstructs injected threat chains with a score of 0.980, 8 points above the strongest baseline. Applied to all 43 unmodified agents, it discovers hundreds of structural vulnerabilities, ten of which we confirm with proof-of-concept exploits.
tldr: ACaM is a neurosymbolic static-analysis-plus-LLM framework that derives the true capabilities of tools invoked by agentic AI systems, exposing description-code inconsistencies and 'capability laundering'.
motivation: Agentic LLM systems grant tools standing access to credentials, data and services, yet security analysis relies on tools' natural-language descriptions, which need not match their implementations; this gap (Description-Code Inconsistency) enables hidden malicious behavior.
method: The authors ground an LLM in code-derived facts from static analysis, compiling agent source into an Agent Capability Property Graph (ACPG) from which multi-tool threat chains are reconstructed, with the LLM supplying only behavioral semantics that static facts cannot express.
result: On 24 manually annotated agents ACaM recovers capability properties with 98.3% macro-F1 and reconstructs injected threat chains at 0.980, 8 points above the strongest baseline; across 43 unmodified agents it finds hundreds of structural vulnerabilities, ten confirmed by proof-of-concept exploits.
conclusion: Code-grounded capability modeling closes the description-code trust gap and provides a practical automated auditing method for agentic AI security.

title: FlowSH: Detecting Web Attacks By Correlating Anomalous Network Flows And Endpoint Logs
authors: Nuno Dur\~ao, Rodrigo Branco, Vinicius V. Cogo, Ib\'eria Medeiros
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23669v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Web applications compose the core of internet services, rendering them prominent targets for audacious attackers. Among web attacks, SQL injection (SQLi) remains a persistent, damaging web applications connected to databases. The widespread adoption of HTTPS has been a critical advancement for online security, ensuring the confidentiality and integrity of communications by encrypting network payloads. However, it also renders traditional Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) less effective, as these typically rely on packet inspection of plaintext traffic. To access encrypted payloads, some NIDS resort to TLS-interception proxies, which leads to data leaks and security risks. This paper presents FlowSH, a system for detecting web attacks that is agnostic to whether the traffic is encrypted (HTTPS) or not (HTTP). Rather than decrypting packets in transit, FlowSH correlates flow-level metadata (NetFlows) with endpoint logs, which inherently contain decrypted payloads after reaching the web server. The system combines unsupervised machine learning to flag anomalous NetFlows and similarity search over server-side logs using Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH) to confirm attacks. We implemented and evaluated FlowSH in a testbed with multiple web scanners and demonstrated its detection effectiveness, detecting 70% of SQLi attacks missed by ModSecurity, a leading web application firewall.
tldr: FlowSH detects web attacks such as SQL injection by correlating flow-level network metadata with server-side endpoint logs, avoiding TLS interception.
motivation: HTTPS encryption blinds traditional network intrusion detection systems to payload contents, and decrypting traffic via TLS-interception proxies introduces data-leak and security risks.
method: The system flags anomalous NetFlows with unsupervised machine learning and then confirms attacks via locality-sensitive-hashing similarity search over the web server's own logs, which contain decrypted payloads.
result: In a testbed with multiple web scanners, FlowSH detected 70% of SQLi attacks that were missed by ModSecurity, a leading web application firewall.
conclusion: Correlating encrypted-traffic metadata with endpoint logs offers an effective, encryption-agnostic detection layer complementary to existing WAFs.

title: Jev Vs. LLMs: A Comparative Analysis For Phishing Email Detection
authors: Muhammad Mahir Malik, Muhammad Moiz Khalid, Hussain Ahmad, Faheem Ullah
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Phishing remains a major source of credential theft and fraudulent payments, and email security systems must classify large message volumes reliably, quickly, and at manageable cost. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer flexible text understanding, but their token-based generation increases response time and API cost, and the reliability of their confidence values requires measurement. Jev 1.13, a typed decision model from TypeSafe AI, instead returns a structured outcome with a confidence value. This paper compares Jev 1.13 with Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra, and Meta Llama 4 Maverick on a labelled dataset of 1500 emails, covering classification performance, decision latency, token consumption, API cost, and probability calibration. Jev achieves the highest accuracy (79.67%), precision (71.43%), recall (97.97%), and F1 score (82.62%). It also records the shortest batch time (173.88 seconds), the lowest token count (597,895), the lowest cost (USD 0.015103 per 1000 decisions), and the lowest Brier score (0.1698) and ECE (0.1594). These results suggest that Jev is a promising option for fast, structured, high-volume triage. LLMs retain the advantage of generating explanations, which we do not evaluate, and all four systems require further validation before standalone deployment.
tldr: A comparative benchmark of a structured typed decision model (Jev 1.13) versus three large language models for phishing email detection, evaluating accuracy, latency, token cost, and calibration.
motivation: Phishing causes credential theft and fraudulent payments, and email filters must classify high volumes quickly and cheaply; LLM token-based generation is slow and costly and its confidence values are unverified, motivating an alternative structured classifier.
method: Jev 1.13 is compared against Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra, and Meta Llama 4 Maverick on a labelled dataset of 1500 emails, measuring classification metrics, decision latency, token consumption, API cost, Brier score, and ECE.
result: Jev attains the best accuracy (79.67%), precision (71.43%), recall (97.97%), F1 (82.62%), shortest batch time (173.88 s), lowest token count and cost (USD 0.015103 per 1000 decisions), and best calibration (Brier 0.1698, ECE 0.1594).
conclusion: Jev appears promising for fast, structured, high-volume triage, while LLMs retain the advantage of generating explanations; all systems need further validation before standalone deployment.

title: Rational Ensemble Logic For Cohort Discovery With Real-World Electrophysiology Data
authors: Guo-Qiang Zhang, Xubing Hao, Yan Huang, Xiaojin Li, Licong Cui
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23708v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Biomedical knowledge representation should make the passage from observations to conclusions transparent, rigorous, understandable, explainable, and reproducible (TRUER). We introduce Rational Ensemble Logic (QEL) for specifying temporal phenotypes in real-world electrophysiology data (RWED), with a meaning independent of the implementation software. QEL combines three parameterized modal operators (exact displacement, bounded existence, and bounded universality) over rational time with Boolean connectives and first-order quantification. Its Labeled Interval Ensemble (LINE) semantics represents annotated records as finite interval ensembles. We relate the operators to morphological operations and develop endpoint-array algorithms and finite rational evidence sets for model checking. We prove closure and semantic correctness of the interval operations, obtain finite evidence sets by quantifier elimination, and establish polynomial data complexity for fixed formulas. On 54 manually constructed records, a prototype agreed with the assigned outcomes for base and strict post-ictal generalized EEG suppression (PGES) queries. A separate feasibility experiment over 1,976 patients identified 37 qualifying patients and 45 annotation patterns in 16 seconds. The released prototype uses endpoint candidates and numerical tolerances. QEL supports the TRUER principle through explicit phenotype definitions, precise semantics, and provably correct evaluation procedures, with rational witnesses for existential queries. These provide a logical foundation for formal specification and correctness of algorithms that are independent of specific clinical interpretation, data annotation quality, and software implementation.
tldr: The paper introduces Rational Ensemble Logic (QEL), a temporal modal logic with interval-ensemble semantics for specifying and querying clinical phenotypes in real-world electrophysiology data.
motivation: Biomedical knowledge representation needs to make the step from observations to conclusions transparent, rigorous, and reproducible, which requires precise, implementation-independent phenotype specifications for messy clinical time series.
method: QEL combines three parameterized modal operators (exact displacement, bounded existence, bounded universality) over rational time with Boolean connectives and first-order quantification, interpreted via Labeled Interval Ensemble (LINE) semantics with endpoint-array algorithms and finite rational evidence sets for model checking.
result: The authors prove closure and semantic correctness of the interval operations, obtain finite evidence sets by quantifier elimination, and establish polynomial data complexity; a prototype matched assigned outcomes on 54 manually constructed EEG records and identified 37 qualifying patients with 45 annotation patterns among 1,976 patients in 16 seconds.
conclusion: QEL provides a provably correct logical foundation for formal phenotype specification that is independent of clinical interpretation, annotation quality, and software implementation.

title: Expressiveness And Convertibility Of Rule-Based Access Control Policies
authors: Amir Masoumzadeh, Paliath Narendran, Padmavathi Iyer
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23738v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rule-based access control models such as attribute-based access control support flexible policies based on rules with conditional expressions. The design choices in those models such as what is allowed in the conditional expressions or supporting deny rules may impact the range of the policies that are expressible. In this paper, we propose a systematic approach to investigate the semantics and compare the expressiveness of various rule-based access control models that can be built based on different design choices of rule structure and rule composition. Furthermore, we investigate the problem of convertibility of a policy from one rule-based model to another. This question is critical for policy migration to ensure that a given policy instance in a source model is expressible in a target model. Some of our major results in this paper include well-formedness properties for policy semantics, expressiveness hierarchy of models, and computational complexity of policy convertibility, all having important implications on the design and application of rule-based access control policy models.
tldr: The paper develops a systematic semantic framework for comparing the expressiveness of rule-based access control models such as ABAC and analyzes the complexity of converting policies between them.
motivation: Design choices in rule-based access control models (conditional expression syntax, deny rules, rule composition) affect which policies are expressible, yet no systematic comparison of expressiveness existed, which matters for policy migration.
method: The authors formalize policy semantics for several rule-based model variants, establish well-formedness properties, and derive an expressiveness hierarchy along with complexity results for policy convertibility.
result: They obtain well-formedness guarantees for policy semantics, a hierarchy ordering the expressive power of the model variants, and complexity classifications for deciding whether a policy in a source model is expressible in a target model.
conclusion: The results give designers principled guidance on rule structure and composition choices and provide a basis for reasoning about policy migration between access control models.

title: When Do Decision Models Help LLM-Driven Network Discovery?
authors: Alperen \"orsdemir, Rochelle Xenia Mendoza Santos, Wen Shei Ong, Matthew Caesar, Ertem Esiner
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23947v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Network discovery, the identification of live hosts and their exposed services, is the first phase of every penetration test, and it is increasingly automated by harnesses driven by large language models (LLMs). To mitigate hallucinated or unsafe commands, recent work proposes inserting fast, non-generative decision models to validate actions prior to execution. This paper quantifies whether such validation improves discovery across three network scales (n = 10, 100, and 1,000) in a simulation calibrated on a 30-node containerized testbed. Our findings show that chunked batch dispatch recovers 92% to 100% of open ports in large-scale networks, whereas single-host dispatch collapses to under 6% due to context saturation and scan latency. Furthermore, at the measured proposal quality of the local model, decision gating increases its port recall from 75.5% to 89.0% on small networks and intercepts costly decoy tarpits, but it imposes additional latency on frontier models during early host discovery.
tldr: The paper empirically evaluates whether inserting fast non-generative decision models to gate LLM-proposed commands improves automated network discovery (host/port scanning) across simulated network scales of 10, 100, and 1,000 nodes.
motivation: LLM-driven penetration-testing harnesses risk issuing hallucinated or unsafe commands, so recent proposals interpose local decision models as validators; it is unclear whether this validation actually helps discovery and at what cost.
method: Simulation calibrated on a 30-node containerized testbed, comparing chunked batch versus single-host dispatch and comparing gated versus ungated (frontier-model) execution for port recall, latency, and decoy-tarpit interception.
result: Chunked batch dispatch recovers 92-100% of open ports at large scale while single-host dispatch collapses below 6% due to context saturation and scan latency; decision gating raises local-model port recall from 75.5% to 89.0% on small networks and blocks tarpits but adds latency for frontier models in early discovery.
conclusion: Decision-model gating is beneficial for weaker local models and small networks and for safety against decoys, but is not uniformly advantageous; dispatch strategy and context limits dominate large-scale discovery performance.

title: Intent Contracts: Taking Tools Away From Agents
authors: Ziyuan Wang, Genliang Zhu, Xiaobo Chen, Chu Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.24025v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Intent contracts are an authorization interface for tool-using LLM agents in which the planning model holds no tools. For each step it submits a short logged contract: a goal, a verbatim quotation of the user, and scope fields. Code validates the contract, and a small trusted model checks it against the user's words and writes the tool call itself. Provided the validation and dispatch code is correct, every executed call is written by the trusted model, the planner's influence on a call is confined to a contract logged before it, and the trusted side decides how much of a request to carry out. We compare contracts with two reviewers of planner-written commands: one sees only the user's words and the command, the information boundary of a reasoning-blind permission classifier, and one also sees the planner's goal and a checked quotation. With gpt-6.1-terra as planner and GLM-5.3-Flash as the trusted model on three AmPermBench task families, every object changed under contracts is named in the goal of the contract that produced the change; under review the planner names objects in its commands and rarely in its goals. When the planner adds work the user never asked for, contracts complete the user's task in 27/30 runs and the intent-visible reviewer in 16/30, because a reviewer can only refuse a whole command. Contracts do not reduce unauthorized actions. They are indistinguishable from blind review, and once the benchmark's environment terms are clarified, every condition that changes state hits a wrong target in 40-49% of those runs. That error is the planner's choice of objects for an ambiguous reference, which no trusted model here can see the environment to check; telling the executor to decline when unsure does not change it. We evaluate benign over-reach with one pair of models, not adversarial planners. We release the plugin and run records.
tldr: The paper proposes 'intent contracts', an authorization interface where a planner LLM that holds no tools submits short logged contracts (goal, verbatim user quotation, scope) validated by code and checked by a small trusted model that itself writes the tool call.
motivation: Tool-using LLM agents expose a risk when the planner directly emits commands; the authors aim to constrain the planner's influence on executed actions and give a trusted component control over how much of a user request is carried out.
method: Contracts are compared against two reviewers of planner-written commands — a blind (reasoning-blind) permission classifier and an intent-visible reviewer — using gpt-6.1-terra as planner and GLM-5.3-Flash as trusted model across three AmPermBench task families, with logging of every executed call.
result: Under contracts every object changed is named in the producing contract's goal, and contracts complete user tasks in 27/30 runs versus 16/30 for the intent-visible reviewer when the planner over-reaches; however contracts do not reduce unauthorized actions and are indistinguishable from blind review, with 40–49% of state-changing runs hitting a wrong target under ambiguous references.
conclusion: Intent contracts improve traceability and task completion for benign over-reach but provide no security benefit against unauthorized actions, and ambiguous-reference errors remain invisible to trusted models that cannot see the environment.

title: Evaluating Lim Trading Agents: A Critical Review Of Backtesting Validity And Reporting Practices
authors: Long Xu, Fuyi Wang, Xiaolu Hu, Chao Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.24133v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in investment research, and many studies report promising historical returns. However, such results are only credible if researchers can demonstrate that the model used only information available at the time, account for how strategies and configurations were selected, and explain how reported returns were generated. We identify six common threats to validity in LLM investment evaluations and apply them to 18 published studies. Across 108 assessments, we find substantial gaps in reporting. No paper fully addresses information timing, model-memory exposure, universe selection, trading costs, or configuration-selection bias. Only four studies provide minimum evidence that results hold across multiple market periods. Our analysis reveals that commonly used safeguards often address different problems than researchers assume. For example, using dated inputs does not guarantee that a pretrained model lacked knowledge of future events, and repeated experimental runs do not correct for strategy-selection bias. We therefore propose an evaluation protocol for future LLM investment research. Rather than judging whether LLMs can generate profits, our study examines whether existing evidence is sufficient to support such claims. We conclude that current reporting practices are generally insufficient for that purpose.
tldr: A critical review identifying six validity threats in evaluations of LLM-based investment/trading agents and auditing 18 published studies against them.
motivation: Many papers claim LLM trading agents yield profitable historical returns, but such claims are only credible if information timing, model memory exposure, configurational selection bias, and cost accounting are properly controlled and reported.
method: The authors define six common threats to validity, then apply them to 18 published studies, producing 108 individual assessments of reporting practice, and illustrate why common safeguards (dated inputs, repeated runs) fail to address the intended problems.
result: Substantial reporting gaps were found: no paper fully addresses information timing, model-memory exposure, universe selection, trading costs, or configuration-selection bias, and only four studies provide minimal evidence of robustness across multiple market periods.
conclusion: Current reporting practices are insufficient to support claims that LLMs can generate profits, and the authors propose an evaluation protocol for future LLM investment research.

title: Guarding The Kingdom Of Skill-Based Agents In The Ai Dynasty Of Computation: Control-Flow Integrity For Agent Skills
authors: Bonan Ruan, Yuhao Sun, Jiahao Liu, Qixiao Lin, Jian Mao, Zhenkai Liang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.24185v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Control-flow integrity (CFI) confines a program to a control-flow graph fixed ahead of time. Procedural agent skills move this control flow into prompt text, and a large language model (LLM) agent decides at runtime whether each step runs in its reasoning, a tool call, or a script. The procedure's control skeleton survives, but its enforceability depends on where each step runs. Many violations, such as overwriting a file before validation, use only operations the skill requires, so permission allowlists admit them. A deviating or prompt-injected model can also evade a monitor by regime migration, for example by claiming that a check passed. We present SkillCFI, which carries CFI over to skill-based agents. Its compiler confines LLM interpretation to compile time and derives the agent's instructions and an executable contract from one skill. By a formal enforceability criterion, it enforces obligations whose evidence crosses the tool boundary and rejects a skill whose mandatory obligation leaves nothing to check. A deterministic runtime enforcer admits a tool request only on trusted evidence and refuses unmediated channels such as inline scripts, so admitted traces follow the contract whatever the model proposes. On eight self-written skills, no compiled contract permits more than its source under 24 source mutations. In 770 agent sessions, SkillCFI blocks before dispatch all 240 such violations, which an allowlist admits, and normal tasks complete nearly as often as without it. Listing the next legal steps in a refusal raises recovery from 21% to 65%. Checking takes about 2% of task time, and a compact command form cuts session slowdown from 1.32 times to 1.08 times. None of 53 public skills is accepted as written. The compiler's diagnostics point to interfaces rather than workflows and guided seven into enforceable contracts.
tldr: SkillCFI adapts control-flow integrity from program analysis to LLM-based procedural agents, compiling skill prompts into enforceable contracts enforced by a deterministic runtime monitor.
motivation: Procedural agent skills encode control flow in prompt text, and permission allowlists fail to catch violations that reuse only permitted operations, while prompt-injected models can migrate between reasoning, tool-call, and script regimes to evade monitoring.
method: A compiler confines LLM interpretation to compile time and derives instructions plus an executable contract from a single skill using a formal enforceability criterion; a deterministic runtime enforcer admits tool requests only on trusted evidence and rejects unmediated channels such as inline scripts.
result: Across 24 source mutations and 770 agent sessions, SkillCFI blocked all 240 allowlist-admitted violations before dispatch, with normal task success nearly unchanged, ~2% checking overhead, and recovery improved from 21% to 65% when next legal steps are listed; none of 53 public skills was accepted unchanged.
conclusion: Control-flow integrity is a feasible and low-overhead defense for skill-based LLM agents, though the strict compiler requires most real-world skills to be refactored into enforceable contracts.

title: Erased But Recoverable: On The Fragility Of Concept Erasure Under Fine-Tuning
authors: Jun Li, Lizhi Xiong, Ziqiang Li, Yu Liu, Zenglin Shi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.24220v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing concept erasure methods for text-to-image diffusion models primarily focus on suppressing target concepts while preserving non-target generation quality. However, in practical applications, open-source diffusion models are often further adapted through DreamBooth, LoRA, or Custom Diffusion. Such adaptations can reshape internal representations, thereby weakening or even reversing the erasure effects achieved by existing methods. We identify erasure persistence as a key yet underexplored dimension of concept erasure and analyze how downstream fine-tuning reshapes internal representations. Our analysis reveals that fine-tuning of the original model does not uniformly modify the model, but preserves certain high-contribution structures, particularly attention heads with stable output subspaces and response magnitudes. We also observe that, after downstream fine-tuning of concept-erased models, these heads' output representations more readily realign with their pretrained counterparts. Motivated by this observation, we propose Stable-Head-Aware Concept Erasure (SHACE), which improves erasure persistence by preserving stable attention structures during concept erasure. SHACE identifies stability-critical attention heads through Attention-Head Stability Profiling and keeps their corresponding parameter blocks unchanged during erasure via Stable-Head Gradient Preservation. Extensive experiments show that SHACE improves resistance to concept recovery across diverse fine-tuning settings while maintaining strong suppression and non-target generation quality.
tldr: The paper studies how concept erasure in text-to-image diffusion models can be undone by downstream fine-tuning, and proposes SHACE, a method that preserves stable attention-head structures to improve erasure persistence.
motivation: Open-source diffusion models are frequently adapted via DreamBooth, LoRA, or Custom Diffusion, and such fine-tuning can weaken or reverse previously applied concept erasure, a failure mode the authors term erasure persistence.
method: The authors analyze how fine-tuning reshapes internal representations, finding that attention heads with stable output subspaces are preserved, and they introduce Attention-Head Stability Profiling plus Stable-Head Gradient Preservation to freeze stability-critical parameter blocks during erasure.
result: Extensive experiments show SHACE resists concept recovery across diverse fine-tuning settings while maintaining strong suppression of target concepts and good non-target generation quality.
conclusion: Erasure persistence should be treated as a key evaluation dimension for concept erasure, and structural preservation of stable attention heads offers a practical route to more robust erasure.

title: Pipette: Prompt Injection Purple-Teaming For Robust Llm Agents
authors: Lipeng He, Yihan Wang, Jiawen Zhang, N. Asokan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.24362v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents routinely interact with untrusted external data, exposing them to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks that hijack agents into executing attacker-chosen tasks. To uncover these vulnerabilities at scale, automated red-teaming methods often leverage reinforcement learning (RL) to generate attacks that achieve high attack success rates (ASR). Model developers use the attacks discovered during internal red-teaming to harden agents through adversarial training before deployment, a collaborative offensive-defensive process known in cybersecurity as purple-teaming. However, we show that achieving high ASR during red-teaming does not guarantee robustness gains from subsequent adversarial training. Specifically, we find that two state-of-the-art RL-based red-teaming methods, RL-Hammer and PISmith, suffer from mode collapse, repeatedly discovering similar attack strategies whose additional successes add no additional robustness improvements to adversarial training. To address this gap, we introduce PIPETTE, a unified prompt injection purple-teaming framework that effectively converts red-teaming discoveries into defender robustness improvements. PIPETTE employs a dictionary learning-based reward that encourages broader coverage of attack strategies during red-teaming. It also integrates an on-policy adversarial training pipeline tailored to IPI defense, enabling agents to resist attacks while completing legitimate user tasks. Extensive evaluations across agentic benchmarks (AgentDojo and ASB) demonstrate that PIPETTE produces defenders that achieve near-zero attack success rates on static attacks and can withstand strong adaptive attacks, while maintaining benign task utility close to that of the undefended baseline.
tldr: PIPETTE is a purple-teaming framework that improves indirect prompt-injection defenses for LLM agents by combining dictionary-learning-based reward shaping for red-teaming with on-policy adversarial training.
motivation: Existing RL-based automated red-teaming methods (RL-Hammer, PISmith) suffer from mode collapse, so high attack success rates during red-teaming do not translate into genuine robustness gains after adversarial training.
method: The authors introduce a dictionary-learning-based reward that rewards coverage of diverse attack strategies during red-teaming, and pair it with an on-policy adversarial training pipeline tailored to indirect prompt injection defense.
result: On AgentDojo and ASB benchmarks, defenders trained with PIPETTE reach near-zero attack success rates against static attacks, withstand strong adaptive attacks, and retain benign task utility close to the undefended baseline.
conclusion: Converting red-teaming discoveries into measurable robustness requires diversity-aware reward design; PIPETTE provides a unified purple-teaming loop for hardening LLM agents against prompt injection.

title: Drift-Aware Explainable Prioritization For Windows Pe Malware Forensic Triage With Semantic Consistency Checks
authors: Toqeer Ali Syed Mohammed A. Alharbi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.24474v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Forensic investigators must decide which suspicious files to examine first. Machine-learning (ML) and deep-learning (DL) malware detectors usually return a bare score that neither explains why a file deserves attention nor signals when changing data make the model unreliable. We present a framework for Windows Portable Executable (PE) malware forensic triage that works only on pre-extracted static features and never executes malware. A calibrated maliciousness score sets each file's triage priority, and a per-sample feature attribution explains the prediction. A per-sample consistency score measures whether the top attributed features agree with documented behaviors from the Malware Behavior Catalog (MBC) and MITRE Adversarial Tactics, Techniques & Common Knowledge (ATT&CK), where the available features support such interpretation. Conformal evaluation and statistical distribution tests flag drift. Each file receives one investigator-oriented triage output. The evaluation protocol, specified before testing, uses a time-ordered split of EMBER2024 as the primary dataset and BODMAS for family disjoint checks, and compares every component with simple baselines on predictive performance, prioritization effectiveness, explanation quality and robustness over time.
tldr: A machine-learning framework for prioritizing Windows PE malware samples in forensic triage, combining calibrated scores, feature attributions, semantic consistency checks against MITRE ATT&CK/MBC, and drift detection.
motivation: Forensic investigators need to know which suspicious files to examine first, but existing ML/DL malware detectors give only opaque scores and no warning when data drift degrades reliability.
method: Uses only pre-extracted static PE features (no execution), producing a calibrated maliciousness score for triage priority, per-sample feature attribution, a semantic consistency score matching top features to documented MBC/ATT&CK behaviors, and conformal/statistical tests to flag distribution drift, evaluated on time-ordered EMBER2024 and BODMAS against simple baselines.
result: The paper specifies a pre-registered evaluation protocol comparing predictive performance, prioritization effectiveness, explanation quality and temporal robustness against baselines across the two datasets.
conclusion: The framework aims to deliver a single investigator-oriented, explainable and drift-aware triage output, but it lies entirely outside quantum information science.

title: Archimedes' Angle Measure And The Fundamental Theorem Of Trigonometry
authors: Omar Hijab Eric L. Grinberg
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23318v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We aim to understand a distant conversation about a trigonometric principle. Although foundational to calculus, this principle and the basic concept of angle measure are often treated tacitly in both elementary and advanced accounts. The primordial idea of counting rotations makes one aware of the integers. In the same vein, Archimedes' measure of partial rotations hints at the completeness of the real numbers. By a less well-known implication, these ideas also lead to the complex numbers and to the Fundamental Theorem of Trigonometry. What does it all mean? And is it true?
tldr: A historical and foundational exposition of angle measure and the 'Fundamental Theorem of Trigonometry', connecting Archimedes' measure of partial rotations to completeness of the reals and to the complex numbers.
motivation: The authors argue that the foundational trigonometric principle underlying calculus, together with the notion of angle measure, is usually treated only tacitly in both elementary and advanced texts, and they wish to make it explicit and interrogate its meaning and validity.
method: Conceptual and historical mathematical analysis, tracing the idea of counting rotations and Archimedes' treatment of partial rotations to derive implications for the real numbers, the complex numbers, and the trigonometric theorem.
result: The paper shows how Archimedes' angle measure hints at completeness of the reals and, via a less well-known implication, leads to the complex numbers and the Fundamental Theorem of Trigonometry.
conclusion: The work is an expository/foundational mathematics essay on trigonometry and the real continuum, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Minimax Estimation For Simultaneous Deconvolution Model In Random Design Using Wavelets
authors: Rida Benhaddou
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23439v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simultaneous deconvolution model is investigated when the design points are random and follow bounded densities and errors are either [MATH] or long-memory dependent. We propose wavelet hard-thresholding estimators, and show that they achieve asymptotically near-optimal convergence rates for the [MATH]-risk when the response function belongs to Besov space under both [MATH] errors and homoskedastic, long-memory errors. However, under heteroskedastic, long-memory errors the estimator is not optimal. For the [MATH] errors, the convergence rates are {identical} to those found in simultaneous deconvolution under regular design {and [MATH] errors}. However, for long-memory dependent errors, the convergence rates are new {and completely different from those in simultaneous deconvolution under regular design and long-memory errors}.
tldr: This paper develops wavelet hard-thresholding estimators for a simultaneous deconvolution model with random design and long-memory dependent errors.
motivation: The work addresses statistical estimation under random design and dependent errors, extending deconvolution theory to long-memory settings where standard convergence results may not apply.
method: The author proposes wavelet hard-thresholding estimators and analyzes their asymptotic convergence rates over Besov spaces for L2-risk under bounded random designs and either independent or long-memory errors.
result: Near-optimal rates are obtained for independent errors and homoskedastic long-memory errors, with rates matching regular-design deconvolution for independent errors and differing for long-memory errors; heteroskedastic long-memory errors yield non-optimal performance.
conclusion: The paper provides new minimax convergence results for simultaneous deconvolution with random design and long-memory dependence, but it is purely a mathematical statistics contribution unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Modeling Fluid--solid Interaction In Three-dimensional Granular Systems: Two-way Coupling Of Sph And Ls-dem
authors: Sebasti\'an Pazmi\~no, Nitin P. Daphalapurkar, Jacinto Ulloa
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23592v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a two-way coupled fluid--solid interaction framework for granular systems based on the level-set discrete element method (LS-DEM) and smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH). The proposed method is mesh-free, fully Lagrangian, and equipped with a seamless description of arbitrary solid shapes. In particular, a level-set representation of grain geometry is used for both contact detection and fluid--solid coupling, allowing for realistic, highly irregular grains to be handled within a unified computational framework. Moreover, the method incorporates a convenient treatment of moving boundaries and admits a simple computational implementation. The capabilities of the proposed SPH--LS-DEM framework are demonstrated through several numerical benchmarks involving dam-break flow, flow through porous media, granular collapse, and cyclic loading of a saturated granular specimen. The study sets the stage for several extensions to multiphysics problems across disciplines.
tldr: This paper develops a two-way coupled SPH–LS-DEM framework for simulating fluid–solid interaction in three-dimensional granular systems with irregular grain shapes.
motivation: The authors aim to handle realistic granular geometries and moving boundaries in fluid–solid interaction simulations within a unified mesh-free Lagrangian computational framework.
method: They couple smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) for the fluid with the level-set discrete element method (LS-DEM) for solids, using a level-set representation for both contact detection and fluid–solid coupling.
result: The framework is demonstrated on numerical benchmarks including dam-break flow, porous-media flow, granular collapse, and cyclic loading of a saturated granular specimen.
conclusion: The proposed SPH–LS-DEM method provides a flexible approach for multiphysics granular simulations and is positioned for extensions to broader multiphysics problems.

title: Averting `Gravity': Launch Control And The Limits Of Collision Avoidance In Low Earth Orbit Operations
authors: Harsha Honnappa Aditya S. Gopalan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23607v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large constellations fill low Earth orbit, the risk of a runaway collision cascade has become a central concern of space operations. Debris population models treat collision avoidance as a fixed input, although the capacity to screen potential collisions and plan maneuvers degrades as debris accumulates. Using a stylized multi-layer queueing network model, we show that collision avoidance capabilities that saturate as the in-custody fragment count increases, can make the orbital shell bistable, with a low-debris and a high-debris equilibrium, and hysteretic. This has two major operational consequences. First, leaving the high-debris equilibrium requires a large cut in launch rates. Second, in the low-debris equilibrium, fragment counts respond with a delay as the launch rate rises past a tipping point. Removing bistability is desirable, and we show that fragment count-indexed admission control can achieve this. The least restrictive such policy lengthens the lag, whereas an exponential tilt of this policy makes the fragment count track its equilibrium with a bounded lag. Furthermore, admitting more launches can reduce the rate of completed missions, and under a unimodality condition a threshold rule on the debris fragment count maximizes this rate at equilibrium.
tldr: The paper models collision-avoidance saturation in low Earth orbit as a queueing network and shows that debris accumulation can create bistable, hysteretic orbital shell dynamics.
motivation: Large satellite constellations increase orbital debris and runaway collision risk, but debris models often treat collision-avoidance capacity as fixed rather than degrading with fragment count.
method: A stylized multi-layer queueing network model is used to represent collision screening and maneuver planning capacity as a function of in-custody fragment count.
result: Saturation of collision avoidance can make an orbital shell bistable with low- and high-debris equilibria; fragment-count-indexed admission control can remove bistability, and an exponential tilt can bound tracking lag.
conclusion: Launch-rate management and debris-indexed admission policies are important for avoiding high-debris orbital equilibria, and admitting more launches can sometimes reduce completed mission rates.

title: Schatten And Weak Schatten Classes Of Composition Operator Differences On Bergman Spaces
authors: Rong Yang Qian Ai
abstract:
ArXiv:2611.23733v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate Schatten and weak Schatten class membership of differences of composition operators on the standard weighted Bergman spaces over the unit disk. We prove that the known sufficient condition for Schatten p-class membership is also necessary for 0

<2, thereby completing the characterization for all p>0. We also characterize when differences of composition operators belong to weak Schatten classes for every p>0. Both results are expressed in terms of local-mass conditions involving the pseudohyperbolic distance between the inducing maps, and yield two-sided (quasi-)norm estimates.
tldr: This paper characterizes Schatten and weak Schatten class membership for differences of composition operators on weighted Bergman spaces over the unit disk.
motivation: The authors aim to complete the characterization of Schatten p-class membership for differences of composition operators by proving necessity of a known sufficient condition for 0<p<2.
method: They use local-mass conditions involving the pseudohyperbolic distance between inducing maps and derive two-sided quasi-norm estimates.
result: They show the sufficient condition is also necessary for 0<p<2, completing the characterization for all p>0, and characterize weak Schatten class membership for every p>0.
conclusion: The work provides a full operator-theoretic classification of composition operator differences in Schatten and weak Schatten classes on Bergman spaces.

title: Protecting Web Applications Using A Multimodal AI-based System For Classifying Web Injection Attacks
authors: Rodrigo Branco, Vinicius Cogo, Ib\'eria Medeiros
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23660v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Web applications have been essential to accessing and managing online services. Made available with weaknesses, much due to their rapid development and human error, they are exposed to frequent web injection attacks, leaving security analysts overwhelmed with threats and alerts that often lack critical details for proper risk assessment. Detecting these attacks requires inspecting the payload of network traffic packets, which becomes inaccessible when traffic is encrypted via HTTPS, as encryption hides the content of the traffic. This paper introduces a Multimodal Artificial Intelligence (AI) system to protect online services that rely on web application security by detecting and classifying web injection attacks, and provides security analysts with information to support attack prevention and incident response. The system employs unsupervised Machine Learning (ML) to flag potentially anomalous Network Flows (NetFlows). The corresponding data recorded in Web Server Logs (WebLogs) is then analysed using a heuristic framework based on Natural Language Processing (NLP) and supervised ML to detect and classify web injection attacks. Finally, the resulting classifications are scrutinised using a Similarity Search Engine (SSE) based on Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH) to validate them. The solution handles encrypted traffic by analysing NetFlows and WebLogs, the latter in their natural, unencrypted form, by leveraging NetFlow-level metadata for anomaly detection and analysing web server logs after TLS termination, thereby avoiding any additional in-network traffic decryption. It was evaluated in the classification of eight web injection attack classes. The results demonstrated its ability to accurately identify attacks and their classes, achieving an F_1 score of 91% and an accuracy of 95%, and offering valuable insights for alert prioritisation.
tldr: A multimodal AI pipeline combining unsupervised NetFlow anomaly detection, NLP-based WebLog analysis, and LSH similarity search to detect and classify eight classes of web injection attacks in encrypted-traffic environments.
motivation: Web injection attacks are frequent and hard to triage because HTTPS encryption hides payloads and analysts face overwhelming, low-detail alerts.
method: Unsupervised ML flags anomalous network flows; corresponding web server logs (available post-TLS termination) are parsed with an NLP/supervised-ML heuristic framework; classifications are then validated by a locality-sensitive-hashing similarity search engine.
result: The system classified eight web injection attack classes with 95% accuracy and 91% F1 score while avoiding in-network decryption.
conclusion: Multimodal fusion of flow metadata and server logs offers a practical, encryption-compatible detection and alert-prioritisation tool for web application security.

title: JITAtlas: Checking Lifetime And Protection Obligations In Compiler Rewrites
authors: Wen Li Baihong Chen (utah State University)
abstract: ArXiv:2611.23715v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Compiler rewrites can preserve returned values while violating object lifetime or ownership. Such failures arise when a rewrite changes when an object remains live, whether a borrowed pointer stays supported, or what ownership reaches the caller. We present JITAtlas, a source-level checker that reconstructs reference and target computations from optimizer code and checks valid uses, continuous borrow support, and caller-visible ownership. On a 58-input benchmark constructed and labeled independently of JITAtlas output, JITAtlas detects all 29 defects and reports none of 29 safe inputs; PyRefcon detects 20 defects and CpyChecker 18. Across three CPython snapshots, JITAtlas extracts 3,332 rewrite alternatives, retains 801 under recovered receiving contexts, and reports 194 violations. Manual review confirms 92 reports, giving 47.42% precision. End-to-end analysis takes 35.56-42.31 s per snapshot. JITAtlas further identifies 15 new bugs across five failure classes, each with a reproducible proof of concept.
tldr: JITAtlas is a source-level checker for detecting compiler rewrite defects that violate object lifetime, borrow support, or ownership obligations.
motivation: Compiler rewrites can preserve returned values while introducing subtle lifetime or ownership bugs, so automated checking is needed to catch such defects.
method: The tool reconstructs reference and target computations from optimizer code and checks valid uses, continuous borrow support, and caller-visible ownership, evaluated on an independently labeled benchmark and CPython snapshots.
result: JITAtlas detects all 29 defects in the benchmark, reports no false positives on 29 safe inputs, and identifies 194 violation reports across CPython snapshots with 47.42% precision after manual review, including 15 new bugs.
conclusion: JITAtlas provides practical detection of lifetime and protection obligation violations in compiler rewrites, though with moderate precision requiring manual review.
